20189-recollections-of-manilla-and-the-p:
Recollections of Manila and the Philippines covers the years 1848, 1849, and 1850. The writer looks back to Spain's first push toward those islands. As Cortez, Pizarro, and Almagro won fame in America, a new idea grew. Magellan, a Portuguese in Spanish service, sought a sea road east.

By sailing south and past the new western world, spices lay within reach. That old story frames a firsthand account of mid-century Manila life. Trade, custom, and Spanish rule fill the writer's daily notes. Readers get a rare English view of the Philippines before American rule.
23180-the-denver-express-from-belgravia-: A. A. Hayes wrote The Denver Express, a story that ran in Belgravia in January 1884. In the town it describes, the train's coming and going ranks among the great events of each day. A local poet even marked it in verse in the town paper. His lines, though, were borrowed without credit from an old eastern magazine. He passed them off as his own work.
abbott-flatland-1884:
Edwin A Abbott, an English schoolmaster and theologian, published Flatland in 1884 under the name 'A Square.' The short novel is set in a world of only two dimensions. It is the founding work of fiction about higher dimensions and a sharp satire of Victorian society.

The Square tells how Flatland's classes are ranked by shape, from lowly lines to priestly circles. A visit from a Sphere of three dimensions blows his mind open to worlds beyond his own. Abbott uses the tale to teach geometry and to mock rank, dogma, and fear of new ideas.
arxiv-2512-00084:
Segmenting medical images means marking exactly which pixels belong to a structure or a tumor. Venkata Siddharth Dhara and Pawan Kumar present a modern BERT-based diffusion model for that task in 2025, guided by text. Diffusion models have done well at generating and cleaning medical images.

Pixel-level labels for training are costly, slow to make, and demand expert knowledge, which limits real clinical use. The authors aim for a faster, more efficient model that uses text conditions to guide segmentation. Their work speaks to hospitals and researchers who need accurate image marking without huge annotation budgets. Speed is part of the point, since clinical tools must keep up with busy imaging workloads.
arxiv-2512-00184:
Convex functions sit at the heart of optimization, the mathematics of choosing the best option. Sergey Bobkov and Friedrich Götze discuss how to build measurable subgradients for convex functions of several variables in a 2025 study. Subgradients generalize slopes for functions that are not smooth.

The authors also study a key growth condition through directional derivatives, and basic properties of Luxemburg and Orlicz pseudo-norms for vector-valued functions. These norms measure the size of functions in flexible ways used across analysis. The work is foundational theory for readers in probability and functional analysis. Vector-valued functions arise whenever several measurements are tracked together, as in imaging. The study collects basic properties that later work can cite rather than reprove.
arxiv-2512-00284:
Molecular clouds collapse into dense cores that become stars, but what sets the spacing between cores is debated. Manuel Zamora-Aviles and co-authors test one popular idea in 2025: that core separation is set by the sonic scale. That scale is where turbulent velocity dispersion equals the sound speed.

The suggestion was recent, and the authors examine whether turbulent clouds actually obey it. Their title gives the verdict plainly: the sonic scale does not determine core separation. Settling this question guides how astronomers model star formation and how they read telescope maps of nearby clouds. The question matters because core spacing feeds estimates of how many stars a cloud makes.
arxiv-2512-00584:
Projective curves with especially simple algebraic descriptions are rare and useful test cases. Hang Huang, Yevgeniya Tarasova, Matteo Varbaro, and Emily Witt study smooth Herzog projective curves in 2025. A Herzog ideal is one whose initial ideal, under some monomial order, is squarefree.

The authors prove that smooth projective curves admitting a squarefree Gröbner degeneration have genus zero. Genus zero curves are the simplest kind, parametrized by rational functions. The result links computational algebra, through Gröbner bases, to the geometry of curves, showing that a computability condition forces a strong geometric restriction. Genus zero is a strong restriction, ruling out most curves a priori. Gröbner degenerations replace a hard ideal with a monomial shadow that is easier to read.
arxiv-2512-00684:
Xu Duan and Dongmei Chen wrote a 2025 machine learning paper on latent spaces. Generative models often lift images into high-dimensional feature spaces, where traits like shape or style become easier to separate. Newer designs, such as representation autoencoders, lean on spaces that line up with meaning.

Duan and Chen argue that these spaces hold patterns that older methods miss. In particular, the directions between features carry useful structure. Their cosine-similarity methods use the angles between feature vectors for training and for sampling new outputs. Using direction well could make training cheaper and samples better in very high dimensions.
arxiv-2512-00784:
Sanjith A and Shantanu Desai test a statistical method on fake pulsar data in a 2025 astronomy paper. Pulsars are spinning neutron stars whose radio beams sweep past Earth. A basic law says a pulsar's flux should fall with the inverse square of its distance, like light spreading out.

The Efron-Petrosian method is meant to uncover such links in survey data with limits and cutoffs. The authors built a synthetic catalog modeled on the Parkes multi-beam survey, using standard simulation software. They find the method cannot recover the inverse-square law, except over a narrow range of flux cutoffs. That warning matters for real pulsar studies.
arxiv-2512-00884:
Samuel Kessler, Menglin Xia, and Daniel Madrigal Diaz study how to grow training data while a model learns, in a 2025 paper. A common trick for improving language models is fine-tuning a small student model on text written by a stronger teacher model. Those teacher outputs are called synthetic data.

Most teams generate all synthetic data before training starts. Some work instead creates fresh samples as training progresses, reacting to what the student still gets wrong. The authors work toward active synthetic data generation, choosing new samples on purpose rather than at random. Smarter data choices could cut wasted training.
arxiv-2512-00984:
Fernando Rosas wrote a 2025 paper on why the world seems organized in layers. Many systems show nested emergent levels, each with its own rules: atoms, cells, organisms, societies. Our knowledge is naturally organized around those levels, and Rosas asks what creates that pattern.

He proposes that hierarchical emergence of this kind arises from underlying symmetries. When a system has the right symmetries, higher layers with their own regularities can appear. The paper develops that proposal as a general account of emergence. If correct, it would give scientists a shared principle for when new levels of description should exist.
arxiv-2512-01684:
Jie Song and co-authors trace how galaxies switch their star birth pattern at early times. They combine sharp JWST and Hubble views of CANDELS fields. For each galaxy they gauge mass, star birth rate, and shape across wavelengths. Radial profiles show where stars are being born.

The profiles hint at a switch from outside-in to inside-out growth near a set epoch. That switch marks a turn in how disks build up. Knowing when it fires tests models of gas inflow and feedback in young galaxies. CANDELS fields have deep multi-band data, which lets mass and star birth be read for the same galaxies across cosmic time slices.
arxiv-2512-01784:
Sebastian Golat, Nathaniel Levy, and Francisco Rodriguez-Fortuno trace the origin of dipolar recoil force and torque. A radiating dipole feels a push back from its own emission. That recoil is often found from momentum balance via the Maxwell stress tensor. The balance gives the outcome, not the cause.

The team digs into which forces produce the recoil. They separate the physical sources of force and torque on the dipole. A causal picture aids design of optical tweezers and nano motors, where recoil sets the limits of control. Torque matters for spinning probes, so the causal split covers both push and twist that a radiating particle feels at once.
arxiv-2512-01984:
Chaotic systems, from weather to turbulent fluids, defeat long-range prediction because tiny errors grow explosively. Andrea Goertzen, Sunbochen Tang, and Navid Azizan present ECO in 2025, a data-driven method that learns how such systems evolve while respecting their energy limits.

Many chaotic systems are dissipative, shedding energy, and ergodic, visiting their states in stable proportions over time. A good model should therefore aim at the long-run statistics, not exact trajectories, and must stay bounded rather than blowing up. ECO builds energy constraints into operator learning to secure those guarantees. The result targets trustworthy long-horizon models of chaotic behavior.
arxiv-2512-02284:
Quantum computers are widely believed to beat classical ones at some tasks, yet proving a clean separation on today's hardware has been elusive. A 2025 paper from the Google Quantum AI team reports such a separation for bounded-resource tasks, powered by measurement contextuality, a distinctly quantum effect.

Using a superconducting qubit processor, the team shows contextuality lets certain tasks be completed with success rates beyond classical limits. The tasks are framed for limited resources, which is what makes a demonstration on current processors possible. A verified separation gives the field a concrete, hardware-level witness that quantum effects do real computational work.
arxiv-2512-02384:
Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling often performs near-optimally in Bayesian inference, for reasons theory has struggled to explain. Amit Rajaraman and David Wu study in 2025 the classical spiked Wigner problem, recovering a planted signal from a noisy matrix, and connect sampling to approximate message passing.

Their framework, Markov Chains Approximate Message Passing, aims to make the samplers' empirical success rigorous. The spiked Wigner problem is the standard test bed because its thresholds are known precisely. A theory that certifies samplers could guide algorithm choice across statistics and machine learning, where MCMC is used on faith daily.
arxiv-2512-02484:
Kazem Bitaghsir Fadafan, Jesús Cruz Rojas, and Jonas Mager use holography to model some of the densest matter known. Their 2025 study builds a quark phase that is hot and dense, yet still made of massive quarks. The setup adjusts a field profile by hand in the deep infrared region to match real behavior.

From that model, the team works out how stiff the matter is under pressure. They find it stiff enough to hold up exotic dense stars as heavy as about two Suns. Such stars, if found, would test both gravity and the physics of quarks. A stiff core is a strong hint that such stars are more than a trick of math.
arxiv-2512-02684:
Navinder Singh and four co-authors extend a classic theory of hot electrons in tilted Dirac cone materials. In these materials, electron energy cones lean to one side rather than standing straight. The Kaganov-Lifshitz-Tanatarov theory describes how hot electrons cool by heating the crystal lattice.

The team points out that this cooling is uneven across the Brillouin zone, the map of electron states. Lattice heating favors certain directions, opposite the tilt among them. Uneven heating could be probed in experiments and may matter for devices that use these tilted materials under strong light or current. Heat that pools in one zone can warp a chip, so maps of that pool are worth the math it takes.
arxiv-2512-02784:
Gabriele Cassese works on Korn inequalities, which bound how much a material can distort overall from how it stretches. In elasticity, the full gradient of a displacement is controlled by its symmetric part alone. That symmetric part has fewer components, so the bound is far from obvious.

Cassese connects the problem to martingales from probability and to laminates from materials science. The aim is minimal constants: the smallest factors for which the inequality still holds. Sharp constants matter when engineers and mathematicians need guarantees, not estimates, for how elastic bodies deform under load. Best marks in such bounds are the ones plant and bone work cite when they need a wall they can lean on.
arxiv-2512-02984:
Duality means two unlike theories can describe the same physics. This 2025 study looks at new dualities in one-dimensional supersymmetric gauge theories. These are theories with a balance between matter and force parts, plus a unitary gauge group.

The authors study matter in two forms, chiral and fermi, with a nonzero extra term in the setup. They find that the ground states of paired theories match exactly. That match is a strong test that the duality holds. Work like this helps map how quantum theories link to each other across dimensions. The match between paired theories also gives a strong sign the duality is no accident.
arxiv-2512-03084:
A family of special functions gets new sum formulas here. Ronald Orozco López presents the work in this 2025 study. He builds a new operator based on a q-derivative, a tool from q-calculus, which handles sums in a shifted way.

With that operator he derives sums for several bilateral basic hypergeometric series. These series are broad tools in math physics and combinatorics. New sum formulas can shorten hard calculations in those fields. They also give other researchers exact results to build on in future work on special functions. Bilateral series appear in many sum problems, so new formulas widen the shared toolkit.
arxiv-2512-03184:
The young Sun blasted its disk with high-energy particles. Steven Desch, Ashley Herbst, Richard Hervig, and Benjamin Jacobsen ask how far that blast reached in this 2025 work. Young stars like the early Sun emit X-rays and fast ions, called solar energetic particles.

Observations of young stars suggest fluxes hundreds to thousands of times today's levels. Such particles can change the chemistry of the disk where planets form. They may leave traces in meteorites that labs can measure. The study helps link those traces to conditions in the early solar system. Meteorite traces give the disk story a check that telescope data alone cannot provide.
arxiv-2512-03484:
A charged particle near a black hole feels gravity and magnetism at once. Ken-ichi Nakao and co-authors study that motion in this 2025 work. Their black hole is static and spherically symmetric, immersed in a monopole magnetic field.

The authors show the radial motion follows exactly the same equation as with no magnetic field. That surprise simplifies the analysis of orbits in this setup. It gives a clean baseline for more complex fields. Such work helps model matter falling into black holes in magnetized space. Monopole fields are idealized, yet they clarify how charge and curvature interact.
arxiv-2512-03584:
Ships report their positions by AIS, but coverage has gaps at sea. Thomas Gräupl and co-authors present VesselEdge in this 2025 work. The system extends AIS coverage through shared learning and smart data compression on tight links.

Ships become mobile sensors that spot odd events in real time. A shared model trains across ships without pooling raw data in one place. A compression method sends odd data first. Better sea awareness aids safety, fishing checks, and care for the marine environment in far waters. The design keeps raw ship data on board each ship, not on shore.
arxiv-2512-03884:
A walker on a circle who jumps by random whole multiples of a fixed irrational step will, over time, visit every arc fairly. Bence Borda asks how fast that fairness arrives in a 2025 probability preprint. The answer lives in pure number theory: the step is a quadratic irrational, satisfying a quadratic equation with integer coefficients.

Borda measures convergence to uniformity with the quadratic Wasserstein metric, also read as a periodic discrepancy. He proves the rate is governed by deep arithmetic features of the number field the step generates. Fundamental units of its ring of algebraic integers and special values of zeta functions both enter the story. The result bridges random walks and analytic number theory. A question about shuffling points on a circle is answered by invariants invented for algebraic numbers. Such links often prove useful in both directions.
arxiv-2512-03984:
Tests for entanglement usually assume the measuring device can point its settings anywhere, but some detectors are stuck with rotational symmetry. Marlene Funck, Ilija Funk, Tizian Schmidt, and René Schwonnek study that restricted case in a 2025 quantum physics preprint. Their test particles are polarised photons, and their devices are rotationally covariant, treating every direction alike.

The authors derive the allowed measurements explicitly: each is fixed by a single measurable parameter. One derivation recasts the classic Klein-Nishina formula for Compton scattering in this language. They add a semidefinite-programming method certifying it from full statistics, including partly untrusted devices. Two such settings can never violate a Bell inequality, they show. Yet EPR steering remains certifiable when it is imposed on one side only. As a showcase, they analyse such tests using polarised light scattered in soft drinks, lemonade included.
arxiv-2601-06684:
Lorenz Zwick tests vacuum-template subtraction for LISA black hole sources in 2026. LISA will observe massive black hole binaries from space over years. A global fit must subtract each source to find the others.

He investigates gravitational wave dephasing due to gas accretion on the binaries. The subtraction is studied over four years of LISA data. Realistic environments, not clean vacuum, are the paper's key focus. Gas can shift a binary's phase enough to leave residuals behind. Those residuals could corrupt the global fit for other sources. His limits show where vacuum templates stop being good enough. Gravitational wave astronomers get a warning calibrated to real astrophysics. Environment effects must enter LISA analysis plans from the start.
arxiv-2601-06884: Masahiro Kaneko and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with paraphrasing adversarial attack on LLM-as-a-Reviewer. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. The use of large language models (LLMs) in peer review systems has attracted growing attention, making it essential to examine their potential vulnerabilities. Prior attacks rely on prompt injection, which alters manuscript content and conflates injection susceptibility with evaluation robustness. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07084:
Melissa Tessa and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with how secure is secure code generation? adversarial prompts put LLM defenses. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. Recent secure code generation methods, using vulnerability-aware fine-tuning, prefix-tuning, and prompt optimization, claim to prevent LLMs from producing insecure code.

However, their robustness under adversarial conditions remains untested, and current evaluations decouple security from functionality, potentially inflating reported gains. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07184: Research by Rafael Bertolotto-Stefanelli and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with stellar initial mass function of nearby young moving groups. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. A possible explanation is that they are remnants of individual stellar clusters and associations, currently dispersing in the galactic disc. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-07684:
Geoffrey J. Taghon introduces AptaFind, a local tool that gathers aptamer knowledge from the research literature. Aptamers are short molecules selected to bind specific targets, used in sensing and medicine. Knowledge about them lies scattered across papers, supplements, and databases. Each literature search can eat hours that scholars would rather spend at the bench. Taghon's 2026 preprint describes the system.

AptaFind uses a three-tier design for automated curation. The author frames research mining as a spectrum, not a simple success or failure. Partial, ranked, and sourced results can still save large amounts of time. A lightweight local interface keeps the tool close to the researcher's own workflow. The paper should interest aptamer scholars and builders of literature mining tools. It treats curation as an ongoing aid, not a one-time scrape.
arxiv-2601-07784:
The Euclid team tests whether simple analytic formulas can capture galaxy intrinsic alignments well enough for their work on the cosmos. Their 2026 preprint models alignments in Euclid's Flagship run and studies the effect on the weak lensing signal. The setup uses facts on galaxy light and color, plus their dark matter host halos. Run settings are tuned against real sightings and large hydro based runs of the cosmos.

Analytic models are fast, which large surveys need, but may miss real depth. Testing them inside a rich simulation shows where they fail. Weak lensing is a flagship Euclid measurement for dark matter and dark energy. Off mark fixes for alignments would skew the end results themselves. The paper serves the Euclid analysis teams and wider weak lensing community. It checks a practical shortcut against a virtual universe. The test uses the same fake sky for both tools.
arxiv-2601-07884:
Xiaodan Wang and colleagues survey how scholars define and fight ideological isolation online. Social networks have reshaped how people access information. They may also trap users among homogeneous content and like-minded contacts. The survey covers computational definitions, metrics, and mitigation strategies for this isolation. It appears in Information Sciences and as a 2026 preprint.

Definitions differ: isolation can mean exposure, interaction, or belief patterns. Metrics follow from whichever definition a study chooses. Mitigation strategies try to widen what users see without destroying engagement. A survey that lines these up exposes where the field agrees and where terms shift meaning. The paper serves computational social scientists and platform designers. It gives the echo chamber debate a more precise shared vocabulary.
arxiv-2601-07984:
Haorui Yu and coauthors test whether vision and language models can judge art like experts who know each culture. These models are strong at sight tasks, but their grasp of cultural meaning in art is not well checked. Cultural grasp and clear reasoning are left out when models are judged. Their 2026 preprint sets out a three tier test scheme for art critique across cultures. Tier one gives auto metrics that show breadth of cultural coverage.

Art carries symbols whose meanings differ across traditions. A model can name objects in a painting yet miss its point entirely. A tiered test splits surface notes from deep readings of a work. That split shows where a model's grasp stops. The framework gives developers targets beyond object recognition scores. The paper serves scholars in multimodal AI and digital humanities. It holds cultural reading is a skill that can be scored, not a bonus.
arxiv-2601-08184: Yixuan Zhang and Qiaomin Xie derive central limit theorem rates in Wasserstein distance for dependent data. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that finite-time rates matter across modern machine learning. The study covers multivariate dependent data in Wasserstein-p distance for general p at least one. Settings range from local dependence to Markov chains. Exact rates tell practitioners how many samples suffice before normal approximations can be trusted. That guidance matters when data arrive as time series rather than independent draws.
arxiv-2601-08384:
Priya Deshwal and Hitendra Malik simulate a Rayleigh-Taylor-like instability in binary complex plasma. Their 2026 arXiv paper uses two-dimensional molecular dynamics simulations. Heavier dust particles sit above lighter ones in a planar setup, with the same charge-to-mass ratio for both.

An external electric field and an equilibrium charge density gradient act on the interface. Langevin dynamics tracks how perturbations at the boundary between the two species evolve. The setup mirrors the classic fluid instability, where a heavy layer over a light one overturns. Complex plasmas let researchers watch that overturning particle by particle, which can test theory in fine detail.
arxiv-2601-08684: Paolo Italiani and co-authors present MemeWeaver for detecting sexism and misogyny in memes. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that women face online harassment at twice the rate of men due to gender. Multimodal moderation has advanced, yet most approaches overlook the social dynamics behind abuse. Perpetrators reinforce prejudices and group identity inside like-minded communities. MemeWeaver reasons over an inter-meme graph to capture those links. Graph context could catch coded memes that single-image classifiers read as harmless.
arxiv-2601-09084:
Wilson Lee asks how many human picks it takes to grade two chat models fair. Such grades ask folk which reply they like more. Labs use them to claim a new model is a bit more good. But a bit is hard to see. If the gain is spread thin over all ask types, no smart pick of asks can find it fast.

Lee proves that in the thin spread case, a plain share of picks is as good as it gets. No scheme can beat it by much. That sets a floor on grade cost for small gains. A reader who grades models gets a bound to plan by. Small claims need vast pick counts, by law, not by poor design.
arxiv-2601-09184:
Yifei Xie and four co-authors speed the leader swap step in a fast form of group vote for block chains. In such a vote, nodes agree on a log with out a boss. When a lead node fails, the group must swap leads. That swap is called a view change. In a parallel form, where many chains run at once, swaps can clog the whole net.

The team finds where the clog forms and gives a lean swap plan. It cuts wait in the swap while it keeps the vote safe. A reader who runs chain nets gets a way to keep pace when leads fail, a case that hits most oft when load is high.
arxiv-2601-09484:
Marouan Mizmizi, Stefano Tebaldini, and Umberto Spagnolini merge radar sensing and data transfer on one surface. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents an echo-side modulation framework for systems that sense and communicate at once. A space-time reconfigurable surface stamps a smooth phase pattern onto the radar echo itself.

That stamped phase carries uplink data, riding on a radar-like waveform. The received signal is thus a product of the sensing wave and the data phase. Using the echo this way avoids a separate radio link for the sensor's reports. The scheme suits smart surfaces that must watch a scene and talk about it too.
arxiv-2601-09584:
S. Marbach, A. Carter, and M. Holmes-Cerfon study how stiff links shape the wander of tiny particles. Their 2026 arXiv paper treats Brownian motion with soft constraints in soft matter. Stiff forces appear everywhere: colloids with short-range attraction, receptor contacts, optical traps, and stretch-resistant fibers.

Treating stiff forces as hard constraints lets the system move only within allowed shapes. The authors assess the long-term effect of that limit on dynamics and structure. The payoff is a cleaner theory for many lab systems at once. It clarifies when the shortcut of strict constraints is safe to use.
arxiv-2601-09684:
Ziyu Yang and four co-authors reduce friction when one adapter learns many tasks. Their 2026 arXiv paper treats multi-task LoRA, where a single low-rank adapter serves several tasks in a large language model. Sharing one adapter cuts storage sharply.

The downside is negative transfer: gradient updates from different tasks clash and drag each other down. The authors project gradients onto orthogonal directions to separate the conflicts. Keeping tasks from fighting should recover single-task quality at shared cost. The method suits online services that must host many skills in very little memory.
arxiv-2601-10384:
Yibo Zhang and co authors test audio models in true sound scenes. Large audio models have grown strong at speech and sound tasks. But lab tests use clean or fake noise. Real scenes layer many sounds at once. A room, a street, and a crowd each have their own mix.

The team call that mix the Acoustic Ecology of a scene. They built RSA-Bench from real scenes. It grades models on layered, true noise, not one fake source. A model that scores well in the lab may fail here. The set shows which models hold up in the wild.
arxiv-2601-10984:
Kamal Maayergi, Devin G. E. Walker, Ora Cullen, and Michael E. Peskin test how well Higgs factories could spot composite Higgs models. A Higgs factory is a future collider tuned to make Higgs bosons in bulk. In composite models, the Higgs is not elementary. It is a bound state, a Nambu-Goldstone boson of a new strong force.

The authors study a representative model of this kind, in the Little Higgs family. Its main shifts from the Standard Model come from vectorlike top quark partners. Precision Higgs measurements could reveal those shifts before any new particle is seen directly. The paper helps planners judge what a Higgs factory must measure, and how well, to settle the question.
arxiv-2601-11284:
Markus Bink, Marten Risius, Udo Kruschwitz, and David Elsweiler design AI copilots. Their 2026 preprint asks how copilots can back human judgment. People now seek facts online with generative AI at hand. Such tools speak in fluent, firm tones on most topics.

That firm tone brings a real risk to users. People may lean on the tool and skip their own checks. The team argues for a shift in how such tools are built. A good copilot should scaffold thought, not replace it. It should keep the user in the work of judging sources. The study sets out design moves toward that goal.
arxiv-2601-11884:
Kashif Imteyaz, Qiushi Liang, Yakov Bart, Maitraye Das, and Saiph Savage study job search for blind and low-vision people in an age of AI hiring. This group faces high jobless rates. More firms now screen CVs with AI before a human sees them.

Such screens could add fresh blocks for these job seekers. The study asks how AI-led hiring shapes their search and odds. It points to where tools and rules could be made fair. The work is set in the CSCW field, on tech and social life.  Fair tools would widen real choice for these job seekers.
arxiv-2601-11984:
Michal Dvořák, Antonín Novák, Přemysl Šůcha, Dušan Knop, and Claire Hanen study the cost of scheduling in robotic process automation. RPA tools run office tasks by script. Their schedules must respect task order, release times, and due dates.

They ask how hard the single-machine case is as key terms grow. This is a parameterized complexity study, which sorts tasks by which inputs drive the cost. Such maps help firms pick tools that scale. They also show which RPA schedules are bound to stay hard.  The maps also show which inputs drive the hard cases.
arxiv-2601-12084:
Shiye Cao, Jiwon Moon, Yifan Xu, Anqi Liu, and Chien-Ming Huang reframe how we design chat for robots. Large models let robots chat in free form, past fixed scripts. But plain model output can be wrong or off-tone for a set place or task.

Tuning by prompt craft is slow and not clear to most builders. The team argue for deliberate design with AI scaffolds in place of ad hoc prompts. Scaffolds could give structure that non-experts can use. The work is set for the HRI 2026 meeting in Edinburgh.  Scaffolds may also make robot chat more safe to test.
arxiv-2601-12584:
Electron backscatter diffraction is a main tool for mapping the crystal grain structure of a material. It reads patterns, called Kikuchi patterns, off a sample under a beam. In the past few years, data driven tools have been used more and more on the raw patterns. Most of those tools still need a user in the loop, though.

The traits those tools pull out can also be hard to read. A user must often guess what a trait means in terms of real grains. The work takes a multi modal data driven route to the task. Joining more than one kind of data may cut the need for user input. It may also yield traits that map more cleanly onto real structure.
arxiv-2601-12784:
Haoyang Li and eight co authors speed up reinforcement learning post training for large models. RL post training is now pivotal for raising model capabilities. A recent trend splits the RL pipeline into three phases: rollout, reward, and training. Those phases run on separate resources and execute asynchronously, a fully disaggregated design.

Asynchrony brings a problem called staleness, where training uses data from older model versions. The team propose staleness constrained rollout coordination to manage that lag. Keeping staleness bounded should keep learning stable while hardware stays busy. Efficient post training lowers the cost of improving large models. The work serves labs that train at very large scale.
arxiv-2601-12884:
Jianshu Wang and a large team study whether motion impairs cognition in human computer interaction. Interaction increasingly happens in motion rich environments, from cars to walking commutes. Responding accurately and rapidly to directional visual cues is critical in these contexts. How whole body motion affects perception and reaction to such cues is underexplored.

The team stress the role of directional congruency between physical motion and visual targets. Individual differences also shape how people cope with motion while thinking. If motion and cue direction align, performance may hold up far better. Their work appeared in a human computer studies journal. Results can guide interface design for users on the move.
arxiv-2601-12984:
Lorenzo Piersante and Anirudh Natarajan tune machine learned models of how atoms push on each other. Such models now serve many tasks in atom scale science. They are fast, yet they can miss the mark on phase change in solids. One such change is precipitation, where a new phase grows inside an alloy.

The team give error scores made for this hard case. They also give plans for the training data such models need. Their focus is alloys with more than one main metal. Good models of this kind speed the hunt for strong, rust proof alloys. Less time goes to trial melts in the lab. The work serves the field that joins computing with metals.
arxiv-2601-13284:
Duygu Nur Yaldiz and co-authors teach decision models to be right and to know when they may be wrong. Large language models now sit in decision chains. In such chains a right pick is not all that counts. The trust score that comes with the pick must be sound too. A sound score lets a down stream tool know when to trust the model and when to pass to a back up.

Past teach can lift pick skill while it bends trust scores, or the next way round. Their teach is calibration aware reward learning. The reward pays for both a right pick and a trust score that fits the true odds. For teams that put models in care, funds, or law chains, that pair is the trust base.
arxiv-2601-13384:
Jiajun Zhang and a large team teach code models to edit in place, not just fill gaps. The stock fill in the middle form asks a model to write the span left blank in a code file. That form is stiff. It cannot fix flaws in the code that is left in place. It also leans on base models that lack safety tune.

Chat models are safe but slow at edits. Agent chains are flex but lag more. The team's swap is search and replace teach. The model learns to state an edit as a find and swap pair, in chat form. That gives in context edits with chat grade safety and less lag.
arxiv-2601-13584:
Niels Goedegebure and Kateryna Marynets study hard math problems at the edge of a region in 2026. Their problems use the Hilfer fractional derivative, a tool that blends two older such tools. Fractional tools track change with memory of the past, not just the near past. The edge rules here are fractional-periodic, a new twist on repeating edge values.

The pair prove when true solutions to these problems must exist. They also give ways to find near solutions by number crunching. Such edge problems show up in models of flow, heat, and growth with memory. Clear rules for when solutions exist help those models stand on firm ground.
arxiv-2601-13984:
Stefano Lanzini and co-authors run lab tests on gravity currents that flow along heated walls in 2026. A gravity current is a flow driven by density gaps, like cool dense air sliding low. Their current is a mix of air and carbon dioxide fed steadily at a channel inlet. Heat at the wall can stir or lift the current as it advances.

They measure two velocity components at high frequency, point by point. Carbon dioxide concentration and temperature are measured at the same time. Full maps of the flow show how wall heat reshapes it. Such flows model smoke, pollution, and industrial leaks.
arxiv-2601-14184: J. McGee and S. V. Dordevic test sparse statistical modeling on two classic problems in condensed matter physics in 2026. Sparse modeling picks a few key variables from many candidates. The problems are elemental superconductors and heavy fermions. In most cases the method was shown to beat other AI methods, such as machine learning and deep learning. Sparse models also stay easy to read, since few terms do the work.
arxiv-2601-14684:
Kanami Imamura, Tomohiko Nakamura, Kohei Yatabe, and Hiroshi Saruwatari study audio source separation in this 2026 paper. Source separation splits a mixed recording into its parts, such as one voice among many. Deep neural network methods for this task are typically trained at a single sampling frequency. To handle untrained frequencies, the input is usually resampled.

Resampling can degrade performance. The harm is worst when the input sampling frequency is lower than the trained one. The team dissects that performance degradation under sampling frequency mismatch. Readers get a careful breakdown of where the loss comes from, a step toward separation models that handle real-world files of mixed rates.
arxiv-2601-15184:
Julius A. Zeiss, Gereon Kossmann, René Schwonnek, and Martin Plávala prove a finite form of a classic theorem about symmetry. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with de Finetti theorems in general probabilistic theories. Such theorems say that exchangeable states look like mixtures of independent copies.

The authors use a recent notion of relative entropy for these theories. They prove a finite de Finetti result for general convex bodies. They then apply it to polynomial optimization. The result bears on when a chain of outer approximations must close in on the true answer.
arxiv-2601-15284:
Anurag Bagchi, Zhipeng Bao, and co-authors teach a video model to step inside paintings. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with world models, systems that predict how a scene changes with each action. A good model should foresee the correct future, not just a plausible one.

The team presents EgoWM, the Egocentric World Model. The method takes any pre-trained video diffusion model and makes it action-conditioned. No new architecture is needed. Fed with internet priors, the model can then walk through paintings from a first-person view, frame by carefully predicted future frame.
arxiv-2601-15584:
Pankaj Kumar and a large team design a waveform for dual-purpose wireless systems in a 2026 arXiv paper. Integrated sensing and communication, or ISAC, needs signals that do two jobs. One job is carrying data. The other is sensing the surroundings, like radar does. A single waveform must serve both well. The team proposes a blend of two known forms.

Their waveform amalgamates CHIRP signals with OFDM, the workhorse of modern wireless. CHIRP forms suit sensing, while OFDM suits high-rate data. The blend aims to lift performance on both sides at once. ISAC is a pillar of planned future networks. A shared waveform saves spectrum and hardware. This paper adds one candidate design to that race.
arxiv-2601-16184:
Vladimir Zyuzin shows that a known twist force can drive a steady spin flow. His 2026 preprint deals with paired anti magnets in a line. The force is the Dzyaloshinskii Moriya force, a twist in how spins link. Zyuzin shows it can call forth a spin flow that holds at rest. The flow is a reply to a built in pull on the wave like spin acts.

He likens the flow to the known flows in super cold wires. It also pairs with the held flows in ring traps. A rest flow needs no drive to keep it up. Such flows could carry spin facts with low loss. The work is a pure theory claim for tests to check.
arxiv-2601-16284:
Ikki Mitsuhashi and a large team find star birth that comes in bursts at high shift. Their 2026 preprint uses UNCOVER and MegaScience views. The views span stars born when space was young, at shifts three to nine. Birth rate through time is called star formation history. The team finds that rate rose and fell in bursts, not in a smooth line.

The burst form holds in much the same way across the set. It also fits tales of how the first star groups grew. Burst births shape how fast young star systems gain mass. A shared burst form hints at a shared drive. The work rests on deep views of far young systems.
arxiv-2601-16784:
Joshua Corneck, Edward Cohen, and Francesco Sanna Passino read nets whose links spark over time. In such nets, link acts come as bursts in a stream. Link types add a next layer to the web. Their 2026 preprint builds a model for such timed, typed webs. It uses point streams, where each act is a blip in time.

Their model finds a low-depth map for each node. That map can flag odd acts and group kin nodes. Timed webs show up in trade, chat, and crime data. A sound stream model helps watch them as they grow. It may catch fraud or faults as they form.
arxiv-2601-16984:
Rahul Ghosh, Chun-Hao Liu, Gaurav Rele, Vidya Sagar Ravipati, and Hazar Aouad make phone rule books search-able by AI. The 3GPP rule books guide all phone nets on Earth. They are vast, dense, and full of charts and tables. Plain chatbots fail on hard asks in them. Their 2026 preprint builds TelcoAI, a search aide for those books.

TelcoAI uses agent steps and rich search in one frame. It reads text, charts, and cross-links as one pool. Staff can then ask hard asks in plain words. Fast true reads cut hours of book work. Phone firms and labs both gain from it.
arxiv-2601-17084:
Iman Peivaste, Ahmed Makradi, and Salim Belouettar let an AI agent hunt light-harvest design rules. Such harvest bits turn light to hydrogen fuel. The search space for good ones is vast. Human hunch has long steered that hunt. Their 2026 preprint shares ChemNavigator, an agent that hunts on its own. It forms guesses, tests them, and learns rules from the loop.

Rules link a bit's build to how well it works. Clear rules beat blind trial lists in the lab. The agent's rules can guide cooks of new bits. Green fuel work gains a tireless scout here.
arxiv-2601-17184:
Adrian Tkachenko and a team of nine co-authors rework how gene read data gets stored. Gene read tools pour out vast data sets each run. The old FASTQ form stores one byte per base. It stores one more byte per grade mark. That waste swells stores and slows each move. Their 2026 preprint, FASTR, packs reads in a shot-like form.

Shot tricks squeeze the data to a leaner size. Lean files move fast and cost less to keep. Pop-scale gene work feels that gain most. The team aims to keep all facts in the pack. No base or grade mark is lost in the squeeze.
arxiv-2601-17384:
John E. Gough and Dylon Rees recast the Diósi-Penrose model as a filtering problem. That model links gravity to the collapse of quantum states. Past forms assumed background gravitational noise. Gough and Rees take a new route. They treat the universe itself as a detector. Space-time homodyne reads a stream of output signals from the system.

The result is a quantum Kushner-Stratonovich equation. It tracks the state as the signal comes in. This frame makes collapse a matter of information gain. It joins quantum optics tools to a deep gravity question. Tests of collapse models gain a cleaner math base. The work may guide how future probes are read.
arxiv-2601-17484:
Pengshuo Li and Lei Wu speed up simulation of oscillating rarefied gas flows. Such flows occur in micro-electro-mechanical systems. Their math rests on the Boltzmann kinetic equation. That equation is high-dimensional and time-bound, so runs are slow. The team focuses on the periodic steady state. That is the settled cycle the flow reaches.

Their frequency-domain scheme solves for that cycle at once. It skips long transient runs that waste time. Fast rarefied flow tools aid design of tiny sensors and pumps. They also help vacuum and chip gear. The work cuts a core cost in kinetic simulation. Design teams can test more shapes in the same time.
arxiv-2601-17884:
John Joseph M. Carrasco, Yaxi Chen, Nicolas H. Pavao, and Aslan Seifi push a famous shortcut in physics past its usual limits. Their 2026 preprint deals with the double copy, a map that turns gauge theory results into gravity results. Most uses of the map are perturbative, built step by step. The team instead gives a first-principles study that does not rest on small steps.

Their tool is the worldline instanton, a path that captures sudden quantum events. They study vacuum decay in a gauge theory set on a black hole background. The color-thermal spectrum of the gauge side appears as a winding mode. The double copy then carries the vacuum response across to gravity. The work links heat, color, and backreaction in one frame.
arxiv-2601-18084:
Zeki Hayran, John B. Pendry, Prasad P. Iyer, and Francesco Monticone study surfaces that change in time as well as space. Their 2026 preprint deals with space-time modulated metasurfaces driven by pulses. Time-varying photonics opens routes to effects like time reflection, frequency conversion, and one-way light flow. These effects arise when the optical traits of a material shift while light is inside it. The shifts can move photons between states of distinct frequency or direction.

Pulse driving gives fine control over when and how the change hits. Nonreciprocity, where light passes one way but not back, is a prized outcome. Such control serves lasers, sensors, and optical circuits. The work maps what pulsed modulation can unlock.
arxiv-2601-18184:
Zhiliang Peng and a large team present VibeVoice-ASR, a speech system built for long recordings. Their 2026 preprint is a technical report. Short-clip speech recognition has improved fast. Long audio, like meetings and podcasts, still trips systems up. Context breaks into pieces across a long file, and many speakers trade turns. The framework builds on the team's earlier VibeVoice work to handle those strains.

A general-purpose design aims to serve many kinds of long audio at once. Keeping track of who said what, and what was said an hour earlier, is the hard part. Progress here serves transcription, search, and meeting tools. The report lays out the system for other builders.
arxiv-2601-18284:
Hsiao-Chuan Chang, Sheng-You Huang, Yen-Chi Chen, and I-Chen Wu present VissimRL, a frame for learning traffic signal control inside a simulator. Their 2026 preprint starts from the cost of congestion: lost time, money, and clean air. Signal control is one of the key tools cities have against it. Reinforcement learning suits the task because lights must adapt as traffic shifts. The authors build their frame on Vissim, a widely used traffic microsimulator, and support multi-agent learning.

Each junction can learn as an agent while the city runs as a whole. Training inside a trusted simulator keeps experiments off real streets. The frame lets researchers compare control ideas on common ground.
arxiv-2601-18484:
Divya Setia studies when a blend of two gem-like maths forms stays a clean sum of like forms. The forms, named Demazure crystals, chart how a big maths house of swaps acts on sets of points. Each gem has a shape set by a high point and by rules for steps up and down. When two gems are joined, the join can break into clean parts or stay mixed.

Setia finds the exact terms on which the join breaks clean. The terms cover a wide house of swap groups, far past the plain case. Past work by two named scholars had settled the plain case. Her terms stretch theirs to the full house. Clean breaks help staff count and sort the parts of big forms with far less work.
arxiv-2601-18684:
Aaron Spector and thirteen colleagues report the first hunt of a device that seeks light bits that may not be in the book of known bits. The bits sought are like ghosts of the field: they would pass through a wall as if it were glass, then turn back to light on the far side. That trick gives the hunt its name, light that shines through a wall. No kit in a smash lab can reach such faint bits.

The hunt ran for a few months in the year past last. A strong beam was fired at a wall, with fine kit on the far side to catch a ghost bit's turn back to light. The first run tests the kit, the noise, and the reach of the hunt. Such hunts probe a part of the dark world that smash tests miss.
arxiv-2601-18784:
MohammadReza Torkamani and eight colleagues build a pure maths path to a key count for fast bursts of radio waves from space. Each burst is bent by the free bits it passes on its way to us. The size of that bend is called its dispersion measure. The spread of that size across many bursts tells us where loose stuff sits in space. Past paths to that spread ran huge, dear sims of how stuff moves.

Their path swaps the sims for sums. It rests on a trick that paints loose stuff onto dark maps by rule, at a far less cost. With sums in hand, the spread can be worked out fast for each world view. Fast counts could let teams test far more world views next to burst data. That could sharpen what bursts tell us of the stuff between stars.
arxiv-2601-18884:
Sally Jiang and many colleagues read a young star's disc with a space dish web to chart its rings and its stuff. The star, GY 91, is still in its first class of youth. Its disc holds rings and gaps that may mark where worlds are being born. Such marks at such a young age would push the birth of worlds far back in a disc's life. The team caught the disc in a new band with both the main dish web and its small mate web.

Their shots show the dust rings in fine form, and their line reads chart the gas that rides with the dust. Gas and dust can part ways as worlds form, so the pair of charts counts. A disc read at this care could help sort which ring tales are true. It could also set when the first worlds start to grow.
arxiv-2601-19384:
Julien Eudine and a large team co-design hardware and algorithms to map paired DNA reads to a genome. Genome sequencing now anchors personalized medicine and outbreak tracking. Mapping, the step that places each short read where it belongs, is a heavy compute cost in that pipeline.

Paired end reads come in twos with a known gap, a clue the mapper can exploit. Their accelerator, GenPairX, is built around that clue from the silicon up. Faster mapping shortens the road from a blood sample to answers a clinician can use. That is the point where sequencing stops being a lab feat.
arxiv-2601-19584:
Zs. Regály and A. Németh model how young planets move inside the disks where they form. Low-mass planets do not stay put. Gas and solid material in the disk push on them with torques, and those forces control how far the planets migrate. Most models assume the disk's mix of solids and gas matches the Sun's composition.

The authors look beyond that solar case. Changing the solid-to-gas ratio changes the push a planet feels. That in turn can change where small planets end up and whether they survive. Migration shapes the layout of whole planetary systems. Testing non-solar mixes matters because real disks vary widely in composition. The work widens the range of disk conditions that planet formation theory covers.
arxiv-2601-19784:
Danilo Lelin Li, Ramtin Rabiee, and Arman Farhang work on channel estimation for future mobile networks. A receiver must know how the radio channel distorts signals before it can decode them. Movement creates Doppler shifts that tangle the signal in time and frequency. New delay-Doppler modulation schemes handle this well, but a full switch is not yet practical.

Current 5G waveforms will carry into the next generation. The authors therefore estimate the channel in the delay-Doppler domain using the sounding reference signals that 5G already sends. Their approach bridges old waveforms and new processing. Better channel knowledge means faster, more reliable links for fast-moving users. The work speaks to high-speed rail, vehicles, and drones.
arxiv-2601-19984:
Dorota M. Skowron and Igor Soszyński review the role of long-period variable stars in observational astrophysics. These stars are evolved red giants and supergiants that pulsate over months or years. Their pulsations probe the late stages of stellar evolution. They are also practical tools used across modern astronomy.

Their period-luminosity relations make them distance indicators, and period-age relations make them clocks. Light curve shapes, amplitudes, and multiple periods reveal the physics of stellar interiors and mass loss. Few star types serve so many purposes at once. The review gathers what decades of monitoring have taught. It is a reference for anyone using these stars as probes or as tracers of galactic history.
arxiv-2601-20084:
Yash Saxena, Ankur Padia, Kalpa Gunaratna, and Manas Gaur make dense retrieval systems explain themselves. Dense retrievers embed queries and documents as vectors and match them by similarity. They power retrieval-augmented generation, yet their matching is opaque. How a query and document interact semantically stays hidden inside static embeddings.

Their method, IMRNNs, modulates embeddings so the interaction becomes interpretable, while staying efficient. Static embeddings cannot show which parts of a query matched which parts of a document. Modulation lets the two sides adapt to each other visibly. Understanding retrieval behaviour helps diagnose failures and improve design. The work targets a central trust problem in search and question answering. The flaw is not small. It hides why a match was made.
arxiv-2601-20184:
Mohsen Hatami and three colleagues survey security risks that arise when AI agents run inside cyber-physical systems, such as factories, vehicles, and power grids. These agents do not just read data; they sense and act on the physical world. New generative tools enable deepfake and manipulation attacks that can fool an agent's perception and reasoning.

The survey also covers how protocols for tool use widen the attack surface, since agents now call external tools and share context across domains. The authors review defenses and design principles for this setting. Their map of threats matters as agents move into systems where a wrong act can cause physical harm.
arxiv-2601-20284:
Debopom Sutradhar and four colleagues present a source-free method for domain adaptation in image classification. Domain adaptation moves knowledge from a labeled source domain to a target domain where the data look different. Many methods need the source data at hand, or rely on adversarial training or heavy pseudo-labeling, all of which cost compute.

Their approach works without access to the source data. It uses multiview image transformation together with consistency in the latent space. Source-free methods suit real deployments, where privacy or storage rules often bar keeping the original training set.
arxiv-2601-20484:
Serena Dipierro, Ovidiu Savin, and Enrico Valdinoci prove regularity results for the traces of nonlocal minimal graphs. Minimal graphs are surfaces that minimize area in a generalized sense; in the nonlocal version, distant points interact. At sticky boundary points, where the surface clings to the boundary of its domain, the trace's smoothness was in question.

The authors prove the trace has one continuous derivative with a Hölder bound at those points. As a result, boundary continuity implies boundary differentiability for these graphs. Such results anchor the theory of nonlocal surfaces, which model long-range effects in materials and image processing.
arxiv-2601-20884:
Atik Faysal and four co-authors propose warming up a model for the task it will actually face. Their 2026 paper concerns multimodal pretraining. Such pretraining builds general-purpose representations from mixed data, like images with text. In many deployments, though, only one modality is heavily used at fine-tuning time. Standard pretraining treats all modalities the same. That can leave the key modality under-optimized.

The authors call their fix finetune-informed pretraining. Knowledge of the downstream task shapes the first training phase. The model then spends its capacity where it will count. The paper reports that this boosts downstream performance. The idea is simple but broad: train for the job you know is coming. It speaks to teams that pretrain once and deploy in a narrow setting.
arxiv-2601-21084:
Amit Meghanani and Thomas Hain make speech enhancement robust to where a speaker sits. Their 2026 paper integrates front-end speech enhancement with self-supervised speech models. Such integration works well for downstream tasks in noisy conditions. Enhancement models are commonly fine-tuned with self-supervised representations. The fine-tuning uses mean squared error between enhanced and clean speech. The authors target position invariance in that tuning.

A system should not degrade when the speaker moves. Position changes alter the signal in ways that can fool enhancement. Position-invariant fine-tuning aims to remove that fragility. Cleaner speech feeds recognition, calls, and hearing tools. The paper is a focused methods study in speech processing. It helps systems that must work in real rooms, not just fixed studios.
arxiv-2601-21184:
Oem Trivedi and Abraham Loeb argue for a joint network to catch visitors from other stars. Their 2026 paper concerns interstellar objects, or ISOs. ISO astronomy has grown over the past decade into a new frontier. Current observations stay limited, though. Short visibility windows cut each visit brief. Inference degeneracies blur what the data mean. Follow-up work is split across telescopes. The authors call these limits structural, not incidental.

Their remedy is a full network for discovery and study. An end-to-end strategy would link detection, tracking, and analysis. Each new visitor could then be caught early and followed well. Such objects carry material from other planetary systems. Losing one to poor coordination wastes a rare sample. The paper makes the case to build the network now.
arxiv-2601-21384:
Hui Ma, Qingzhong Li, Jin Wang, Jie Wu, Shaoyu Dou, Li Feng, and Xinjun Pei forecast network traffic with little real data to learn from. Traffic forecasts guide smart network operations, but new services often lack long records. Models that juggle several traffic types at once also suffer when tasks clash.

Their model learns first in simulation, then transfers to the real network. It handles space and time patterns for many service types together. The design fights task imbalance so common services do not swamp rare ones. Better forecasts help operators plan capacity and catch strain before users feel it.
arxiv-2601-21484:
Xiuyu Li, Jinkai Zhang, Mingyang Yi, Yu Li, Longqiang Wang, Yue Wang, and Ju Fan align language models at test time without any retraining. Standard alignment training works but is costly and can be unstable. Their method instead samples directly from the policy that training would have produced.

An energy term guides each sampling step, combined with a reference model. The sampling runs inside a masked language model setup. Skipping training saves the full cost and risk of a training run. If the samples match trained quality, alignment becomes a setting teams can adjust on the fly rather than a project they must fund.
arxiv-2601-21684:
Xinglin Wang, Jiayi Shi, and eight co-authors recycle search effort to make test-time reasoning cheaper. Giving a model more compute at answer time broadens its search for a solution. Standard search treats each trial as disposable, throwing away the partial insights inside it.

The authors save and reuse that experience across trials. Lessons from dead ends can steer the next attempt away from the same walls. Reuse turns a pile of failed tries into a growing asset. More solved problems per unit of compute is the goal, which matters as reasoning features scale to everyday use.
arxiv-2601-21884:
Pratik Ingle, Jørn Lambertsen, Kasper Støy, and Andres Faiña build surfaces that move objects without grabbing them. A manipulation surface controls items by deforming its own shape, tipping and rolling things across itself. Dense arrays of actuators can make rich shapes, but they bring many degrees of freedom and hard control problems.

The team's MANTA-RAY platform takes a modular route. And this 2026 preprint describes a multi-modular version for handling several objects at once in a distributed way. Soft, modular surfaces could one day sort fragile goods. They could feed parts to assembly robots. They could move items where grippers are too clumsy. All this works by spreading control across simple repeating units.
arxiv-2601-21984:
Jian Gao and co-authors let a search process hunt for better power circuits. A power converter is a circuit that changes electric power from one form to a new form. The set of good designs is huge. In the past, this search was work for skilled human experts. Past AI tools just picked from fixed designs that men had drawn first.

Their tool is called PowerGenie. It pairs firm checks based on math with a search that breeds new designs from old ones. Weak designs die out, and strong ones change and mix. The team claims this can find new top designs at a large scale. Good converters sit in cars, solar kits, and data halls. Small gains in how well they work can save a lot of power when they are used by the millions.
arxiv-2601-22084:
Alfredo Gurrola, Robert Scherrer, and Oem Trivedi propose listening for dark energy from the Moon. The sound speed of dark energy carries basic information about what drives the universe's accelerating expansion. Existing observations barely constrain it at all.

The authors show that a laser interferometer on the Moon, such as the proposed Laser Interferometer Lunar Antenna, could measure that sound speed directly. It would do so by detecting how dark energy responds in gravitational wave observations. Their 2026 preprint turns a planned lunar instrument into a probe of cosmic acceleration. The Moon offers a quiet, seismically calm platform that Earth-based detectors cannot match.
arxiv-2601-22184:
Ido Aharon, Emanuele La Malfa, Michael Wooldridge, and Sarit Kraus ask how language models coordinate without talking. In tacit coordination games, several good outcomes exist, and pure logic gives no reason to pick one over another. Everyone must somehow converge on the same choice.

Humans solve this with focal points, options that stand out as salient to everyone, an idea from Schelling's classic theory. The authors test whether large language models do the same. Their 2026 preprint matters as model-based agents begin to interact in markets and negotiations. Agents that share human focal points will coordinate smoothly with us, while agents with alien salience could talk past everyone while sounding reasonable.
arxiv-2601-22284:
Yixuan Wang, Omkar Patil, and Warren Dixon build one frame that holds many classic tools for model tuning. Their 2026 preprint names the family Riemannian Lyapunov Optimizers. Most new tuners grow by trial tweaks to old ones, with thin grounds for why they work.

The new family grows from control theory, the study of how to steer a system. It treats tuning as a steered system that moves on a curved space of settings. That view yields tuners in a planned way, not by guesswork. A shared frame can help users pick and trust a tuner.
arxiv-2601-22384:
Ziming Li and six co-authors argue that graphs should be a shared base across all kinds of data. Graphs show links between things, and such links arise in text, images, and records alike. Their 2026 preprint notes that graph learning is now done task by task, then thrown away.

The team call for a common graph substrate: learn the link layout once, and reuse it across tasks and data types. A shared base could cut waste and lift weak tasks with help from strong ones. It could also make results easier to compare. The work is a stance paper for the field.
arxiv-2601-22784:
Viktor Stein and José Manuel de Frutos offer a simpler way to measure how far apart two data distributions are. Such gaps, called f-divergences, are usually found by first guessing density ratios, a step that can go wrong. Their method skips that step and works with ranks instead.

They turn the gap between two distributions into a histogram of ranks, then measure how far that histogram sits from flat. Rank-based tools are robust and easy to compute. The approach could serve tests for drift, fairness, and model fit.
arxiv-2601-22884:
Ana Arribas-Gil and Sara López-Pintado build a robust way to find the main pattern in multi-part curve data. Such data arise when several signals are recorded over time, each warped in its own way. A shared template may hide underneath, stretched differently in every part.

Their depth-based method estimates that template while coping with both individual and cross-part time warping. Depth methods resist outliers better than simple averages. Good templates help compare growth curves, motion traces, and other repeated signals across people or trials.
arxiv-2601-22984:
Yuhao Zhan and four co-authors ask why deep research agents go wrong. These AI agents search and write long reports, and their failures are hard to diagnose. Most benchmarks grade only the final report, hiding errors made along the way, like flawed planning that piles up quietly.

The authors argue for process-aware checks that audit the whole research path. Catching a bad plan early is easier than fixing a polished but wrong report. Better diagnosis should lead to research agents that users can actually trust. Flawed planning is singled out as the kind of intermediate error that end-to-end grading hides until the final report fails.
arxiv-2601-23284:
Iman Abdoli, René Wittmann, and Hartmut Löwen build a theory for dense fluids with odd diffusion. Odd diffusion breaks time-reversal symmetry through sideways chance currents, while keeping a steady balance state. Such behavior appears in systems of spinning or chiral grains.

Their dynamical density functional theory handles dense, interacting odd-diffusive fluids. They apply it to very soft grains on a flat plane. The framework predicts how strange diffusion reshapes clustering and flow in active matter. Ultrasoft grains on a flat plane provide the test system where the new density functional theory is exercised. Transverse chance currents are the odd signature, flowing sideways while the steady state stays at balance.
arxiv-2603-01484:
Signals that change over time on a network, such as sensor readings, need math tools that respect both space and time. Mingzhi Wang, Manjun Cui, Feiyue Zhao, and colleagues extend those tools in this 2026 work. Older fractional transforms force one shared setting across both dimensions, which limits how well they fit mixed patterns.

Their new transform gives each dimension its own fractional order while keeping key traits like reversibility. A second version links graph and time bases along a smooth path on a curved space of transforms. On top sits a filter whose orders are learned from data end to end. Tests on real time-varying graph data and on image repair show steady gains over top fractional methods.
arxiv-2603-01984:
Xiaoyu Yi, Gus Xia, and Ziyu Wang give composers a visual way to control instrumental texture in generated music. Their 2026 work identifies instrumentation, which instruments play and in what roles, as a natural control axis. Text prompts and metadata cannot shape a multi-track piece with that directness.

Their representation, ViTex, draws texture as an image-like score for the model to read. Color encodes instrument choice, position encodes pitch and time, and stroke traits encode local texture. A discrete diffusion model, conditioned on ViTex plus chord progressions, writes short multi-track symbolic pieces. Texture-level control stays explicit while unconditional generation quality remains strong in their tests. The demo and code are public, which invites hands-on trials of visual music control.
arxiv-2603-02184:
Jinqi Wu, Sishuo Chen, Zhangming Chan, and colleagues build a public test set for ad prediction in this 2026 paper. Online ads earn credit for a sale through rules called attribution, and rules differ. Learning from several rules at once can help predict conversion rates. Public data sets, though, carry labels from just one rule.

Their benchmark, MAC, is the first public set with labels from many rules. A companion library gathers standard methods so results can be compared fairly. Learning from many rules helped most users with long paths to a sale. Adding extra targets sometimes hurt, so targets must be chosen with care. Their new model, which mixes expert parts unevenly, beat the prior best method by a wide margin.
arxiv-2603-02584:

bailly-rapport-commissaires-magnetisme-a:
In 1784 the French king set a royal commission to test Mesmer's animal magnetism. Jean-Sylvain Bailly drafted its report, and Benjamin Franklin, Antoine Lavoisier, and Joseph Guillotin were among its signers. The commission ran careful trials, blindfolding patients and swapping magnetized objects for plain ones.

The verdict was firm. No fluid could be found, and the effects came from imagination alone. The report is a landmark of scientific testing, a debunking carried out with wit and rigor. It did not end mesmerism, but it set the standard for judging such claims. Enlightenment reason speaks here at its most decisive.
beal-buddhist-records-western-world-vol1:
Samuel Beal translated the Si-yu-ki, the record of the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang's journey to India, as Buddhist Records of the Western World. Volume one appeared in 1884. Xuanzang traveled from 629 to 645, crossing Central Asia to study at the great Indian monasteries.

The record describes kingdoms, roads, relics, and monasteries of seventh-century Asia in a pilgrim's faithful detail. Xuanzang names the doctrines he heard, the stupas he worshipped at, and the rulers who fed his party. Historians of India and China alike mine Beal's volumes for facts found nowhere else. Beal's notes name modern places for the pilgrim's ancient stops.
bovet-pandaemonium-english-1684:
Richard Bovet published Pandaemonium, or the Devil's Cloyster, in 1684. The title page promises a further blow to modern Sadducism, the age's word for doubting spirits. Bovet wrote as Joseph Glanvill's popular successor in the English war for belief in the invisible world.

Apparition stories and witchcraft cases pile up as his evidence. Each tale is told with gusto and offered as proof that spirits walk among us. Bovet presses ghost stories into the service of theology. Doubters, he argues, will end by doubting God himself. The book shows popular print defending the spirit world with narrative firepower rather than dry argument.
britten-nineteenth-century-miracles-1884:
Emma Hardinge Britten swept the globe for marvels in Nineteenth Century Miracles, her vast book of 1884. Her faith held that the dead speak and heal in her age. She set out to prove it with tales from land past land, faith past faith, town past town.

Each part gives names, dates, and sworn tales of cures and ghosts. The sheer bulk is her case. She meant the book as a store of proof no foe could shrug off. It is the faith's world tour in one tome. She knew the chief names of the faith at first hand in her tours. That close reach gives her vast claims a weight mere hearsay lacks.
bruno-de-infinito-1584:
Giordano Bruno wrote these talks in Italian in 1584, while he lived in London. The full title speaks of the vast whole, the world, and the worlds. Bruno held that the stars are suns with worlds of their own. The Church later burned him at the stake in Rome.

Five talks pit Bruno's voice against men who cling to the old closed cosmos. He says space has no edge and no core point. Earth is one world among a vast host of worlds. The book is a root text for the claim that life fills the sky.
burnet-sacred-theory-of-the-earth-vol1-1:
Thomas Burnet's Sacred Theory of the Earth reached English readers in 1684. Volume one holds the two first books of his four part theory. The first book treats the Deluge, the second treats Paradise, the Earth as it first was. Burnet pictures the young Earth as smooth, fair, and without seas or mountains.

The Flood, in his telling, cracked that smooth shell and drowned the world. Ruined fragments of the crust became our mountains and ocean beds. The work founded modern catastrophist cosmology, Earth history by great sudden blows. Its grand style won readers across Europe for a century. The English translation spread the theory widely. Few books shaped early geology so much.
cavendish-experiments-on-air-1784:

His work bore on the great fight over phlogiston that then split chemistry. Few trials of that age can match his for care, and few men hid from fame as he did.

Cavendish joined two gases with a spark and got pure water, weight for weight. The result showed water is a compound, not a base stuff as men had long held. He also wrote back to Kirwan in the same work. The proof shook the old scheme hard.
