Stalin replied to Roosevelt on 27 December 1944, and the voting plan hit its wall. His top secret message answers the proposal Harriman had delivered on 14 December. It is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume of Foreign Relations of the United States.

Stalin fully agrees that the questions left open at Dumbarton Oaks must be settled before a United Nations conference, voting first of all. The first two points of Roosevelt's proposal, he says, meet no objections and can be accepted. The third point is different. With regret, he sees no possibility of agreeing to its wording, because it weakens the rule that the permanent members must act in unanimity.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d184:
British Minister John Balfour proposed two United Nations items for the agenda in a letter dated July 5, 1945. The letter to Matthews, with its enclosure, is document 184 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. The new world organization was still being set up, and its first posts were unfilled.

London wants the leaders to settle two posts before that body meets in early August. One is who chairs the Executive Committee. The other is who serves as Executive Secretary of the Preparatory Commission. Agreeing among the Big Three first would let France and China be approached by month's end. The enclosure also proposes an early exchange of views on where the world organization should have its seat. But no final decision should be taken at Terminal, since other countries' views must count.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d284:
John Erhardt, the political adviser for Austrian affairs, reported the planned entry into Vienna in a telegram from Florence on July 15, 1945. The message is document 284 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. General Clark had left for Brazil and would return July 26.

In Clark's absence, Erhardt reports, the deputy commanders are to confer with Soviet officers in Vienna to settle the details for taking over the national sectors. The Berlin entry taught the need for careful planning and full agreement first. The talks will be purely military, with no political advisers present. If the zones and control agreements are ratified by July 26, the American, British, and French commanders, with their political advisers, hope to enter Vienna soon after and remain there permanently.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d384:
Joint control of German external assets is pressed in a Washington memorandum by Oliver, acting chief of the Division of Economic Security Controls, dated July 7, 1945. It was written for Collado and Despres, the Department's economic officers. American policy, Oliver states, was to control German assets abroad, and to make that control a joint one, headed by the Allied Control Council.

It would be most unfortunate, he argues, if control fell to zone commanders alone, wherever the parent firms or marks of ownership happened to sit. A common policy had to be pressed for. The memo then lists the problems in the way of agreement among the occupying powers.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d484:
Recognition of Poland's new government moves forward in Grew's cable to Harriman of June 22, 1945. The Department concurs, Grew writes, in Harriman's action as commissioner in accepting the settlement reached in Moscow. For his information, he has telegraphed the President an outline of Harriman's message of June 21 on the agreement on the Polish government.

In that telegram Grew recommended that the President look favorably, if the British government concurs, on granting recognition to the newly constituted government. It would be recognized as the new Polish Provisional Government of National Unity. As soon as he hears from the President, Grew promises, he will inform Harriman of the decision.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d584:
Ambassador Sato answered Foreign Minister Togo from Moscow on July 12, 1945, with blunt advice. His very secret cable, in translation, is document 584 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. It pours cold water on Tokyo's hope of using Moscow to end the war.

Sato says the chance of winning the Soviet Union to Japan's side is next to nothing. Fine phrases about peace in Asia, he warns, are mere theory. Britain and America mean to strip Japan of its role in East Asia, and Japan's home islands are themselves in peril. Burma, the Philippines, and part of Okinawa are already lost. The Soviet leaders, Sato adds, are realists whom empty words will not move. Japan must first resolve itself to end the war.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d684:
Ambassador Edwin Wilson reported Soviet demands on Turkey from Ankara on June 18, 1945. His secret priority wire is document 684 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Turkey's acting foreign minister had briefed him that morning.

The Turkish ambassador in Moscow had seen Molotov on June 7 at his own request. Molotov said outstanding questions must be settled before a new treaty could be concluded. First came the 1921 treaty, under which Russia ceded eastern lands to Turkey. The Soviet Union, Molotov said, desired those lands returned. The ambassador refused to discuss Turkey's territorial integrity at all. Molotov set the point aside, but warned it remained unsettled. He then turned to the Straits, where Turkish good will, he said, was not enough to guarantee Soviet security.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d84:
Edward Page recorded a turning point in the access fight in a Moscow memorandum dated June 21, 1945. The memo is document 84 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Ambassador Harriman met Vyshinsky, who handed over a written reply about the American advance group waiting to enter Berlin.

Vyshinsky explained that the delay came from Zhukov being in Moscow until June 28. But if Washington wished to start without him, it could send its group whenever it liked. He also shared the first firm site plans. Each delegation would get its own zone, as at Yalta. And since Berlin was destroyed, the conference would sit at Babelsberg near Potsdam, in the Crown Prince's palace. The Americans had their opening at last.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1084:
The Acting Secretary of State cabled George Kennan in Moscow on July 31, 1945. Kennan is to inform the Soviet Foreign Office of America's answer to Yugoslavia's protest notes on Greek Macedonia. Belgrade has been told that Washington will recommend a tripartite commission to test the charges.

The commission would mix military and political officers from the Allied missions in Belgrade and Athens. Moscow would need to name a special group to work beside the Athens team. Washington now asks whether the Soviet government will collaborate in the inquiry and in framing advice for Athens and Belgrade. The Greek government has already been told of the Belgrade reply.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1184:
Churchill wrote to Truman on 25 July 1945, his final day as a Potsdam principal. The next day's election results would replace him with Clement Attlee at the table. Few summits have changed a chief player in the middle of the game.

The message is among the last words of Churchill's wartime leadership. He had helped design the summit system itself, meeting Roosevelt and Stalin across the war years. Now the system went on without him. This letter marks the changing of the guard in the British team. It also shows the talks pausing for no man, however large his part had been.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1284:
On 18 July 1945 the United States Chiefs of Staff issued this memorandum. It followed their opening-day paper in the volume's run. The staff's work of framing the summit's military questions continued into the second day.

Papers of this kind weighed what the services could do and what they feared. They gave the envoys facts with a soldier's edge. This memorandum is part of that early stack. Read with its neighbors, it shows the chiefs' office building its brief day by day, as the shape of the talks came into view.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1384:
The communiqué of the Berlin Conference, issued on 2 August 1945, told the world what the Potsdam leaders had decided. Unlike the protocol, which recorded the bargain in full, the communiqué was written for the press and the public. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

Comparing the two closing texts is a lesson in how governments speak. The communiqué smooths hard edges and stresses accord; the protocol keeps the fine print. Readers get both the public face of the settlement and, elsewhere in the volume, the record behind it. This public statement closed the last wartime summit and opened the uneasy peace that followed in Europe.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-84:
Secretary of State James Byrnes wrote to John Winant, the United States ambassador in London, on July 23, 1945. Byrnes was at Potsdam with President Truman for the Big Three conference. Winant held the London embassy, a key post for work with the British ally. The letter was later printed in the second Potsdam volume of the official Foreign Relations series.

Such letters kept an absent ambassador in step with the talks he could not attend. London still ran much joint work on Europe through its own channels. The message shows the conference's reach beyond the meeting rooms. It also shows how Byrnes used his ambassadors as a link between Potsdam and the wider alliance.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d784:
Document 784 is a working paper of the United States delegation dated July 27, 1945. It comes from the conference's final week. Staff drafted it as the talks turned toward closure. The paper stayed in the delegation files and was printed in the second Potsdam volume.

Final-week drafts have a different grain. The writers know the end is near and write for the record as well as the moment. Readers can spot lines meant to last. The document shows the American team polishing its positions for the protocol. It belongs to the last, careful stage of the paper war.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d884:
President Harry Truman signed this letter to Secretary of War Henry Stimson on July 29, 1945. It gives the War Department its orders on German interim financing. Truman quotes the goals of a minimum import program, drawn from principle 14 approved by the foreign ministers at Potsdam.

The goals include disarmament, reparations, and care for occupying forces and displaced persons. Living standards in Germany should not pass the average level in Europe. Truman directs the War Department to handle buying and first financing for imports America accepts. Advances should be a first charge against exports of German goods and stocks.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d984:
The Acting Secretary of State cabled William Clayton at Potsdam on July 18, 1945, about a Soviet move in Rumania. Bucharest had seen a Russian letter to the Rumanian prime minister. It declared that German-held shares in Rumanian oil firms pass into Soviet ownership, as partial payment for war damage done to the USSR.

Washington lists why the claim is objectionable and drafts arguments to use at Potsdam. Shares might be looted property, barred by the Allied declaration of January 5, 1943. Even proven German shares must await four-power rules for assets in former enemy and neutral lands. America denies that the USSR may assert ownership alone. It holds such assets in trust for all four occupying powers.
galdos-trafalgar-bell-1884:
Benito Pérez Galdós began his Episodios Nacionales in 1873 with Trafalgar, and Clara Bell Englished it in 1884. The cycle grew to forty-six novels tracing Spain's nineteenth century. Gabriel Araceli, a cabin boy from Cádiz, tells this first tale from his old age.

Gabriel ships aboard the Santísima Trinidad at the battle of Trafalgar in 1805. Nelson's fleet, Spanish pride, and shattering cannon fire fill his boy's-eye view. Galdós mixes history with a servant's plain witness of great events. Bell's translation opened the cycle to English readers early. The series became Spain's national epic in prose, and Trafalgar is still its most read door.
gao-gaoreports-b-296984: WorldWide Language Resources and SOS International tangled six dockets in November 2005 — a multi-firm protest pile — and GAO's combined ruling settles all. The firms challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Mega-filings get one careful answer. Six dockets, one fair verdict.
gao-gaoreports-b-297084: IAP World Services took its November 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-305484: The National Mediation Board's arbitrator pay got a fiscal ruling in this 2006 GAO call, which tests compensating the neutral arbitrators. The decision reads the money law. The ruling decides whether the pay was legal. The law had the final word.
gao-gaoreports-b-306284: The Capitol architect's electrical and security payments got a fiscal ruling in this 2006 GAO call, which tests the judiciary building charges. The decision reads the money law. The ruling decides whether the payments were legal. The law had the final word.
gao-gaoreports-b-309784: A Government Accountability Office bid-protest ruling dated October 19, 2007, covering two filings by CAMSS Shelters. The shelter manufacturer contested a federal contract award, and the consolidated decision works through each protest argument. The published ruling shows how GAO judges competitions for specialized equipment — and gives future bidders a map of what wins and what fails.
gao-gaoreports-b-311284: This 2008 GAO ruling is about designated Employee Agent at Mark Whetstone. The decision answers a legal question about spending public funds. The library keeps it in the public record of federal fiscal decisions. The library keeps it as part of the public record.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-684: Student aid tax breaks lacked effectiveness research in 2005, and GAO's report says limited research existed on the tools. The findings demand the study. The report warns that the students deserved proven help. The research had to be done. The students deserved proven help.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-984: The 2004-05 flu vaccine shortage underscored poor preparation in 2005, and GAO's report says the shortfall showed the need for better readiness. The findings deliver the verdict. The report warns that the next season should not run dry. The preparation had to improve.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-184: Financial system modernizations kept failing in 2006, and GAO's report says more effort was needed to address the key causes. The findings diagnose the disease. The report warns that the money machines' upgrades should not keep crashing. The causes had to be addressed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-284: The Army's contract guard program needed oversight in 2006, and GAO's report says the program required greater supervision and a reassessed acquisition approach. The findings demand the watch. The report warns that the hired sentries needed proper management. The program had to be reassessed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-784: Military families' housing aid eligibility needed a fix in 2006, and GAO's report says excluding housing allowances from income tests would expand access. The findings do the math. The report warns that the service families deserved the rental help. The allowances should not disqualify.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-84: The Navy's fleet response plan needed better management in 2006, and GAO's report says a comprehensive approach and rigorous testing would help. The findings prescribe the discipline. The report warns that the surge-ready fleet needed proving. The approach had to be comprehensive.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-384: Veterans' college aid was a bureaucratic maze in 2007, and GAO's report says management action was needed to cut the overlap in approving programs. The findings target the duplication. The report argues the benefit should not require a second education to claim.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-584: Dangerous truckers were on GAO's radar in 2007 — the safety agency could name the risky carriers but would not say the maximum fines. The report finds the watchers spotting trouble yet pulling punches on penalties. The findings ask why the hammer stayed holstered when the bad actors were known.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-84: Doctor-shortage maps were still broken in 2007, and GAO's report says problems remained with the primary care shortage designation system. The findings target the flaws. The report warns that the neediest towns were missing from the map. The designations had to be honest.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-984: The Guard and Reserve's future had fine print in 2007 — GAO's report says money, security, and people puzzles should shape the force's redesign. The findings lay out the trade-offs. The report treats the citizen-soldier bargain as a contract worth reading closely.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-284: This 2008 GAO report takes a hard look at federal Workers' Compensation: Better Data and Management Strategies Would Strengthen Efforts to Prevent and Address Improper Payments. Congress relies on GAO for straight fact-finding on federal programs. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-384: GAO published its findings on aviation and the Environment: FAA's and NASA's Research and Development Plans for Noise Reduction Are Aligned but the Prospects of Achieving Noise Reduction Goa in 2008. GAO digs into federal programs at Congress's request and reports back what it learns. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-684: The Government Accountability Office dug into federal Real Property: Property Conveyances between the District of Columbia and the Federal Government Await Completion, and Development Will Take Many Years in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-84: A 2007 Government Accountability Office report assessing the United Nations' management reform efforts. Congress, which funds a large share of the UN budget, wanted to know whether promised reforms were working. GAO found progress had varied — some initiatives moved forward while others stalled. The report gives American lawmakers a scorecard on an institution they fund but do not control.
hartmann-philosophy-unconscious-vol1-188:
Eduard von Hartmann, a young German ex-officer, published his Philosophie des Unbewussten in 1869 and startled Europe. W C Coupland's English translation of 1884 fills three volumes, and volume one here treats the phenomenology of the unconscious. That is: Hartmann gathers the signs of unconscious mind at work in body, instinct, and feeling.

His claim is large: an unconscious will and idea steer nature and human life beneath our waking thought. Decades before Freud, Hartmann made the unconscious a central concept of philosophy. The first volume builds his case from reflex, instinct, and the healing wisdom of the body. It is a strange, powerful book that its century could not ignore.
hartmann-philosophy-unconscious-vol2-188:
Volume two of Coupland's 1884 Hartmann turns from the signs of the unconscious to its metaphysics, its inner nature and law. Eduard von Hartmann's Philosophy of the Unconscious, first published in German in 1869, argues that one unconscious principle works through all nature. Volume one had surveyed its effects; this volume asks what that principle is.

Hartmann joins Schopenhauer's blind will to Hegel's unfolding idea, and finds both at once in the unconscious. From atoms to human genius, one striving, knowing power drives the whole, on his account. The system swept Germany and reached England in Coupland's careful English. Volume two is where the bold architecture stands tallest.
hartmann-philosophy-unconscious-vol3-188:
Coupland's third volume of Hartmann, from 1884, carries the Philosophy of the Unconscious into religion and history. Eduard von Hartmann's German work of 1869 had grown through many editions into a system touching everything. Having traced the unconscious in nature and in mind, he now asks what it means for faith and for the fate of mankind.

Hartmann reads history as the unconscious slowly schooling humanity out of its illusions of happiness. Religion, on his view, moves through stages toward a clear-eyed, somber wisdom. His pessimism, argued at full scale, made him one of the most debated thinkers of his age. Volume three completes Coupland's English Hartmann, system and all.
hering-condensed-materia-medica-1884:
Hering's guiding symptoms filled ten big volumes, and The Condensed Materia Medica of 1884 shrinks that wealth to pocket size. The second edition keeps Constantine Hering's marks and choices, so the strongest signs still stand out. A prescriber could carry the great man's life work in a coat pocket.

Condensing meant hard choices: only the symptoms Hering trusted most survive the cut. What remains reads like the distilled voice of the larger set, terse and ranked. Country doctors riding between patients prized such books, and this one ranks among the most portable forms of the great materia medica.
huysmans-against-grain-1884:
Joris-Karl Huysmans published Against the Grain in 1884, a French novel with almost no plot in the usual sense. Its hero, Des Esseintes, is a rich and tired nobleman. He shuts himself away in a house outside Paris. There he surrounds himself with rare books, scents, jewels, and art.

Most of the book lists what Des Esseintes loves and what he hates. His tastes stand against the plain tastes of the world outside. The novel became a guide for the Decadent movement, which prized art and artifice over nature. Its strange hero still draws readers who like beauty pushed to an extreme.
jacko-ape-man-yale-british-colonist-1884:
A Victoria newspaper told British Columbia a strange tale on July 4, 1884. The Daily British Colonist reported a creature called Jacko, caught by a train crew above Yale. The headline asked what the thing was, and the report calls it a kind of gorilla.

Jacko was small, hairy, and strong, the crew said, and was kept in town for show. No trace of him stands past the news reports of that summer. Most now take the tale for a hoax or a tall yarn of the rails. Still, the report is read as the first draft of the Bigfoot legend.
jevons-investigations-currency-finance-1:
Jevons died in 1882, and his Investigations in Currency and Finance appeared in 1884, edited by H. S. Foxwell. The volume gathers the papers Jevons had written on money, prices, and trade crises across his career. Foxwell, a fellow economist, arranged them as a memorial to the marginal revolution's most empirical mind.

The papers track the value of gold, chart price movements with early index numbers, and test the idea that trade cycles follow a rhythm. Jevons even tried to link commercial crises to sunspots and harvests, a bold guess that later scholars judged wrong but fertile. Throughout, statistics serve theory: he hunts patterns in the numbers the way a detective hunts clues. The book preserves the working side of a founder of modern economics, counting and measuring where his rivals only reasoned.
jewett-country-doctor-1884:
A Country Doctor, printed in 1884, opens with chapters named The Last Mile and The Farm-House Kitchen. Later heads follow a great change, a stay at Dr. Leslie's, and new outlooks for its heroine. The book grew from Jewett's own life beside a country physician father.

Nan Prince, a bright farm girl raised by that doctor, resolves to study medicine herself. Her choice costs her a marriage offer and the good opinion of proper society. She holds her course all the same. When women doctors were still rare, the novel gave American readers a serious and early portrait of a professional woman.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lumbrozo-jacob-:
Jacob Lumbrozo, a Lisbon-born physician, planter, and trader in colonial Maryland, is the subject of a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906 by Cyrus Adler and J. H. Hollander. He reached Maryland on January 24, 1656, by way of Holland. He built a profitable medical practice, took up land, and grew wealthy.

Lumbrozo is the first Jew in Maryland whose faith is proven by documents, the article stresses. In 1658 he was arrested for blasphemy under the Toleration Act of 1649, a charge that carried death and loss of property, after denying the Trinity. A general amnesty freed him ten days later, and no new attempt followed. He later traded with the Indians by commission and exercised most rights of a citizen. The entry uses one man’s case to test how far religious toleration in Maryland really reached.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ma-oz-zur-10384:
Ma'oz Zur, the great Hanukkah hymn, is examined in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. The hymn was first sung at home after kindling the festival lights. It later entered the synagogue service as well. Its acrostic spells the name Mordecai. Zunz placed its author in the middle of the thirteenth century.

Much of the article is given to the famous tune. The bright melody became so bound to the feast that four other Hanukkah hymns are sung to it. Gottheil's English paraphrase, Rock of Ages, carried it into the Union Hymnal. Scholars traced the air to an old German folk song known among Jews by 1450. Luther used the same melody for one of his first chorales. The entry thus follows a hymn from a medieval Jewish home into churches and hymnals far beyond it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mah-nishtannah-: Mah Nishtannah, literally wherein is distinguished, is given a stub entry in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. The words open the child's questions to the father in the Passover Haggadah. By extension, the whole home service of Passover is sometimes familiarly called by this name. The questions are often chanted in the study chant of the Talmudical schools. The intoned text appears elsewhere in the encyclopedia's pages.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mattersdorf-joa:
Joab ben Jeremiah Mattersdorf was a Hungarian rabbi who died about 1807. Gotthard Deutsch and S. Mannheimer profile him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He owed his pulpit to family connections. Aaron Chorin had been a disciple of Joab's father, and through his influence Joab became rabbi of Deutschkreuz. The town lay near Mattersdorf, from which his name is taken.

Two books define his record, among them “Hen Tob,” printed at Zolkiev in 1806, which comments on part of the marriage-law code Eben ha-Ezer. The printed volume adds a companion work by his son-in-law. His earlier “Sha'are Binah” offers fresh readings of an older legal work. The entry also catches him in a shared scholarly error. Like Joseph Caro and others, he mistook the author Isaac ben Reuben for a grandson of Isaac Alfasi.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meir-ben-simeon:
Meir ben Simeon of Narbonne was a Talmudist and controversialist of the later thirteenth century. Solomon Schechter and Isaac Broydé profile him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was a disciple of Nathan ben Meir of Trinquetaille. He corresponded as an equal with Nahmanides and enjoyed a high reputation as a commentator. His fame in his own day, though, rested on religious disputation with Christians.

His “Milhemet Mizwah,” the War of the Commandment, survives in a Parma manuscript and falls into five parts. It opens with his account of a formal disputation held in 1245 before the bishop of Narbonne. It collects his controversies with churchmen. It explains the messianic passages Christians pressed into service, and comments on the Shema and the thirteen attributes of God. It ends boldly, with a letter declaring the revered “Sefer ha-Bahir” a forgery.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-menken-ada-isaa:
Ada Isaacs Menken was an Anglo-American actress. One daring role made her name. Joseph Jacobs and Edgar Mels profile her in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. She was born in Louisiana in 1835. She began as a child dancer in New Orleans, survived capture by Indians in Texas, and wrote for newspapers. In 1856 she married Alexander Isaacs Menken, publicly embracing Judaism. In 1861 the Mazeppa of Albany's Green Street Theater made her famous. She rode strapped to a horse in the part. It made her famous on two continents. The entry calls the part more acrobatic than histrionic.

The life that follows is restless. She married the prize-fighter John Heenan, the humorist Orpheus C. Kerr, and James Barclay, played the London and Paris stages, and wrote two books of poems. The last, "Infelicia," was dedicated by permission to Dickens. She died in Paris in 1868. Dickens, Swinburne, Dumas, and Hugo admired her.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-michael-max-107:
Max Michael, a German painter born in Hamburg on March 23, 1823, is profiled in a Jewish Encyclopedia entry by Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman, published in 1906. He studied at Dresden's art academy, spent five years in Paris, and then twenty years working in Rome and Venice. His first known work, Country Girl Writing, dates from 1866.

Michael returned to Berlin in 1870 and, five years later, became professor of painting at the Royal Academy, a post he kept until his death in 1891. The entry names his Girls' School in the Sabine Mountains, now in Hamburg's Kunsthalle, a cardinal visiting a monastery, Job disputing with his friends, and Bertini painting an altar-piece among the Camaldolites.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-miter-10884:
The miter is the priestly head-dress of the Bible. Joseph Jacobs and Judah David Eisenstein sort it out in a Jewish Encyclopedia article published in 1906. The high priest's miter, the miẓnefet, was fine linen. It carried a gold diadem engraved Holiness to the Lord, tied on with a purple cord. Ordinary priests wore the migba'ah, likewise of linen.

The article then follows the word pe'er beyond the sanctuary. It was a festive head-covering for a bridegroom and for the daughters of Zion. Precisely because it was an ornament, mourners took it off. The Bible never describes the miter's shape. Its names suggest a turban wound round the head. Exodus, Ezekiel, and Isaiah supply the evidence throughout.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mordecai-10984:
Mordecai, in this Jewish Encyclopedia entry by Cyrus Adler and A. S. W. Rosenbach, published in 1906, is not the biblical hero but an American family of German origin settled in the United States in the later eighteenth century. Its fame is military, and its brightest name is Alfred Mordecai of Warrenton, North Carolina, born January 3, 1804.

Alfred entered West Point at fifteen and graduated first in his class in 1823, into the engineer corps. He taught natural philosophy at the academy, built Forts Monroe and Calhoun in Virginia, and rose to captain of ordnance. For two decades he sat on the Board of Ordnance, inspected arsenals, and toured Europe's cannon-foundries. He died at Philadelphia in 1887.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-hasid-110: Moses Hasid was an Austrian ethical writer who lived at Prague in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. Kaufmann Kohler and Isaac Broydé give him a short entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His one work is a Zawwa'ah, a book of ethical instructions, printed at Prague in 1717. Part of it, as Iggeret ha-Musar, was reprinted with Moses Alshech's commentary on the Prophets in 1720.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mother-hebrew-e:
Mother, in Hebrew em and in Aramaic imma, is treated here as a subject in Bible and rabbinic teaching. Wilhelm Bacher and David Philipson wrote the Jewish Encyclopedia article. Legally the father headed the Hebrew family, and the mother stood below him. In the honor owed her by her children, though, she stood on his level.

The article gathers the texts: the Decalogue bids children honor mother and father alike, and Proverbs sets a mother's teaching beside a father's. Scripture pictures God's comfort as a mother's comfort and grief as Rachel weeping for her children. Rabbinic tales add Tarfon's devotion to his mother. The entry closes on the mother's supreme place in rearing and teaching the young.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-natronai-b-nehe:
Natronai b. Nehemiah, called Mar Yanka, headed Pumbedita's academy. Wilhelm Bacher and S. Mendelsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was gaon there from 719 to 730. He married into the exilarch Hasdai's family. Pride in that tie marked his rule.

Sherira Gaon reports that students fled his arrogance. Many left the academy and returned only after his death. Two responsa are ascribed to Natronai by name. One readmits followers of the false Messiah Serenus. The other bars children of heretics who renounced Judaism. Weiss, though, gives both rulings to Natronai b. Hilai. Many more responsa under his name remain uncertain.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-neuwiedel-elias:
Elias Neuwiedel was a Russian teacher of Hebrew grammar. Crawford Howell Toy and Max Rosenthal wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Neustadt-Sugind in 1821. He died at Warsaw on Sept. 16, 1886. He studied Talmud at the yeshivah of Volozhin.

Neuwiedel taught Hebrew and modern languages after Volozhin. Rossieny, in Kovno, and Warsaw were his school towns. At Warsaw he published his Hebrew grammar in 1874. More Sefat Ibrit follows the method of Ollendorf. In 1882 came Ab le-Banim, talks for the young. Its title means a father to his children. He was grandson of Benjamin-Benish Neustädter, a noted name. The entry keeps his record in these few firm lines.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-noph-11584:
Noph is a name for an ancient Egyptian city. Isidore Singer and W. Max Muller wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel all name the place. Every ancient version renders the name as Memphis. The form, scholars hold, was worn down in copying. Hosea keeps the truer form, Mof, for it.

Some scholars tried to rescue the letters as written. They read Noph as Napata, far off in Ethiopia. Ezekiel's list, though, puts the city in Egypt itself. Jewish colonies at remote Napata are also unlikely. Jeremiah's exile towns all lie on Egyptian soil. The entry therefore keeps the old reading: Memphis.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-oldenburg-11684:
Oldenburg was a grand duchy in the north of Germany. Gotthard Deutsch and Abraham Lewinsky wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It held nine Jewish groups within its bounds. Delmenhorst, Jever, and Varel were among those towns. Vechta and Wildeshausen were two more of them.

Jews lived in Oldenburg in the Middle Ages, the piece shows. An old bronze seal ring was found near the town. It bears the name of Reuben, son of Jeremiah. It shows two frogs that swim side by side. In 1350 the Jews were cast out of Wildeshausen. In 1365 the counts of Oldenburg gave rights to Jews. Three Jewish homes stood at Vechta in later years. They had to pay a tax for the costs of war.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-oser-leopold-11:
Leopold Oser was an Austrian doctor in Vienna. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Nikolsburg, in Moravia, in 1839. He read cures at the University of Vienna there. He took his degree and set up practice in 1862.

In 1872 Leopold became a teacher at the university. He was chief of a ward at the general clinic too. He was a doctor at the Rothschild Hospital in Vienna. In 1885 he was named to a higher post there. That post was as an assistant professor of his school. He wrote for the great hand books of his field. His own works treat the womb and its moves in birth. They treat the gut and its ills, and the cholera plague.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-phabi-12084:
Phabi was a high-priestly family of the late Second Temple age. Richard Gottheil and Samuel Krauss wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Three high priests carried the family name. They were Jesus ben Phabi and two Ishmaels. Its story is one of names, not deeds.

Josephus names all three of these high priests. The Mishnah and Talmud also recall Ishmael ben Phabi. The name itself seems Egyptian in origin. Greek writers spell it in several different ways. Rabbinic books show the same uncertainty in their spelling. The family rose just before the Temple fell.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-porges-porjes-a: Aaron ben Benjamin Porges was a rabbi in Prague in the seventeenth century. The Editorial Board and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His one known work is called Zikron Aharon. It forms the first part of a book on Jewish customs at death. The book also gives counsel to the sick. It was first printed at Prague in 1682. It has been reprinted many times since then.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pronunciation-m:
Modern Hebrew is spoken in two main ways, Ashkenazic and Sephardic. Crawford Howell Toy and Caspar Levias wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Like Syriac, Hebrew came down with a twofold sound, they say. The Ashkenazic way is traced to Babylonia. The Sephardic way is traced to Palestine.

Proof for that split is thin, the writers admit. The Sephardim came to Europe from Palestine, it is known. The Ashkenazim came in part through southern Russia. Those paths may explain the two sounds of Hebrew today. The article sets out the sounds letter by letter. It shows where the two traditions part ways.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rabbah-b-nahman:
Rabbah bar Nahman was a Babylonian teacher of the third set of amoraim. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was of an age with Rabbah bar Huna. The two men were close in work and in life. Rabbah bar Huna came to his house as a guest. He once sent him a question in learned form.

May our teacher teach us, the question began in respect. Later the bond between the two men broke down. Rabbah bar Nahman had some trees of his friend cut down. The trees stood on the banks of a stream. A claim over that ground drove the two apart. The entry tells the tale from Talmud records.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-representative-:
Representative themes are melodies borrowed between synagogue services. Cyrus Adler and Francis L. Cohen wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Cantors used them once chant traditions were fixed. That fixing came by the early sixteenth century.

The article explains the practice in plain terms. A snippet of melody points worshipers to another day. It can signal an approaching holy occasion. In Sephardic use, one service quotes another service's tune. A New Year prayer takes three different melodies in turn. Each tune recalls a different part of the season. Ashkenazic cantors used the practice more widely still. Certain melodies became signs for days and seasons. The entry shows music doing the work of memory.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-robbery-or-1278:
Robbery is the taking of another's goods by force or fear. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Lewis N. Dembitz wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. In the Bible the word can cover land or slaves too. Leviticus sets the penalty for this offense.

The article notes that stripes are excluded from that penalty. A suspect robber swore an oath under the rules. Perjury added its own penalty if he later confessed. The robber restored what he took, plus a fifth part. He also brought a ram as a guilt offering. Then he was forgiven, the text says. Oppression differs, since goods were held lawfully at first. The Talmud treats robbers even less severely, they note. Its sages had tax tools, not bandits, in mind.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosewater-andre:
Andrew Rosewater was an American engineer born in Bohemia on October 31, 1848. Cyrus Adler and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. His family settled in Cleveland, where he went to public school.

At sixteen Rosewater joined the Union Pacific Railway's engineer corps. He settled in Omaha in 1868 and became its city engineer in 1870. He held that post three separate times across his career. Between terms he edited The Omaha Bee and built a railroad and water-works. He also advised twenty-five cities on sewerage as a consulting engineer.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-sanwel-b:
Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, issued with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board in 1906. It profiles Samuel, called Sanwel, ben Aaron Benjamin. He worked as a scribe at Worms in the seventeenth century. After the great fire of 1689 he left Worms. He settled in Hamburg, in the north of Germany.

In Hamburg, Samuel turned from copying to writing verse of his own. His Ḥidah Mezuḳḳaḳah u-Ẓerufah is a riddle in rhyme about tobacco. It was printed at Hamburg in 1693. His Shir is a poem on the Pentateuch. He dedicated it to the Talmud students of Worms. Its acrostic spells out Samuel of Worms. That poem appeared at Hamburg in 1692. The entry preserves the trace of a working scribe who also wrote poetry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-santarem-13184:
Joseph Jacobs and Meyer Kayserling wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Santarem. The Portuguese city had a Jewish quarter even before 1140. That year the Portuguese took the city. Its synagogue was the oldest in all Portugal. The city was also the seat of the district rabbi for Estremadura.

An early charter set rules for debts between Christians and Jews. Payments had to be made before witnesses of both faiths. In lawsuits, only the Christian's word was believed. In November 1490 the Jews met a royal bride with Torah scrolls and gifts. After the expulsion, many secret Jews stayed in Santarem. A quake struck on January 26, 1531. Fanatic monks blamed the hidden Jews for it. Mobs drove the Maranos from their homes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schloessinger-m:
Cyrus Adler and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Max Schloessinger. He was a German philologist and theologian. Schloessinger was born at Heidelberg on September 4, 1877. He studied at Heidelberg, Vienna, and Berlin. He took his doctorate in 1901. He was ordained a rabbi in 1903, after training in Vienna and Berlin.

In 1903 Schloessinger came to New York. He joined the editorial staff of The Jewish Encyclopedia itself. In 1904 he left that post for Cincinnati. There he became librarian at the Hebrew Union College. He also teaches Biblical exegesis at the college. His published work treats Ibn Kaisan's commentary on an old Arabic ode. It rests on a Berlin manuscript. The piece appeared in a journal of Assyriology in 1901.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-seesen-13384:
Isidore Singer and Lesser Knoller wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on Seesen. The town sits in the Harz Mountains. In the fall of 1801 Israel Jacobson founded his famous school there. Endowments from Jacobson, his family, and other givers kept it strong. The school took in free scholars. From 1805 many of them were Christians from Seesen itself.

In 1810 the school became an elementary common school. That year Jacobson built a temple for it. It was the first Jewish house of worship with German sermons, choral singing, and an organ. The school later matched the Prussian plan for Realschulen. In 1905 it holds 275 pupils in ten classes. Of those, 123 are Jews and 152 are Christians. Meyer Jacobson founded an orphan asylum there in 1852. Seesen's Jews number only 69.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shadrach-13484: Shadrach was the new name given to Hananiah in the book of Daniel. Emil G. Hirsch and M. Seligsohn wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on the name. The chief of the eunuchs at Babylon's court assigned it. Scholars have offered many views on what the name means. The likeliest, following Delitzsch, reads it as Babylonian for the command of the moon god.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simeon-b-akashy: Simeon ben Akashyah was a tanna, or early rabbinic teacher, of the second generation. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. Only one of his homiletic sentences has been preserved for readers. It explains verses in Job about wisdom and old age. Untaught people lose intelligence as they grow old, he taught. Scholars, by contrast, grow more intelligent with advancing years. His saying stands in the tractate Kinnim of the Mishnah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sippurim-ma-asi:
Hasidic sippurim are stories told by or about the Hasidic rebbes. Joseph Jacobs and Judah David Eisenstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. The rebbes were also called zaddikim or holy men. These tales differ from tales of other heroes or saints. They were never meant as mere stories for amusement.

One class of tales was invented as parables by the rebbes. They taught Hasidic ideas through those invented tales. The other class told true-seeming events from a rebbe's life. Disciples told them in praise of their masters. Telling such tales counted as a merit, like study itself. Rebbes often left the moral unsaid for hearers to debate.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solomon-myer-13:
Myer Solomon founded the St Alban's Place Synagogue in London. Joseph Jacobs and Israel Cohen wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born in the last quarter of the eighteenth century. In 1824 he became head of the Denmark Court Congregation. He helped found the new Western Synagogue, opened in 1826.

Solomon often led services as preacher and as hazzan. He was also a competent mohel and shohet in practice. He wrote two scrolls of the Law for his synagogue. His bric-a-brac store stood at 119 Pall Mall in London. His sukkah there was open to all congregation members. He preached a funeral sermon on the death of George IV.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tabernacle-1418:
The Tabernacle was Israel's portable sanctuary in the wilderness. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Eduard König wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. It served during the wanderings and early settlement years. Exodus chapters 26 and 36 describe its building. A frame of acacia wood formed its shell.

Each board stood ten cubits long in the frame. Twenty boards lined the north and south sides. Six more closed the western end of the structure. Silver sockets held the boards by their tenons. Five cross-bars kept each side from falling apart. The eastern side stayed open as the entrance. Inner curtains gave the tent its true form. Exodus calls them the dwelling of the Lord itself. The entry rebuilds the shrine board by board from scripture.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-teheran-14284:
Teheran is the capital and trade center of Persia. Joseph Jacobs and A. V. W. Jackson wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. It sits about seventy miles south of the Caspian Sea. The city grew chiefly in the late 1800s. Shah Nasir al-Din's reign drove that growth.

Teheran's own antiquity is not very great. Its existence barely traces past the twelfth century. It slowly replaced the ancient city of Rai nearby. Rai is now a mass of ruins in its suburbs. That older city was Media's ancient metropolis. The Apocrypha calls it Rages, and the Avesta Ragha. A Jewish trader's report names it an emporium early. The shah's court physician, J. E. Polak, was a Jew. The entry layers a young capital over an old one.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-traubel-horace-:
Horace Traubel was an American editor bound closely to Walt Whitman's legacy. Cyrus Adler and Frank H. Vizetelly wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Traubel was born at Camden, New Jersey, in 1858. Public schools there gave him his education. In 1892 he became a literary executor of Whitman.

He shared that trust with two co-executors. Together they edited a memorial volume on the poet. Traubel wrote many essays on Whitman for the press. He founded Philadelphia's Contemporary Club in 1886. He edited The Conservator from 1890 to 1905. He also led The Artsman, founded in 1903. The International Walt Whitman Fellowship made him its secretary. Few editors served one poet so fully.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-verveer-elchana:
Elchanan Verveer was a Dutch painter and engraver. He was born at The Hague on April 19, 1826. Isidore Singer and Frank Cramer wrote this short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His brother Samuel taught him art, as did H. F. C. Ten Kate. In 1845 he went to Brussels to work.

At Brussels, Verveer engraved pictures for a famous novel. The book was Eugène Sue's Le Juif Errant. Back home, he drew for a Dutch magazine series. His paintings include The First Pipe and Winter. Both hang in the museum at Rotterdam. Other works belong to The Hague's city museum. He held honors from two royal orders.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-weyl-walter-edw:
Walter Edward Weyl was an American economist. Cyrus Adler and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Philadelphia on March 11, 1874. He attended that city's public schools. The University of Pennsylvania gave him two degrees. He took his doctorate there in 1897.

Weyl studied further at Halle, Berlin, and Paris. He has published articles on railway labor. Passenger traffic on railways is another of his topics. He takes a deep interest in organized labor. He has worked with United States labor bureaus. He also serves federal statistics offices in Washington.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wolfenstein-mar:
Martha Wolfenstein (born 1869) was an American writer of tales of Jewish life. Cyrus Adler and Frederick T. Haneman wrote her entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in Prussia, she came to the United States as a small child. Her family settled in Cleveland, Ohio. She was schooled in the public schools of that city.

Her short tales ran in near all the top Jewish journals. Big magazines took her work as well. Two tales named in the entry ran in Lippincott's Magazine. A third tale ran in the Outlook. In 1901 a Jewish press in America brought out her book. Its name is Idyls of the Gass. A German form of the book ran in a Vienna paper. The entry marks her as a voice for Jewish street life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zox-ephraim-lam:
Ephraim Lamen Zox was a communal worker and lawmaker in Melbourne, Australia. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in London in 1837, he died on October 23, 1899. He reached Melbourne at thirteen and worked at gold digging, auctioneering, clothing, and finance.

Zox stood near the center of almost every Melbourne charity. He served his Hebrew congregation as treasurer, president, and trustee. He backed the Jewish Philanthropic Society and led the local Anglo-Jewish Association branch. He also cared deeply for the Discharged Prisoners' Aid Society. In politics he held an East Melbourne seat in the legislature for twenty-one years and chaired the Charities Commission.
johannis-segeri-weidenfeld-de-secretis-a:
Johann Seger Weidenfeld's De Secretis Adeptorum is a Latin work in four books, printed at London in 1684. Its subject is the use of the spirit of wine of Lully, the old alchemical writer. Weidenfeld calls it a practical work. He built it by gathering the adepts, old and new, and fitting their clashing views together.

The title page promises help for beginners learning to judge preparations. Readers would learn to tell true vegetable, animal, and mineral preparations from false and sophistical ones. That skill served both medicine and metal work. It also guarded purses against wandering deceivers and imaginary processes. The book shows practical alchemy trying to sort real craft from fraud.
jussieu-rapport-magnetisme-animal-1784:
Antoine Laurent de Jussieu, a noted botanist, served on the royal commission that judged animal magnetism in 1784. He alone refused to sign the majority report. His separate report of that year is a formal dissent, careful and calm in tone.

Jussieu granted that much of mesmerism was imagination. Yet he thought the trials left room for some unseen influence that science could not yet explain. His dissent kept a door ajar while his colleagues shut theirs. It stands as the lone minority voice in the famous debunking. Doubt, stated with dignity, gives this short report its lasting interest for readers of the affair.
kabbala-denudata-knorr-tome2-1684:
Knorr von Rosenroth issued the second tome of the Kabbala Denudata at Frankfurt in 1684, seven years after the first. The text is in Latin, like its predecessor. Tome two adds commentaries, further Zoharic treatises, and the Siphra de Zeniutha, the Book of Concealment, with the commentary ascribed to Luria's school.

The Siphra, a brief and dense Zoharic text on the divine kings before creation, anchors this volume's mysticism. Around it Knorr sets dissertations that argue Kabbalah and Christian doctrine toward each other. No English translation exists in the public domain. Together the two tomes formed early modern Europe's library of Kabbalah in one place. Christian Kabbalists cited Knorr for two centuries after.
kalpa-sutra-jacobi-1884:
The Kalpa Sutra of Bhadrabahu is a Jain scripture, here in Hermann Jacobi's translation from Prakrit. It forms part of the Jaina Sutras in volume twenty-two of the Sacred Books of the East. Oxford's Clarendon Press issued the volume in 1884, under F. Max Muller's editorship. The same volume holds the Akaranga Sutra, the other great Jain text in this set.

The Kalpa Sutra records the lives of the Jinas, the Jain teachers who conquered rebirth. It tells of their births, renunciations, and deaths in set, solemn patterns. Jacobi's translation made this canonical text readable for Western scholars of religion. The edition preserves a scripture central to the Svetambara Jain tradition, in the form English readers first studied it.
lang-custom-and-myth-1884:
Andrew Lang wrote these 1884 essays to defend a bold claim: that Greek and other classic myths began as the wild tales of early peoples. Against scholars who saw myth as high poetry spoiled, Lang saw survivals of savage custom and thought.

Essay by essay he takes up totemism, the bull-roarer used in secret rites, and the cruel or absurd elements in the tales of gods. He argues these oddities make sense once their origin in early ritual is seen. Lang wrote with wit and wide reading across folklore and anthropology. The book helped found the anthropological study of myth.
lanier-poems-1884:
Sidney Lanier died of tuberculosis in 1881 at thirty-nine, worn out by poverty and the illness he had carried since his Civil War prison days. His widow gathered his poems, and the posthumous collection appeared in 1884. It made the South's poet-flautist famous after his death.

The Marshes of Glynn, his greatest poem, moves through Georgia's salt marshes at sundown into a meditation on faith and freedom. The Symphony gives each instrument of the orchestra a voice against commerce and greed. Sunrise, Corn, and other lyrics show his musical line at full stretch. Lanier's verse sings even when it argues. The 1884 volume fixed his place as the leading Southern poet of his century.
life-of-johnson-volume-4-1780-1784:
Boswell's fourth volume carries Johnson from 1780 to December 1784. Appendices include Miss Burney's account of Johnson's last days. Notes on Johnson's will and Parr's epitaph also appear. The Ivy-Lane and Essex Head clubs receive their own appendices.

Boswell opens disappointed at missing Johnson's company that year. He compensates with sayings collected by his friend Langton. Langton rarely wrote the sayings down when he heard them. His memory, Boswell says, treasured a Herculaneum of Johnsonian wit. Altercations with Dean Barnard and Priestley fill two more appendices. Herculaneum's buried treasures supply Boswell's comparison for Langton's store.
lotze-logic-bosanquet-1884:
Hermann Lotze, a German doctor turned philosopher, built his System of Philosophy in three parts, and the Logic came first. Bernard Bosanquet translated it for the Clarendon Press in 1884. The three books of the Logic treat thought, investigation, and knowledge in turn.

Lotze starts with the forms of thinking, concepts, judgments, and syllogisms, then asks how inquiry in law, history, and science really works. He ends with the question of what knowledge is and what it is worth. British idealists and the first analytic philosophers both learned from Lotze. Bosanquet's version was the form in which the English world read him.
lotze-metaphysic-bosanquet-1884:
The Metaphysic is the second part of Hermann Lotze's System of Philosophy, in Bernard Bosanquet's English version of 1884. Its three books treat ontology, cosmology, and psychology: what there is, how the world hangs together, and what the soul is. Lotze wrote as a trained doctor who refused to cut mind off from nature.

He argues that the mechanical order of science is real but not the whole truth: things act as they do because of what they are for. That blend of science and purpose made Lotze a bridge between German idealism and the new logic of his age. Bosanquet's translation spread his system through the English universities.
lotze-outlines-metaphysic-1884:
Ladd's English version of Lotze's Outlines of Metaphysic appeared in 1884. Lotze, the Göttingen philosopher, trained first as a physician, and he brought a scientist's respect for fact into the deepest questions of philosophy. Metaphysics, the study of what reality is at bottom, was the heart of his teaching.

The Outlines seek a middle way between a world of mere matter and a world of mere mind. Lotze argues that mechanism explains how things happen without exhausting what they mean, leaving room for spirit and purpose. The argument is compressed, since the book began as lectures, but the balance is the point. Readers have praised it as the most humane account of first principles the 1800s produced. In Ladd's clear translation, it served a generation of students in America and Britain.
mars-exploration-remote-viewing-1984:
A remote viewer sat in a plain room in 1984 and described Mars as it was a million years past. The session transcript of May 22, 1984, freed from the STAR GATE files, is that record in full. A monitor fed the viewer map coordinates and took the words down as they came.

The viewer tells of pyramids, a dying race, storms of dust, and a world in its last age. The tale reads like science fiction stamped and filed as spy work. It is the most famed single session of the whole program. No file shows the remote viewing faith at full stretch like this one.
memoir-correspondence-and-miscellanies-f:
Volume four of Jefferson's papers opens at Monticello in 1803. Thomas Jefferson Randolph edited the set from the 1829 issue. Letter one goes to Levi Lincoln on August 30, 1803.

Jefferson asks Lincoln to speak for him in Boston, in soft terms. He will not let his own birthday be used for public honors, he says. Then he turns to a change in the Constitution for Louisiana. He would give Congress the same powers there as in the rest of the Union. A few named bars would stand as the sole bars to that power. State craft and private honor mix in a few short pages.
moody-prevailing-prayer-1884:
Dwight Moody was the great American revival preacher of the late nineteenth century, founder of schools and mass meetings across two continents. His Prevailing Prayer: What Hinders It, published in 1884, asks why so many prayers seem to go unanswered. It became the most widely read evangelical tract on prayer of its era.

Moody lists the hindrances plainly: cherished sin, cold hearts, haste, doubt, and prayers that ask only for selfish ends. He mixes short Bible lessons with stories from his own campaigns and converts. Revival-minded readers used the book as a checklist for clearing the way to answered prayer.
nadaillac-prehistoric-america-1884:
The Marquis de Nadaillac, a French scholar of prehistory, published Pre-historic America in 1884. He gathered what Europeans then knew about the deep past of the New World. Mound-builders, cliff-dwellers, and cave finds all pass through his survey.

Nadaillac weighs how long people had lived in the Americas and what they left behind. He writes as a well-read Victorian synthesizer rather than a field digger. Much has been superseded by later archaeology. The book remains a clear window onto nineteenth-century thinking about America's first peoples. French readers received here one of the first broad surveys of the subject.
openalex-w1999835984:
Holger Unger, Maria Ome-Kaius, Regina Wangnapi and colleagues ran a pregnancy trial in Papua New Guinea. Their paper appeared in BMC Medicine in 2015. Low birth weight is common there. Malaria and infections of the reproductive tract both play a role.

The trial randomly assigned pregnant women to one of two drug plans. One group got a malaria drug pair plus an antibiotic each month. The other group got standard care given once. Babies in the first group had lower rates of low birth weight. Early births were also less common in that group. The treatment was found safe in the trial. The authors noted that many women were lost to follow-up.
openalex-w2011607584:
Christian Bunn, Peter Laderach, Oriana Ovalle Rivera and Dieter Kirschke profiled climate risks for world coffee. Their paper appeared in Climatic Change in 2015. Coffee is highly sensitive to climate change. Coffee plants live for about thirty years. So future climate already matters for planting choices today.

The team used machine learning with records of coffee growing sites. They modelled where Arabica and Robusta coffee could grow. Hotter weather may cut Arabica yields. Robusta may suffer from more uneven temperatures within seasons. Across scenarios, land suited to coffee shrank by about half. Low places and low latitudes faced the worst losses. Higher places fared less badly, but still lost ground.
openalex-w2106069784:
Juliana Quintero, Helena Brochero, Pablo Manrique-Saide and colleagues studied dengue mosquito breeding in five Latin American cities. Their paper appeared in BMC Infectious Diseases in 2014. Dengue is a growing problem across the region. Control programmes need cheaper ways to cut mosquito numbers. Breeding sites differ between neighbourhoods and seasons.

Each city survey covered twenty selected clusters. Homes, businesses and public spaces were inspected. Teams counted mosquito young in water containers. Surveys ran in both dry and wet seasons. Household and background surveys ran alongside. Most clusters were low-to-middle income urban areas. Breeding patterns tied to water storage and services. Targeted clean-up can focus on the riskiest settings.
openalex-w2119349084:
Edgardo Rivera and Henry Gomez reviewed treatment options when breast cancer resists chemotherapy. Their paper appeared in Breast Cancer Research in 2010. About a third of early breast cancers later spread. Standard drugs often work only briefly then. Tumours develop resistance to the drugs used.

First-line treatment usually uses anthracyclines or taxanes. Responses there last only months in many cases. After resistance, several backup drugs are available. Response rates in that setting are low. The review focuses on ixabepilone, a newer option. It was designed to evade common resistance routes. Trial results for taxane-resistant disease are summarised. Choosing the sequence of drugs remains a key challenge.
openalex-w2138504084:
Debra Wunch, Geoff Toon, Paul Wennberg, and colleagues published this study in Atmospheric Measurement Techniques in 2010. They calibrated the Total Carbon Column Observing Network, a worldwide set of ground instruments that track greenhouse gases. The network reads sunlight passing through the air, but its readings must be tied to official measurement scales.

Aircraft carrying trusted instruments flew profiles above four network stations in 2008 and 2009. The team compared those flights with earlier calibration checks from 2004 and 2006. They found that a single global calibration factor for each gas fits the network data within its error range. That result lets stations worldwide report on one shared scale.
openalex-w2593074884:
Roman Thibeaux, Sophie Geroult, and Claire Benezech, with colleagues from Institut Pasteur in New Caledonia, published this 2017 study in PLOS Neglected Tropical Diseases. The metadata record leaves its title and author fields blank; the sample itself supplies both. The team hunted for the environmental source of leptospirosis, a disease people catch from contaminated surroundings. Infection comes from indirect exposure to the bacteria waiting in the environment.

Leptospirosis is described in the paper as an important re-emerging disease affecting humans worldwide. Where its bacteria wait between outbreaks was the open question. The study's title reports its central finding: the bacteria stay viable for a long time in river soils. Durable survival there points to a lasting environmental reservoir. Knowing where the bacteria persist helps explain exposure risk around rivers. It also gives health teams a clearer target for warnings and prevention work.
openalex-w2886636784:
Mónica Rosenblueth, Ernesto Ormeño-Orrillo, and Aline López-López lead this 2018 review in Frontiers in Microbiology, on nitrogen fixation in cereals. Maize, rice, wheat, and sorghum feed most of humanity. Their yields hinge on nitrogen, which industrial fertilizer supplies at great cost and pollution. Overuse is already widespread, yet projected food needs for 2050 demand still more production.

Some bacteria fix nitrogen from the air, and legumes famously host them in root nodules. Cereals lack that partnership, but they do host nitrogen-fixing microbes on and inside their tissues. The review surveys those diazotrophs and endophytes in cereal systems. It asks how much nitrogen they realistically contribute today. Engineering stronger fixation into cereals could cut fertilizer dependence substantially. The authors weigh the biology's promise against its current limits. The stakes are feeding billions with less environmental damage.
openalex-w3000301584:
Stuart Tangye, Waleed Al-Herz, Aziz Bousfiha, and colleagues report this updated classification in the Journal of Clinical Immunology in 2020. It comes from the expert committee of the International Union of Immunological Societies. The subject is inborn errors of immunity, inherited defects that leave the body open to infection.

The update documents four hundred thirty such disorders, with their key clinical and lab features. Sixty-four gene defects were new since the prior update two years earlier, or were confirmed and expanded in that time. Fast gene sequencing keeps speeding these discoveries and broadening known conditions. The authors note that the advances now allow therapies aimed at a patient's exact gene defect.
openalex-w3033499384:
Cristina Taddei, Bin Zhou, Honor Bixby, and colleagues of the NCD Risk Factor Collaboration published this study in Nature in 2020. It redraws the world map of unhealthy cholesterol. High blood cholesterol is usually pictured as a problem of wealthy western countries.

An earlier global analysis tracked total cholesterol up to 2008 but skipped key fractions, such as protective HDL and harmful non-HDL cholesterol. Diets, body weight, alcohol use, and drug treatment have all shifted since then, unevenly across the world. The team pooled fresh data to estimate the fractions country by country. Their results show the center of the cholesterol problem moving, with high levels now rising fastest outside the traditional western core.
openalex-w3165898284: T. M. C. Abbott, M. Aguena, Alex Alarcon, and the Dark Energy Survey team published these results in Physical Review D in 2022. The paper reports year three findings on the cosmos. It draws on how galaxies cluster and how gravity bends their light, an effect called weak lensing. The preserved sample holds only the title page and author list, with no readable abstract or results.
openalex-w7135014884: Curing hepatitis C is now possible, but metabolism can get in the way. This study tracked metabolic syndrome risk against adherence to direct-acting antiviral therapy over six months. The authors examined the two-way relationship. A hepatology study of treating the virus while the body complicates.
openalex-w7168300184: Batteries and electrolysis matter more every year, and this Japanese-language paper rethinks how we study them. The authors developed new analytical methods for electrode reactions that drop the old idealized assumptions. They aimed at real-world conditions like uneven pH. An electrochemistry methods paper for the energy age.
openalex-w7204176384: Bentham's panopticon was a prison of total watchfulness; today's workplace is its digital heir. This law article studies the new digital panopticon, constant monitoring of workers through software, and the challenges it poses to labor law. The authors trace the idea from Bentham through Foucault to the modern office. A sharp study of surveillance sold as productivity.
openalex-w7204997184: Dyslexia makes reading a daily struggle, and teachers need strategies, not just sympathy. This article examines how dyslexia affects teaching and learning, then lays out pedagogical approaches that help educators and schools support dyslexic students in the classroom. The authors focus on what actually works day to day. A practical guide that treats dyslexia as a teaching challenge with answers, not a verdict on a child's ability.
openalex-w7206159784: Medical school is famously grueling, long hours and early contact with suffering, and students pay a mental price. This study measures how common anxiety and depression are among medical students and what drives them. The authors frame the findings as a public-health concern inside the profession that treats everyone else's health. The paper adds hard numbers to a problem medical schools can no longer treat as background noise.
openalex-w7214972884: Zeolites are crystal sponges with molecule-sized holes, and tuning them tunes chemistry. This paper tells how iron was put back into zeolite beta and flaws were healed after the build. The team polished the active spots. A stuff-chemistry study of perfecting holey crystals.
owen-antiquity-of-man-1884:
Richard Owen, the great English master of bones, gave his late word on man's age in this book of 1884. Its spark was a human frame dug from the Thames bank at Tilbury. Owen was old, and his fame as the chief judge of such finds stood high.

He sets out the frame bone by bone and weighs how old it may be. His word counts, since for years his no had held back claims of deep age for man. The book is the old master's last word on a theme that had moved past him.
parkman-montcalm-wolfe-1884:
Francis Parkman published Montcalm and Wolfe in 1884, the climax of his series France and England in North America. The book covers the Seven Years' War in America, ending at Quebec in 1759. Generals Montcalm and Wolfe, French and British, both die in the final battle. The fate of a continent turns on their contest.

Parkman worked from archives in France, Britain, and America for decades. Forests, forts, and snowbound campaigns fill his vivid narrative. His sympathies favor British order, yet he honors Montcalm's courage. The two volumes of this title close a life's work. Parkman remains America's great romantic historian of the frontier wars.
peucer-les-devins-french-1584:
Peucer's commentary on divination reached French readers as Les devins in 1584. The translation spreads his fifteen books on the principal kinds of divination across the French-reading world. It is the vernacular version of the Lutheran demonology of foretelling, made for readers beyond the universities.

Every sort of prediction gets sorted, weighed, and judged by Lutheran lights. Astrology, dreams, omens, and lots each face the same question: lawful sign or devil's art? The French dress gave pastors and magistrates a handbook in their own tongue. Translations like this one carried Reformed doctrine into daily practice. Peucer's fences around the future stood, in French, for a generation of readers.
plos-pbio-0020384:
James A. Fraser, Stephanie Diezmann, Ryan L. Subaran, and their team compared sex-determining regions across kingdoms in PLOS Biology in 2004. In animals, sex chromosomes set sex. In some fungi, a mating-type region does a like job. The authors found these systems share surprising traits, a case of convergent evolution.

Both kinds of regions limit shuffling with their partner region, collect repeat DNA, and degrade over time. Those parallels arose on their own in each kingdom. They suggest any genome region that stops shuffling follows the same path of decay. The insight helps read the future of young sex chromosomes, including our own aging Y. It also guides work on fungal mating, which matters for crop disease.
plos-pone-0000184:
Jan A. van Gils, Vincent J. Munster, Reinder Radersma, and colleagues published this bird flu study in PLOS ONE in 2007. Swans infected with low-pathogenic avian influenza A virus, a mild strain, were tracked during migration. The authors found the infection hampered the birds' foraging and their migratory performance.

Even a mild infection can tax a bird that must feed heavily and fly far. The study quantifies that cost in wild swans. The results matter for predicting how bird flu moves with migration, since sick birds travel differently. They also reveal the hidden toll of low-grade infections in wild animals.
plos-pone-0000284:
Rajesh Kumar, Jing Qiu, Trupti Joshi, and colleagues published this rice genomics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It presents single feature polymorphism discovery in rice, a way to find DNA differences between rice varieties using microarray features rather than full sequencing. Each differing feature marks a spot where the varieties' genomes diverge.

Rice feeds half the world, and breeders need cheap markers to track traits. Polymorphism discovery by microarray offers markers at a fraction of sequencing cost. The authors demonstrate the approach in rice, adding tools for breeding programs that work with limited budgets.
plos-pone-0000384:
Yasuhiro Kitazoe and colleagues revisited one of evolution's dating disputes in PLOS ONE in 2007: when placental mammals first arose. Fossils and DNA-based clocks have given different answers, with DNA studies often pointing to a much older origin. The team set out to estimate the timing in a more robust way.

Molecular clocks convert DNA differences into years, but they are sensitive to how the math is done. By making the time estimates sturdier, the authors argue the two views can be reconciled. The paper matters because the age of the mammal family tree shapes how scientists explain the rise of mammals alongside, and after, the dinosaurs.
plos-pone-0000484:
Andreas Sundquist and colleagues reviewed a turning point in DNA sequencing, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. New high-throughput, short-read technologies could sequence DNA far faster and cheaper than older methods, but they produced millions of short fragments. The paper covered whole-genome sequencing and assembly with these technologies, the puzzle of stitching short reads into a genome.

Assembly is the hard part: short reads repeat and overlap ambiguously. Getting it right decides whether cheap sequencing is also trustworthy. Papers from this period mark a turning point. Genomics shifted from a few flagship projects to a routine tool. Any lab could now aim it at any organism.
plos-pone-0000584:
Leonid I. Brodsky and colleagues designed a method to find genes that matter in antiviral defense without prior guesses, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Their novel unsupervised method identifies genes important in the anti-viral response, and they applied it to patients receiving interferon and ribavirin for hepatitis C.

Unsupervised means the method finds its own patterns in the data rather than testing a preset list. In hepatitis C, only some patients respond to interferon therapy, and the gene signature of response was unclear. A method that surfaces the important genes could predict who benefits and reveal new drug targets.
plos-pone-0000684:
Gernot G. Supp, Alois Schlögl, Nelson Trujillo-Barreto and colleagues followed information flow in the brain during object recognition, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Familiar, meaningful objects reliably boost induced gamma-band responses in EEG recordings. These fast oscillations, above 30 hertz, appear at distinct scalp locations. They are thought to mark local cell groups forming on the fly.

The team analyzed the responses in the brain's source space, estimating where signals originate. Directed flow shows which areas drive which others as an object is recognized. That direction matters: recognition is not one area lighting up, but a conversation. Mapping its direction helps connect EEG patterns to real brain circuits.
plos-pone-0000784:
Brian J. North and Eric Verdin tracked a longevity-linked enzyme as it shuttles in and out of the nucleus, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Human SIRT2 is an NAD+-dependent protein deacetylase residing mainly in the cytoplasm, where it removes acetyl tags from tubulin, the cytoskeleton protein. They report SIRT2 keeps that cytoplasmic address during interphase by active nuclear export, in a manner dependent on the export machine Crm1.

During mitosis, its localization changes. An enzyme that moves between compartments can do different jobs at different cell stages. Sirtuins attract attention for roles in aging and metabolism, so mapping where SIRT2 sits, and when, is groundwork for that larger story.
plos-pone-0000884:
Janet Young, Hang Waters, Cora Dong and colleagues traced the decay of a smell gene across primate history, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The sense of smell rests on several subsystems, each tuned to its own set of chemical cues. In the main smell tissue, at least three types of sensing cells can be told apart by the genes they use.

One of those genes, for an enzyme called guanylyl cyclase D, has been breaking down in primates. The team followed that decline across species. A gene that fades this way tells a story about changing needs: as sight grew stronger in primates, some parts of smell may have mattered less.
plos-pone-0000984:
Sven Letourneau, Eung-Jun Im, Tumelo Mashishi and colleagues designed a universal HIV vaccine candidate and tested it before clinic, in PLOS ONE in 2007. HIV varies enormously, and that diversity can sink any single vaccine. A design that covers many variants at once was badly needed.

The team built an immunogen called HIV CONSV from the parts of the virus that change least across strains. Aiming T cells at conserved regions could give protection no matter which variant a person meets. Their paper covers the design and pre-clinical evaluation. Universal thinking, rather than strain chasing, is the paper's main bet.
plos-pone-0001084:
Tadashi Iwami, Osamu Kishida and Kinya Nishimura studied how salamander larvae offset the costs of a defense, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Animals often change several traits at once when danger looms, a package called phenotypic plasticity. The package arises from tangled ecological and physiological causes.

In Hynobius salamander larvae, an inducible defense brings costs. The team distinguish direct and indirect routes by which a compensatory phenotype develops and eases those costs. Compensation matters because a defense that bankrupts growth is no defense at all. Their analysis shows how trait packages are assembled, not just switched on.
