Pond predators made this system a sharp test case.
plos-pone-0001184:
Most CpG sites in mammal genomes carry methylation marks, but the CpG-rich stretches called CpG islands usually resist them, and nobody fully knows why. Shicai Fan, Fang Fang, and Xuegong Zhang searched the human genome for a clue, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They examined the boundaries of methylation-resistant CpG islands.

The authors found that binding sites for putative zinc finger proteins are over-represented at those boundaries. Zinc finger proteins grip DNA at specific sequences, so their clustering at island edges hints at a protective fence. Their result gives the methylation-resistance puzzle a concrete suspect to test.
plos-pone-0001284:
San Francisco has the highest tuberculosis rate in the United States, with recurrent outbreaks among homeless and marginally housed people. Brandon Higgs and colleagues studied how to detect outbreaks early in that population, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Outbreak detection trades off spatial resolution against temporal scale: finer geography can mean slower signals.

The authors analyze those trade-offs, building on syndromic surveillance work that uses patients' exact coordinates. For a disease that spreads in shelters and single-room hotels, knowing where to draw the detection boundary matters. Their study aims at earlier warnings for a hard-to-reach population.
plos-pone-0001384:
Francesc Garcia-Gonzalo and Juan Carlos Izpisúa Belmonte wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on human embryo stem cells. These cells can grow into many cell types, so they hold great hope for future cures. But labs still lack a clean, fixed food mix to grow them well. The pair studied fats bound to a common blood protein.

The authors show that these fats help the stem cells renew themselves and stay in their early state. That is a step toward defined growth mixes with no unknown parts. Such mixes are key for safe use in clinics. The work helps move stem cell growth from art toward a set, shared method.
plos-pone-0001484:
Hiroki Nakagawa and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a shared gene switch in mammals. About one in ten gene pairs sit head to head on facing DNA strands. A shared switch drives both genes, which often work as a pair. The team studied one such region, kept across species, between two named genes.

They mapped what turns this shared switch on and off. Kept regions like this tend to hold core control logic. The work shows how two genes can be tuned as a unit. That tuning helps cells keep paired jobs in step, a theme that recurs across the genome.
plos-pone-0001584:
Elizabeth Dinsdale and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on microbes at four coral atolls. Microbes run much of the life of both sound and worn coral reefs. The team sampled four atolls in the Northern Line Islands, from a tiny empty one to peopled ones. They mixed gene reads, scope work, cultures, and water tests.

Microbe mixes shifted sharply from the pristine atoll to the used ones. Human use left a clear mark in the unseen life of the reef. Those marks may warn of reef decline before coral loss shows. The set forms a base line for reef health work.
plos-pone-0001684:
Jianwei Jiao, Akira Nakajima, William G. M. Janssen, and their co-authors linked one brain receptor to how practice improves movement, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Motor skills are learned by training, and genes and environment are thought to interact in that learning. The receptor is NR2B, a part of the NMDA receptor, a key molecular switch for learning in the brain.

Working with cerebellar granule cells, the team reports that NR2B expression specifically helps motor training improve motor learning. The full text gives the training tests, the brain measurements, and the comparison across animal groups. The cerebellum fine-tunes movement. A receptor there that gates the benefit of practice helps explain why the same training yields different gains in different learners.
plos-pone-0001784:
Anilkumar Pillai studied brain tissue from people with schizophrenia and bipolar disorder in a 2008 PLOS ONE research report. Current theories blame altered brain plasticity: reduced nerve cell growth and migration, slow myelin growth, and abnormal synapse reshaping. BDNF, a growth factor for neurons, had shown changes in schizophrenia.

Pillai measured Sprouty2, a regulator of growth factor signaling, in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and found lower Sprouty2 levels in both, tied to BDNF levels. The full text gives the tissue readings and the strength of the link. Linked changes in a growth factor and its brake support the plasticity theory. They also mark a pathway that treatments might aim to restore.
plos-pone-0001884:
Sara Batelli and colleagues studied two proteins tied to Parkinson disease in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. In this illness, brain cells die off slowly, and clumps of a protein called alpha-synuclein are a hallmark. A second protein, DJ-1, is linked to rare family forms of the disease, but its exact job was unclear.

The team used a cell model of oxidative stress, the kind of chemical strain thought to harm brain cells in this disease. They report that DJ-1 shifts the clumping state of alpha-synuclein, and that a heat-shock helper protein, HSP70, plays a part. The link gives drug work a fresh target: keep the clumps from forming.
plos-pone-0001984:
Charles Shelburne and co-authors found a blood sign that predicts gum health in at-risk patients, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Periodontitis is a chronic gum infection tied to the bacterium Porphyromonas gingivalis. Helper proteins called chaperones keep other proteins in shape and also act as strong immune targets.

The team measured antibodies in blood against one chaperone from this bacterium, called HtpG. As the title states, those antibodies predict health in patients prone to gum disease. A blood marker that flags who stays healthy could guide how often at-risk patients need care, and which ones need more.
plos-pone-0002084:
Laurent Bogdanik and co-authors studied a muscle protein at the fly's nerve-muscle junction, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The dystrophin-glycoprotein complex links a muscle fiber's inner frame to the matrix outside it, guarding the fiber from strain. One part, dystroglycan, sits in that complex in muscle.

The team asked what dystroglycan does at the synapse itself, in the fruit fly. As the title states, muscle dystroglycan organizes the postsynapse and regulates how much neurotransmitter the nerve side releases. A protein known for muscle strength thus also tunes talk between nerve and muscle.
plos-pone-0002184:
Kristen Barthel and Xuedong Liu reported a surprise hiding place for a gene switch, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The human genome holds only about 25,000 genes, far too few to explain human complexity on their own. Much of the answer lies in how genes are regulated, and switches called enhancers are a big part of that control.

Enhancers are usually found outside genes. The team found one inside the coding region of ADAMTS5, a gene whose protein cuts other proteins outside cells. A switch buried in a gene's own text blurs the line between code and control. The find adds to the case that gene regulation is layered and dense.
plos-pone-0002284:
Mao Chen and co-authors reviewed whether Bt crop plants harm the insects that attack crop pests, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Transgenic plants that make crystal toxins from the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis kill target pests, and their ecological safety is still debated. Much of that debate centers on non-target organisms, above all the parasitoid wasps that naturally control pests.

The authors critically assessed the studies on Bt plants and parasitoids. Parasitoids can meet the toxin through the hosts they live in, so effects may be indirect. A clear-eyed review helps regulators weigh real risks to the farmer's smallest allies against the gains of pest control.
plos-pone-0002384:
Research by Greene and co-authors came out in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Justin M. Greene, Benjamin J. Burwitz, Alex J. Blasky, and others. Its subject is allogeneic Lymphocytes Persist and Traffic in Feral MHC-Matched Mauritian Cynomolgus Macaques. Thus far, live attenuated SIV has been the most successful method for vaccinating macaques against pathogenic SIV challenge; however.

Each part of the study builds on the part before it, in the order the team carried it out. In short, the piece gives a clear, short route into a field that can seem hard to enter from the outside.
plos-pone-0002484:
Jiang and colleagues set out their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. The author list runs from Hongying Jiang, Jigar J. Patel, Ming Yi, and others. Its subject is genome-Wide Compensatory Changes Accompany Drug- Selected Mutations in the Plasmodium falciparum crt Gene. Mutations in PfCRT (Plasmodium falciparum chloroquine-resistant transporter), particularly the substitution at amino acid position 76, confer chloroquine (CQ) resistance in P.

What the team did, and why they did it that way, forms the core of the piece. For science readers, it shows how a small, well framed question can add a firm piece of knowledge to a much larger field.
plos-pone-0002584:
Led by Medina, a team of researchers published its study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Reinhold J. Medina, Christina L. O'Neill, Adrian B. Devine, and others. Its subject is the Pleiotropic Effects of Simvastatin on Retinal Microvascular Endothelium Has Important Implications for Ischaemic Retinopathies. Current guidelines encourage the use of statins to reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease in diabetic patients.

Each part of the study builds on the part before it, in the order the team carried it out. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time.
plos-pone-0002684:
Work by Marc-André Prost and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was implication of new WHO growth standards on identification of risk factors and estimated prevalence of malnutrition in rural malawian infants. Authorship is credited in the record to Marc-André Prost and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. The World Health Organization (WHO) released new Child Growth Standards in 2006 to replace the current National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) growth reference. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002784:
Work by Steven D. Wiederman and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was a model for the detection of moving targets in visual clutter inspired by insect physiology. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Steven D. Wiederman, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. We present a computational model for target discrimination based on intracellular recordings from neurons in the fly visual system. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002884:
Tali Sharot, Matthew L. Davidson, Meredith M. Carson and co-authors tested in 2008 whether eye movements can predict rich recall. A past item can feel vividly remembered, with its setting brought back to mind, or merely familiar. Earlier work hinted that more focus at first sight leads to the richer kind of memory later.

In the PLOS ONE study, how the eyes moved while people first saw items was tracked against later reports of remembering versus just knowing. The title states that eye movements did predict the richer experience. Memory researchers get a simple outward sign of how deep a memory is being laid down.
plos-pone-0002984:
Anders Løbner-Olesen, Monika Slominska-Wojewodzka, Flemming Hansen and co-authors profiled E. coli cells blocked from starting DNA copying in 2008. Starting chromosome replication needs the proteins DnaA and DnaC, and faulty versions are often used to synchronize cell populations. The team focused on the dnaC mutant.

Using DNA microarrays, they measured RNA levels in cells unable to initiate replication. Inactivation of DnaC induced the SOS response, the cell's DNA damage alarm, plus genes for building nucleotides. Published in PLOS ONE, the profile shows how tightly copying, damage control, and raw materials are linked. Anyone can read the full text free of charge through the journal's open access site.
plos-pone-0003084:
Manuel Gonçalves, Maarten Holkers, Gijsbert van Nierop and co-authors targeted large DNA inserts to chosen chromosome sites in 2008. A prominent gene therapy goal is vehicles that integrate added DNA at specific loci. That precision would prevent insertional cancer risk and provide long-term expression of the therapeutic gene.

Their system uses a fiber-modified, high-capacity adenovirus-based vector to insert large DNA into the human genome at targeted spots. Published in PLOS ONE, capacity plus targeting is a rare pairing. It speaks to therapies needing whole genes, not just small patches. The full text gives methods, results, and references for readers who want to check each step.
plos-pone-0003184:
Tiny Boumans, Sharon M. H. Gobes, Colline Poirier and colleagues image songbird brains hearing sounds in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Male songbirds learn their songs from an adult tutor when young. A network of brain nuclei called the song system is the likely base for learning and producing song, but the networks that process auditory feedback signals were less clear.

Using functional MRI of auditory responses in the zebra finch forebrain, the team find a hierarchy based on signal strength but not selectivity. Readers learn how hearing areas are organized in a bird that learns by listening. The results inform wider work on learning complex sounds, including speech.
plos-pone-0003284:
Aki P. Järvinen, Jukka Hiissa, Laura L. Elo and colleagues predict genetic interactions in yeast in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Despite new lab techniques for changing multiple genes and measuring their effects on traits, genetic interactions have remained very hard to predict on a large scale. The team use a recent high-resolution screen of genetic interactions in yeast as their basis.

They propose predicting quantitative genetic interactions by means of sequential matrix approximation. Readers get a shortcut by computer for a huge test space, since gene pairs grow far faster than labs can test them. Good predictions let labs spend their tests on the pairs most likely to matter.
plos-pone-0003384:
Asish K. Ghosh and co-authors asked what a quiet gene does in normal cells in 2008. The gene makes MBP-1, a protein that turns other genes down. Extra MBP-1 was known to kill cancer cells and shrink tumors. But its day-to-day role in healthy cells was still unclear.

The team lowered MBP-1 levels in normal human skin cells called fibroblasts. Those cells then aged early, a state known as senescence. The aging ran through two guard proteins, p53 and p21. So normal levels of MBP-1 seem to hold cell aging back.
plos-pone-0003484:
Rubén Rabaneda-Bueno and co-authors studied mate-eating in a wild population for this 2008 paper. Sexual cannibalism pits female feeding gains against male survival. Females may gain more from eating a male than from mating with him. Males, in turn, may shun aggressive females.

In this natural population, cannibalism occurred at a high rate. The team measured the benefits that flowed to females. Eating mates brought real gains, not just a odd accident. The study weighs an extreme case of conflict between the sexes. Such findings test how far one sex will go at the other's expense.
plos-pone-0003584:
Sabine Telle and Marco Thines read DNA from old plant specimens in this 2008 methods paper. Herbarium sheets are dried plants kept for study, some very old. Molecular work on them had usually needed large amounts of material. The team worked with just two milligrams per sample.

They amplified a cox2 gene stretch of about 620 base pairs. Specimens up to 129 years old yielded readable DNA. Nineteen extraction methods and fifteen polymerases were compared. Museum collections thus become a time machine for plant evolution. Old sheets also hold species that are now extinct in the wild.
plos-pone-0003684:
Andrea C. Tricco, Jamie Brehaut, Maggie H. Chen, and colleagues published this research study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Cochrane reviews are trusted as careful summaries of medical evidence. Each one starts as a published protocol. No one had tracked how many of those protocols reach a finished review.

The authors followed 411 Cochrane protocols to see which ones were completed. They also looked for factors that predicted finishing. The audit measures the gap between starting a gold-standard review and publishing it, a gap that matters to everyone who funds or uses these reviews.
plos-pone-0003784:
Vera Halpern, Folasade Ogunsola, Orikomaba Obunge, and colleagues published this trial report in PLOS ONE in 2008. A vaginal gel that blocks HIV could give women a prevention method they control. The team ran a Phase III, double-blind, randomized trial in Nigeria of six percent cellulose sulfate gel.

The trial tested the gel's safety and its power to prevent male-to-female transmission of HIV. It also tracked gonorrhea and chlamydia infections. Big trials of this kind give the hard answers that smaller safety studies cannot, whatever the outcome turns out to be.
plos-pone-0003884:
Jack Kent and Andrea L. Meredith studied the brain clock in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. Daily rhythms near 24 hours come from a small brain area called the suprachiasmatic nucleus. Clock genes inside its cells set the basic beat of that rhythm. Less was clear about how firing patterns of the cells add to timing.

The authors focused on BK channels, which help control when nerve cells fire. They found these channels shape the rhythm of bursts in the clock nucleus. The work links a single channel type to the pace of daily activity. It adds a cell-level piece to the story of how the brain keeps time.
plos-pone-0003984:
Eti Ben-Simon, Ilana Podlipsky, Amos Arieli, and co-authors studied the resting brain's alpha rhythm in 2008. Brain activity keeps changing even when a person rests. The alpha rhythm, at 8 to 12 hertz, marks that idle state. Whether it reflects one spot or a wide network was debated.

Their PLOS ONE article reports two alpha processes present at once. Both showed in recordings from resting human subjects. Two distinct rhythms suggest rest holds more than one active process. The result complicates the simple picture of an idling brain. The full report sits in PLOS ONE, free to read with all its data shown.
plos-pone-0004084:
Daniel Oro, Antoni Margalida, Martina Carrete, and co-authors tested feeding sites for an endangered vulture in 2008. Conflicts with predators push many species toward extinction. Supplementary feeding at set sites is a popular simple fix. Such fixes can bring unforeseen conservation outcomes, though.

Their PLOS ONE article asks whether feeding truly boosts vulture viability. Feeding stations gather birds where food is predictable. Benefits must be weighed against risks like crowding and dependency. Evidence from this test guides vulture programs across Europe. It was printed in PLOS ONE, where the full text stays free to read.
plos-pone-0004184:
Arikuni Uchimura and colleagues published this genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2009. DNA polymerase delta is one of the main enzymes that copy DNA in eukaryotic cells, and it also helps repair and reshuffle DNA. Its working part, the p125 subunit, is encoded by the Pold1 gene. What this enzyme does for a developing mammal was not thoroughly known.

By disabling Pold1 in mice, the team shows that polymerase delta is required for early embryonic development. Embryos cannot get far without working DNA copying. The study pins a basic housekeeping enzyme to the very first chapter of life.
plos-pone-0004284:
Eun Chan Park, Doreen Glodowski, and Christopher Rongo published this neuroscience study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Ubiquitination, the tagging of proteins, happens at synapses, yet its role there was unclear. Earlier work showed the ligase RPM-1 organises the sending side of junctions between nerve and muscle in the worm C. elegans.

Here the team find a novel postsynaptic role for RPM-1 in interneurons. Together with the p38 MAPK called PMK-3, it regulates trafficking of AMPA receptors, the main receivers of the excitatory signal glutamate. Moving receptors in and out of synapses is how brains tune connection strength.
plos-pone-0004384:
The H5N1 bird flu virus raised fears of a human pandemic. A vaccine that trains lasting, broad immunity would be a strong defense. Angelika Banzhoff, Roberto Gasparini, Franco Laghi-Pasini, and co-authors tested such a vaccine in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper covers adults in two age bands. One group was aged eighteen to sixty, the other over sixty.

The vaccine used an added booster ingredient called MF59. In total, 313 younger adults and 173 older adults took part. The authors report the shot built immune memory. It also raised antibodies that respond across differing strains, called heterotypic responses. Broad memory of that kind is what pandemic planners hope to bank ahead of time.
plos-pone-0004484:
In salt-loving microbes called haloarchaea, the ends of gene messages must work as a pair, show Mariam Brenneis and Jorg Soppa in PLOS ONE in 2009. Gene messages carry untranslated regions at both ends, called the 5' and 3' UTRs. A genome-wide study had shown that control of translation, the reading of messages into protein, plays a big role in these microbes.

The team tested the two end regions directly. They found both are essential, and that they have to interact with each other in the living cell for translation to work well. That is a neat mechanical insight: a message's head and tail cooperate. It also matters for engineering these hardy microbes, which thrive in brine that would kill most life.
plos-pone-0004584:
Spotting a specific mutation amid a sea of normal DNA is made simpler by a real-time PCR method from John Morlan, Joffre Baker, and Dominick Sinicropi in PLOS ONE in 2009. Molecular tests are gaining acceptance for disease diagnosis, especially in cancer, where they guide prognosis and treatment choice. Genetic mutations are key parameters in that molecular characterization.

The authors describe their method as simple, robust, and highly selective. Real-time PCR watches DNA being copied and can be tuned to detect a mutant sequence even when normal copies vastly outnumber it. Selectivity is the whole game in such tests: a false signal can steer a patient's treatment wrong. A sturdier method widens access to mutation-guided care.
plos-pone-0004684:
Miao He, Jane Gitschier, Tatiana Zerjal, and colleagues checked where HapMap samples truly come from, for PLOS ONE in 2009. The HapMap set was built for medical gene studies across world groups. It is also used widely in studies of human history and trait spread.

Yet the way the samples were picked differs from most field studies of groups. Those studies tend to pick people who live in one local place. The team checked how well sample labels match real roots. Clear roots matter, since loose labels can skew claims about group traits and past moves. These findings offer a firm starting point for the next round of testing.
plos-pone-0004784:
Benoît Carpentier and colleagues built artificial focal tools to link T cell surface contacts with cell response, in PLOS ONE in 2009. T cell activation is a key immune event built on contacts with antigen presenting cells. Several receptor and ligand pairs meet in a complex contact zone whose components have been partly identified by past research.

The team created tools that trigger defined spots on the T cell surface. That lets them map which contacts cause which responses. Cleaner causal maps can improve vaccine and cell therapy design. They also reveal basic rules of immune recognition. Replication in other settings will show how robust the findings really are.
plos-pone-0004884:
Francis Willard and colleagues showed regulator of G protein signaling 14 is a selective H-Ras effector, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Regulator of G protein signaling proteins are accelerators of G alpha GTP hydrolysis. Proteins with complex builds regulate much more than GTPase activity. RGS14 was studied for how it binds Ras family proteins. Those proteins drive growth signals in many human cancers and growth disorders.

Selective H-Ras binding distinguishes RGS14 function. It may integrate two major signaling systems. Ras effector diversity expands treatment options. Specificity arises from extra domains. Further tests can show how widely the pattern holds beyond the cases studied here. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field.
plos-pone-0004984:
The eye has light sensors beyond rods and cones. Certain ganglion cells sense light themselves. They use a pigment called melanopsin. Gary Pickard and colleagues studied these cells in mice lacking melanopsin. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They measured light-induced Fos expression. Fos is a marker of cell activity.

Even without melanopsin, the ganglion cells still receive signals from rods and cones. The study asked how much of their light response remains. The answer maps the pigment's true contribution. These cells help set body clocks and pupil responses. The work dissects the eye's hidden light sensors with care.
plos-pone-0005084:
Proteins are built from modules called domains. Drawing domain borders is tricky when domains intertwine. Existing databases disagree on the hard cases. Indraneel Majumdar, Lisa Kinch and Nick Grishin built a curated resource in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their database holds domain definitions for proteins with complex geometry.

Structural domains are necessary for understanding evolution and folding. Sequence-based definitions often miss the truth. The new database gives researchers a shared map for the puzzles. Definitions were chosen with structural care. The resource serves anyone who classifies proteins. It also helps train the algorithms that predict domains. Better definitions mean better comparisons across the protein universe.
plos-pone-0005184:
Friendly gut bacteria can calm swelling in the bowel, partly through substances they release into their surroundings. One such bacterium is Bifidobacterium breve, whose released factors lower harsh signals from immune cells. Heuvelin and colleagues asked in PLOS ONE in 2009 how those factors act on the gut lining itself.

The study traced the steps by which the bacterial factors quiet the intestinal surface cells. Knowing the pathway helps explain how a common gut microbe keeps peace with its host. It may also guide new treatments for bowel diseases built on bacterial products rather than live bacteria.
plos-pone-0005284:
Oxidative stress helps drive cancer, and raising the body's own antioxidant enzymes can suppress tumors in tests. Liu and colleagues tested a supplement called Protandim on that principle in PLOS ONE in 2009, using a two-stage mouse skin cancer model.

Rather than supplying antioxidants directly, the approach turns up the enzymes the body makes itself. The model applies a tumor starter and then a promoter to mouse skin. If enzyme induction prevents tumors there, it supports a chemoprevention strategy based on the body's own defenses. Most cancer drugs try to kill cells that have already turned bad. A food-based plan that stops the turn in the first place would work in a whole new way.
plos-pone-0005384:
Cilia and flagella are built by a shuttle system called intraflagellar transport, which moves parts between the cell body and the tip. The shuttles are organized into complexes A and B with at least eighteen proteins. Wang and colleagues characterized one of them, IFT25, in PLOS ONE in 2009.

In the alga Chlamydomonas, IFT25 proved to be a phosphoprotein, carrying phosphate tags. It belongs to complex B and physically interacts with another component, IFT27. Each mapped interaction helps complete the parts list for how cells build and maintain their flagella. Algae with twin tails are a clean test bed for cilia, the same hairs that sweep mucus in our lungs and move eggs in the body. So each part found here may count for human health too.
plos-pone-0005484:
Lee Baugh and Jonathan Marotta studied movement learning in older adults for a 2009 PLOS ONE report. People adjust their movements when the world changes what they see, such as when a tool shifts their view of their hand. Studies disagreed on whether older people adjust more slowly.

The authors used a setup where the needed change played to a strength rather than a weakness. Older adults adapted well when the task was framed in the right way. The result suggests that aging does not simply dull movement learning; the design of the task matters a great deal.
plos-pone-0005584:
Stéphane Vuilleumier and co-authors published genome sequences for bacteria that eat one-carbon foods, in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Some bacteria can live on compounds with a single carbon atom, such as methanol. The pink-tinted genus Methylobacterium is a well-known group of them, found in soil, water, and industry.

The genomes give a reference map for studying how these bacteria feed and grow. That knowledge serves both basic science and industry, since such bacteria can turn cheap one-carbon feedstocks into useful products. These bacteria also clean up one-carbon waste gases, which gives their metabolism an environmental value as well.
plos-pone-0005684:
Kamille Smidt and colleagues studied a zinc carrier gene in insulin-making cells in 2009. The carrier, from the SLC30A3 gene, moves zinc into storage spots inside the cell. Beta cells need zinc both to pack insulin into crystals and to control their own numbers.

The team varied sugar and zinc levels and watched how the gene and its protein responded. They also tested what happens when the carrier is missing under cell stress. Their findings mark the carrier as key for insulin output and for blood sugar control in the whole body. The work adds one more zinc link in diabetes science.
plos-pone-0005784:
Santiago Rodriguez and co-authors checked in 2009 whether two common skin-gene faults also affect children's hearing. Filaggrin is a key skin protein; its mutations cause several skin conditions. The protein also appears in the eardrum, where it might change how the drum flexes.

In a cohort of more than five thousand children, carriers of the two mutations showed no hearing differences. A clear no is useful: clinics need not flag these children for hearing checks on this basis alone, saving needless worry and testing. The large, well-known ALSPAC cohort gives the negative result its weight.
plos-pone-0005884:
Saroj Basak and co-authors proposed in 2009 that fluid gathered from lung cancer patients' chests can serve as a living sample of tumor diversity. This fluid, malignant pleural effusion, contains shed cancer cells. Tumors are not uniform; they hold subpopulations, possibly including stem-like cells.

The team sought evidence of cancer stem cells and varied cell states in the effusion. If the fluid mirrors the tumor's hierarchy, doctors could sample diversity without repeated biopsies. That would help track how a cancer evolves under treatment. The model turns a drained waste fluid into a research asset.
plos-pone-0005984:
A flu shot that sprays into the nose could guard without a needle. Julia Romanova, Brigitte Krenn, Markus Wolschek and colleagues built such a vaccine against H5N1 bird flu in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper reports preclinical tests of a virus with its whole NS1 gene removed, a change that stops it from copying itself in the body.

A virus that cannot copy itself can still teach the immune system its shape. Given through the nose, it meets the flu at its usual door. The team checked how safe the vaccine was and how strong a response it raised in lab models. The work supports a needle-free route for guarding against a feared flu strain.
plos-pone-0006084:
A scaffold protein best known in young, growing cells also works as an anchor for a hormone receptor. Rudolph Reimer, Heike Helmbold, Beata Szalay and colleagues showed that in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper studies nestin, the marker filament of progenitor cells, and its grip on the glucocorticoid receptor, the switch that answers stress hormones.

Nestin holds the receptor in the cytoplasm, away from the genes it would switch on, the title reports. Anchoring thus tunes how strongly a cell answers its stress signal. The finding links the cell's inner frame to hormone control, a pairing that may matter in growing tissue and in tumors where nestin returns.
plos-pone-0006184:
Human African trypanosomiasis, known as sleeping sickness, is a deadly disease spread by tsetse flies. Caroline Boda and colleagues profiled immune cells in patients for a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Little was known about human immune responses to the parasite. The germ lives outside cells in the blood, yet the body still struggles to clear it.

Using flow cytometry, a method that sorts and counts cells by their markers, the team charted lymphocyte patterns in patients. Those patterns show which branches of the immune system react most strongly. A clearer immune portrait can guide better tests and future treatments. It also helps explain why the illness harms the body as it does.
plos-pone-0006284:
Whooping cough has returned in many countries despite infant vaccination, prompting adult booster debates. Laurent Coudeville and colleagues ran an economic evaluation of adult vaccination strategies for the United States in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Earlier evaluations disagreed, partly because static models missed indirect effects.

Their model includes dynamic population effects, including protection passed to others when spread slows. Counting herd benefits changes the value of vaccinating adults and teens. The fuller accounting gives policymakers a better basis for booster decisions. It shows why method choices can flip economic verdicts on vaccines.
plos-pone-0006384:
Sending video costs more energy than sensing it, a problem for tiny camera systems. Yu Chi, Ralph Etienne-Cummings, and Gert Cauwenberghs present compression built into the image sensor itself in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Embedded compression saves transmission energy but the encoder itself consumes power.

Their architecture detects change at the focal plane and compresses around it. Analysing energy trade-offs shows where the design wins. Low-power vision sensors serve wildlife monitoring, security, and medical devices. Doing less work per frame extends battery life in all of them.
plos-pone-0006484:
Nalini Raghavachari and colleagues tackled a technical problem in blood gene studies for PLOS ONE in 2009. Reading all gene activity in whole blood with microarrays is proven to be challenging. Globin transcripts, from the oxygen-carrying protein, make up most of the RNA in blood. They swamp signals from other genes. Reducing globin message is a common fix, but it may distort the rest.

The team characterized whole blood gene expression profiles after globin reduction in patients. They checked what the fix does to the remaining profile. Their results help labs worldwide read immune and disease signals from a simple blood draw.
plos-pone-0006584:
Márta Gácsi and co-authors compared dogs and wolves on human gestures in PLOS ONE in 2009. Comparing human-related communication skills of socialized canids may help understand evolution and development of gesture comprehension in humans. Dogs famously follow human pointing, while wolves do less well even when raised by people. The team sought to explain dog-wolf differences in utilizing human pointing gestures.

They argue for selection for synergistic shifts in the dog lineage during domestication. In other words, several traits changed together to make dogs cooperative partners. The study uses canids to ask how communication with another species evolves.
plos-pone-0006684:
Anupam Nath Jha, G. K. Ananthasuresh, and Saraswathi Vishveshwara searched protein sequences by energy in PLOS ONE in 2009. Proteins fold into shapes that determine what they do. The authors asked whether natural protein sequences are picked for low energy. In other words, a sequence may be favored because it sits comfortably in its target shape. They tested that idea with computer methods.

The team used real protein shapes stored in the Protein Data Bank. They presented efficient ways to find sequences that minimize energy for a given shape. Their numerical evidence supports the idea of minimization in sequence space. That principle could help scientists design new proteins. It also clarifies how evolution may have shaped natural protein sequences.
plos-pone-0006784:
Michael Koeppen, Tobias Eckle, and Holger K. Eltzschig identified the receptor behind adenosine's slowing of the heart in PLOS ONE in 2009. Adenosine given into a vein briefly slows heart rate. It acts through four possible receptor types on cells. Earlier work outside living animals implicated the A1 receptor. Proof inside a living animal was still needed.

The team deleted the A1 adenosine receptor selectively in mice. Without it, intravenous adenosine no longer slowed the heart. That abolished effect confirms A1 as the responsible receptor in vivo. Doctors use adenosine to reset certain fast heart rhythms. Knowing its exact receptor sharpens both use and drug design.
plos-pone-0006884:
Lei Jiang and colleagues studied how leptin helps mice adapt to a fatty diet in PLOS ONE in 2009. Leptin is a hormone made by fat cells. It plays a critical role in energy balance and lipid metabolism. Obesity from overnutrition usually comes with high leptin levels. What leptin actually does during high-fat feeding was the question.

Leptin contributed to adaptive responses by suppressing the lipogenic pathway. Lipogenesis is the body's fat-making process. Suppressing it limits further fat storage during rich feeding. The finding refines leptin's role beyond appetite control. It may help explain why leptin resistance matters in obesity.
plos-pone-0006984:
Rod Dawson, Rany Condos, Doris Tse, and colleagues trialled an immune booster for tuberculosis in PLOS ONE in 2009. Standard treatment for lung tuberculosis takes at least six months of therapy. A lab-made immune signal, recombinant interferon-gamma 1b, might shorten that course. It could calm lung inflammation and clear infectious sputum sooner.

The team added the booster to standard drug treatment. They then measured whether patients improved faster. Even a modest shortening would matter for tuberculosis control. Long courses are hard to finish, and unfinished courses breed drug-resistant bacteria that endanger whole communities.
plos-pone-0007084:
Claudia Orelio, Paul Verkuijlen, Judy Geissler, and colleagues studied a rare syndrome's protein in PLOS ONE in 2009. Shwachman-Diamond syndrome is an inherited disease caused by mutations in the SBDS gene. Patients show pancreas failure, bone defects, and bone marrow dysfunction. Low white cell counts and poor neutrophil movement are common.

The team tracked where SBDS protein sits in human myeloid progenitor cells. They found it at the mitotic spindle during cell division. That address ties the syndrome's blood problems to division errors. It also gives researchers a concrete place to test what the healthy protein does.
plos-pone-0007184:
Yasuyuki Suda, Rachael K. Rodriguez, Alison E. Coluccio, and colleagues published a 2009 PLOS ONE paper on yeast spores. Spores of the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae sit inside a complex wall. That wall protects them from heat, chemicals, and other stresses in the environment.

The outer wall layer is built from a polymer containing the amino acid dityrosine. The authors screen for mutants with faulty spore wall permeability. Their screen finds a secreted protease needed for proper wall assembly. Yeast biologists get a new gene-level lead on how protective spore coats form.
plos-pone-0007284:
Andrew Chi-Ho Chan, Rhona H. Borts, and Eva Hoffmann studied chromosome sorting in yeast meiosis in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Matching chromosomes rely on crossover links to segregate accurately at meiosis. Crossovers are recombination events that physically connect chromosome pairs until division pulls them apart correctly.

Two conserved proteins, Msh4 and Msh5, promote crossover formation. The authors examine msh4 mutants of budding yeast at different temperatures. They report temperature-dependent changes in chromosome segregation. Their work shows that environment can modify genetic defects in meiosis, a caution for interpreting mutant studies.
plos-pone-0007384:
Maria Armesto, Dave Cavanagh, and Paul Britton identified a virulence gene in a bird coronavirus in PLOS ONE in 2009. Infectious bronchitis virus is an avian coronavirus that harms poultry. Earlier work swapped the spike gene between harmless and virulent strains, changing which cells the virus could infect in culture dishes.

The authors now test the replicase gene, which copies the viral genome. They report the replicase gene is a determinant of pathogenicity. That finding shifts attention beyond the spike protein. It may help design safer live vaccines for chickens against this costly disease.
plos-pone-0007484:
Sonia Saxena and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on children's hospital admissions in England. Good primary care keeps children out of hospital and gives families continuity. Yet short, unplanned hospital stays for children rose over the decade studied. The team analyzed time trends from 1997 to 2006 to find the pattern and its likely causes.

The rise in brief emergency admissions was sharp, not gradual background noise. The authors link part of it to a 2004 contract change. That change let family doctors opt out of after-hours care, thinning community treatment at night and on weekends. When local care is harder to reach, hospitals absorb the cases. The findings show how a primary care policy can ripple into hospital wards.
plos-pone-0007584:
Juliette Ben Arous, Sophie Laffont, and Didier Chatenay published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how a tiny worm budgets its behavior. Most animals divide time among states, shifting with their surroundings. The roundworm C. elegans switches between dwelling, lingering where food is, and roaming, ranging widely. The team built a new quantitative method to analyze these states. They then traced the sensory and molecular basis of the two-state pattern.

The worm's time split between dwelling and roaming follows measurable rules. Senses report the environment, and molecular pathways set the balance. In a nervous system of just a few hundred neurons, the whole decision loop can be mapped. That makes the worm a model for a universal problem: how brains allocate time. Even simple animals weigh staying against exploring, and this study shows the weighing in detail.
plos-pone-0007684:
Dongmei Zhu, Junshun Fang, Yanxin Li and their co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on mouse embryonic stem cells. Stem cells can turn into many cell types, including tissues outside the embryo itself. Known factors such as Oct4 and Nanog help keep them in their flexible state.

The team studied a protein called Mbd3, part of a larger complex named NuRD. They found that Mbd3 helps hold stem cells in their unspecialized state. It does so by blocking a path toward trophectoderm. That tissue is the layer that helps form the placenta.
plos-pone-0007784:
Alice Nemajerova and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It deletes a gene called p73 in mice to see what it does. In human leukemias and lymphomas, p73 is often silenced by methylation. Its role in causing cancer was still unclear.

The targeted deletion revealed roles that silencing studies could not. The gene helps guide T cell development in the immune system. It also guards against lymphoma, acting as a T cell-specific tumor suppressor. The mouse work gives this relative of the famous p53 gene its own clear place in cancer biology.
plos-pone-0007884:
Patrick Brunner and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It links wheat farming to faster evolution in a wheat pathogen. The fungus Mycosphaerella graminicola attacks wheat leaves. Its wall-degrading enzymes can trigger plant defenses, putting them under strong selection.

Host and pathogen are locked in an antagonistic arms race. The authors tested one enzyme, a beta-xylosidase, for signs of that race. They found wheat domestication accelerated the enzyme's evolution. Positive selection acted on it as farming spread. The study shows how agriculture itself reshapes the evolution of crop diseases.
plos-pone-0007984:
Ingrid Arijs and colleagues read gut lining genes before and after a strong drug, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The drug was infliximab, given for the first time to people with inflammatory bowel disease. The genes in view make antimicrobial peptides, small proteins that guard the gut wall.

In sick gut lining, some of those guard genes ran at odd levels. After treatment, the pattern shifted as the lining healed. Comparing before and after helps tell whether the odd levels cause the disease or merely follow it. The answer guides both drug choice and the search for new targets.
plos-pone-0008084:
Matthew Davies and colleagues hunted for vaccine helpers that work by blocking one immune receptor in PLOS ONE in 2009. The receptor, CCR4, helps calming T cells reach their posts. If those cells are held back at the right moment, a vaccine's alarm rings louder.

Computer screening picked candidate blockers, and dish tests checked how well they grip the human and mouse forms of the receptor. Hits that grip both forms can move from mouse trials toward human use with fewer surprises. The paired hunt is a model for adjuvant searches.
plos-pone-0008184:
Eva Maria Hodel and colleagues studied malaria patients in Tanzania in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. In places where malaria is common, people often take malaria drugs on their own. They may also have had recent treatment for repeated fever episodes. Such drug use can linger in the body before a trial begins.

The authors measured leftover antimalarial drugs in patients entering an in vivo study. Leftover drugs can change treatment results and confuse readings of efficacy and safety. They can also affect how drug resistance spreads among parasites. The work warns trial designers to check for prior drug intake.
plos-pone-0008284:
Eric Haÿ and his co-workers wrote in PLOS ONE in 2009 about the cells that build bone. These cells are called osteoblasts, and new bone can not form without them. How their numbers are kept in check is a key point for care of bone disease. Sick bones may grow too much bone or too little. The team looked at a glue-like protein on the cell surface, named N-cadherin.

They found that this protein slows the growth of bone cells and cuts their chance to live. It does so by blocking three growth signal paths inside the cell. If that brake could be eased, lost bone might grow back. The work names a clear target for bone care.
plos-pone-0008384:
Harold D. Love and colleagues studied prostate growth genes in mice in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Benign prostatic hyperplasia and prostate cancer are both linked to aging and androgens. Androgen-regulated genes likely play a major role in these common diseases. Prostate growth and development depend on androgen presence. The team used human prostate xenografts grown in mice.

They cataloged genes that androgens switch on or off in the grafts. Relating that list to benign growth and cancer separates shared from distinct pathways. Such knowledge may point to drug targets. It also clarifies how male hormones drive prostate disease.
plos-pone-0008484:
Johan Rebetz and co-authors study virus therapy for cancer in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Their agents are adenoviruses bred to copy only in tumor cells. Each round of infection should spread and kill new cancer cells. In animal tumors, such viruses slow growth but rarely wipe it out. The team find a reason in cells near infected ones. Those bystander cells have not been infected at all.

A viral fiber protein masks receptors on bystander cells. Masked cells resist new infection, which limits viral killing. Yet the same masking may let virus and host coexist longer. The trade-off shapes how such therapies should be designed.
plos-pone-0008584:
Melissa Friswell and co-authors compare gut germs in lab mice in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The gut microbiota is a complex community of microbes in mammals. Its composition influences gut development, immunity, nutrition, and drug metabolism. It remained unclear whether dominant gut communities are consistent across labs. Mouse strain and housing site could each shift the mix. The team profile microbiota and metabolism in experimental mice from different sites and strains.

They find both site and strain cause specific variation in gut profiles. The same strain can host different germs at different facilities. That variation can confound experiments that ignore it. Researchers must account for gut germs when comparing mouse studies.
plos-pone-0008684:
Christopher Cotter, Marie Nguyen, Jacob Yount, and colleagues studied how herpes simplex virus hides from sentries. Their work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Dendritic cells are sentries that should sound an alarm after meeting the virus. Yet a normal infection often leaves them quiet. A viral protein called vhs, short for virion host shut-off, was the prime suspect.

Removing vhs let the sentry cells wake up and respond. The team traced the alarm route that vhs blocks in human and mouse cells. Oddly, that route does not use the usual TLR alarm sensors. Learning how the virus mutes its host may point to better vaccines.
plos-pone-0008784:
Vanesa Sanchez-Guajardo, Fabia Febbraro, Deniz Kirik, and colleagues staged how brain cleaner cells react in Parkinson disease. Their rat study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Microglia are the brain's resident immune cells. Post-mortem Parkinson brains show them switched on near damage. The protein alpha-synuclein, which clumps in the disease, likely triggers them. A virus-based rat model lets damage grow in steps.

As synuclein damage worsened, microglia took distinct activation profiles. Early and late stages differed rather than simply growing stronger. Staged profiles suggest treatment should match disease phase. Blanket calming of microglia may help at one stage and hurt at another.
plos-pone-0008884:
Abraham Peedicayil, Robert Vierkant, Lynn Hartmann, and colleagues asked whether relapse-linked genes also predict ovarian cancer risk. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The team had earlier found genes tied to how ovarian cancer patients fare. Inherited variants in those same genes might raise the chance of getting the disease. The study compared hundreds of women with cancer against more than a thousand controls.

Variants were tallied across the relapse-associated gene panel. Any variant tracking with disease risk marks a candidate for risk screening. Separating risk genes from outcome genes matters for prevention. Negative results, too, steer future hunts away from dead ends.
plos-pone-0008984:
Sohela Shah and co-authors showed that a mouse's family background changes how a liver disease plays out, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The mice lack ATP8B1, a gene faulty in some human bile-flow diseases. Those human diseases range from mild, coming-and-going attacks to steady, worsening liver damage. The mouse was built to model that range of illness.

The same gene fault caused different severity in different mouse strains. Other genes in each strain's background softened or sharpened the symptoms. So two mice with the identical defect did not get equally sick. The lesson matters for anyone using animal models to test liver treatments.
plos-pone-0009084:
Rosa Jimenez and co-authors mapped how a growth controller rewires gene activity in liver cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The controller is mTOR, a hub for nutrient and growth signals. Its blocker, rapamycin, is a drug used against cancer and rejection. Two liver cell lines were compared, one normal and one cancerous.

The cancerous line resists rapamycin's growth-stopping effect. Comparing both lines showed which genes mTOR commands in liver cells. The resistant line's wiring explained part of its indifference to the drug. Gene maps like this help predict which tumours rapamycin-like drugs can slow.
plos-pone-0009184:
Jamie Lukos and colleagues published this neuroscience study in PLOS ONE in 2010. It asks how Parkinson's disease changes the way people grip objects. Healthy hands place their fingers in advance, using memories of earlier lifts. That planning lets a lift feel smooth instead of clumsy.

Earlier research had shown that the basal ganglia, deep brain structures hit hard by Parkinson's, help store these grip memories. The team tested how patients placed their digits when grasping, compared with healthy people. They found that the advance placement of fingers is affected by the disease. The result points to a planning problem, not just a strength problem, in Parkinson's grip.
plos-pone-0009284:
Cornelia Kranczioch and co-authors published this brain study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Picturing a move and making that move feel much alike. One theory says both acts use much the same brain paths. The team tested that claim for the stage just before a move starts.

They placed many sensors on the scalp to track brain waves tied to getting ready to move. People got set for real moves and for moves they only pictured, at tasks of more or less hard steps. Task hardness changed the two kinds of prep in unlike ways. So picturing is not just doing minus the motion, most of all when the task is hard.
plos-pone-0009384:
Ann-Kristin Mossberg and co-authors published this cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2010. HAMLET is a complex made from a milk protein, alpha-lactalbumin, joined with oleic acid. Partially unfolded, the protein becomes lethal to tumor cells while sparing healthy ones. How it kills was the open question.

The team studied how HAMLET meets lipid membranes, the films that wrap cells. HAMLET interacts with those membranes and disturbs their structure and integrity. A leaky, disordered membrane could explain how the complex harms tumor cells. The work brings a curious milk-derived substance closer to a understood cancer treatment.
plos-pone-0009484:
Ildefonso De la Fuente and co-authors took a whole system view of cell chemistry in PLOS ONE in 2010. A cell runs thousands of chemical reactions at once. Yet its core chemistry stays steady even when food or conditions change. The team studied how enzyme activity organizes itself across the cell. They looked for a set of reactions that stays active at all times.

Their work supports the idea of a stable metabolic core. Other reactions switch on or off around that core as needs change. So the cell tunes itself, rather than following a fixed plan. That picture helps explain how cells stay steady in a shifting world.
plos-pone-0009584:
Ahmedin Jemal, Elizabeth Ward, and Michael Thun read United States cancer death rates in PLOS ONE in 2010. Debate has long surrounded the war on cancer, declared in 1971. Trends in death rates are cited both as proof of success and as proof of failure. The team examined rates for all cancers combined and for the nineteen most common types. They followed the trends over recent decades.

Death rates fell for cancer overall and for many major types. The authors read those falls as real progress from prevention, screening, and treatment. Hard trend data cut through claims on both sides. The paper gives the public a grounded measure of what decades of effort have bought.
plos-pone-0009684:
Coronary heart disease remains a leading cause of death in China. Meian He and colleagues looked for genetic clues in a Chinese population sample for a 2010 PLOS ONE report. They focused on HSPA8, a gene that helps cells handle stress from heat and other damage.

Certain variants of the gene turned up more often in people with the disease. That pattern tied the gene to higher risk in this population. Genetic risks can differ between ancestries, so findings from one group do not always carry over. The result adds one more piece to the search for inherited heart risk.
plos-pone-0009884:
Proteins that spill from damaged cells may help clog arteries. Alan Pemberton and Jeremy Brown tested how one such protein family meets the cholesterol carrier LDL. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The proteins are extracellular histones, DNA-spooling proteins found outside cells after injury. LDL is the blood fat often called bad cholesterol. In vitro tests showed the two interact in ways that suggest a pro-atherogenic role. Pro-atherogenic means helping build the plaques that narrow arteries. The work was done in vitro, in lab glassware, not in patients.
plos-pone-0009984:
A common pollutant in smoke and charred food can reach and harm the brain. Kallol Dutta and colleagues showed how it kills neurons in mice. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The carcinogen is benzo[a]pyrene, found in tobacco smoke and grilled foods.

A carcinogen is a substance that can cause cancer. The neuronal death ran via microglial activation, the switching on of the brain's immune cells. Activated microglia can attack the neurons they normally protect. The pathway links air and food pollution to brain damage. Neurons are the brain's signaling cells.
plos-pone-0010084:
The authors were Anette Gjesing, Lesli Larsen, Signe Torekov, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study tested a hunger gene against obesity measures. The ghrelin receptor tells the brain about hunger when the hormone ghrelin activates it. That made its gene locus a natural candidate for weight differences between people.

Using family and population studies, the team checked common and rare variants in that locus. They asked whether those variants track with obesity and overweight. The work helps separate a plausible hunger story from genetic evidence that actually holds up in people.
plos-pone-0010184:
The authors were Meghan Maher, Rigen Mo, Annette Flozak, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study looked at two jobs done by one protein, beta-catenin. Beta-catenin both glues cells together and carries growth signals. Worms and flies make separate forms for those jobs, but vertebrates have a single beta-catenin gene.

The team asked whether chemical tags create the separate forms in vertebrates instead. They found beta-catenin tagged at one site sits apart from protein tagged in another region. That spatial split suggests signaling and adhesion pools are kept distinct by modification, not by separate genes.
plos-pone-0010284:
The authors were Guillaume Laval, Etienne Patin, Luis Barreiro, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study modeled recent human history from DNA resequencing data. Estimating the sizes and splits of past populations is fundamental to reconstructing our species' story. A good model must also explain the neutral genetic diversity seen in people today, without cherry-picking single genes.

The team used resequencing data from noncoding regions, DNA that does not build proteins. Such regions carry cleaner traces of population history than selected genes. Their historical and demographic model gives later studies a baseline for judging unusual patterns.
plos-pone-0010384:
Shirley Mihardja and colleagues tried to grow new blood vessels in damaged hearts, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2010. After a heart attack, muscle is starved of blood and scarred. The body's own scaffolding material, the extracellular matrix, helps tissues regrow. The team asked whether pieces of that scaffolding could be sent to the injury. Antibodies were used as guided carriers to the damaged zone.

In rats, the targeted fragments reached the hurt heart muscle. New vessel growth there increased, aiding repair. Sending material only where it is needed limits effects elsewhere. That targeting idea is central to modern drug delivery. The study offers a proof of concept in a living heart model.
plos-pone-0010484:
Kaushal Gandhi and colleagues searched blood for signs of who will benefit from a multiple sclerosis drug in PLOS ONE in 2010. Interferon beta is the most common treatment for the relapsing form of the disease. Some patients, however, gain little from it. The team looked for marker molecules in blood serum and plasma. Such markers could flag responders before months of futile treatment.

Finding response markers early would spare non-responders side effects and cost. It would also speed their move to other therapies. The study tested new detection approaches on patient samples. MS treatment is a crowded field where matching patient to drug matters hugely. A blood test for that matching is the prize here.
plos-pone-0010584:
Man Charurat and colleagues followed patients in a large HIV treatment program in Nigeria, reported in PLOS ONE in 2010. Antiretroviral drugs work only if people keep taking them and keep returning for refills. The team used pharmacy records to see who stopped coming back.

Certain patient traits raised the risk of dropping out of care. Missed refills, an early warning sign, also clustered in identifiable groups. Knowing who is most likely to disengage lets clinics spend follow-up effort where it helps most. Better retention means fewer treatment failures and less chance for drug-resistant virus to emerge.
plos-pone-0010684:
Mochan Li and colleagues surveyed the genes of a prized wild mushroom in southern China, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Local people call it Dahongjun, or Big Red Mushroom. It grows with tree roots, is picked for food, and is sold abroad at high prices. Almost nothing was known about its biology.

DNA samples from many sites showed how varied the mushroom is across its range. Some areas held rich variety, while others were narrow. Variety is the raw stock that lets a species cope with change. The survey gives harvesters and officials a basis for picking rules that do not strip the richest stands first.
plos-pone-0010784:
Dik Heg and Michael Taborsky tested helping behavior under staged danger in a cichlid fish, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Neolamprologus pulcher lives in family groups where young helpers aid the breeding pair. Helpers feed and defend fry that are often their kin. Raising the threat of predators tests how much risk helpers will accept.

Caged predators of two sizes were placed near natural groups underwater. Helpers adjusted their work as danger changed. Help did not simply vanish under threat; it shifted in form. Cooperation, in other words, is priced against risk in a finely graded way. Such pricing helps explain when helping evolves and when it collapses.
plos-pone-0010884:
Shannon McNulty, William Bornmann, Jill Schriewer and co-authors published this virus study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Vaccinia, the virus used in the smallpox vaccine, builds its offspring by wrapping itself in membranes taken from the host cell. The authors screened a library of kinase-blocking drugs to find which cell enzymes the virus depends on.

Several hits blocked a family of enzymes called PI3Ks, already known to help the virus enter cells. Using drug tests, growth curves, and electron microscopy, the team showed these enzymes also govern two later steps: the ripening of immature virus particles and their wrapping into an extra membrane layer. Cells missing part of the enzyme machinery showed the same defects. McNulty and colleagues reveal that the virus leans on one host pathway at several stages, a possible target for antiviral drugs.
plos-pone-0010984:
Ron Pinhasi, Boris Gasparian, Gregory Areshian and co-authors reported this archaeology find in PLOS ONE in 2010. In 2008 excavators recovered a complete, well-preserved leather shoe from a pit in the Areni-1 cave in Armenia. The authors dated it and placed it in context as the first direct evidence of footwear from the Chalcolithic period in the Near Eastern highlands.

Radiocarbon tests on leather and grass samples in two laboratories converged on a range in the fourth millennium before the common era, making it among the oldest shoes known. The shoe, about twenty-five centimeters long, was stuffed with loose grass, likely to hold its shape or ready it for storage. Pinhasi and colleagues give the evolution of footwear a firm, dated anchor. The find also shows how dry cave pits can preserve everyday objects lost elsewhere.
plos-pone-0011084:
Imaizumi, Monnier, Hegi and colleagues published a mouse cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Radiation is used to kill tumors, but the team asked whether it also cuts off the new blood vessels that tumors need to grow. They traced the signals that let vessel cells sprout and spread.

In mice, radiation held back new vessel growth. The effect ran through a receptor path that blocked sprouting by the cells that line vessels. That finding adds a second way radiation may fight tumors, beyond direct cell killing. It could help doctors pair radiation with other drugs in smarter ways.
plos-pone-0011184:
Wertheim re-examined a flu puzzle in PLOS ONE in 2010. An H1N1 flu strain vanished for about twenty years, then returned in 1977 almost unchanged. The likely source was a frozen lab strain. The author used that odd history to test methods that date virus splits from gene data.

If sampling dates ignore gaps like a frozen interval, dating methods give wrong answers. The case is a cautionary tale for anyone timing virus family trees. It also touches lab safety, since a stored strain apparently re-entered people. Careful assumptions, the paper argues, are part of honest virus history.
plos-pone-0011284:
Lee, McGlone, Bailey and colleagues modeled flu strategy in PLOS ONE in 2010. When flu patients arrive, clinics must choose: test first to confirm flu, or treat at once with antiviral drugs. Both paths cost money and time, and each misses some cases. The team compared strategies with an economic computer model.

Their tool weighs drug costs, test costs and outcomes to find the smarter choice under different conditions. The best strategy shifts with drug price and how much flu is circulating. Pandemic planners can use such modeling to save money and lives at once. It turns a daily clinic dilemma into a policy question with numbers.
plos-pone-0011384:
Zhong Wang and co-authors built a general math model in 2010 for finding gene combinations that raise disease risk. Many common diseases arise not from one gene alone but from genes acting together, a pattern called epistasis. Standard tests that scan one gene at a time miss those partnerships, which may hold much of the inherited risk.

Their model works on case-control data, comparing patients with healthy volunteers, and can handle interactions among several gene sites at once. A flexible model matters because the true pattern of interaction is rarely known in advance. The paper gives geneticists a broader net for hunting combined effects. If more risk partnerships are found, prediction of who will develop complex diseases, and insight into how they start, should both improve.
plos-pone-0011484:
Aude Aumeunier and co-authors tested in 2010 whether stimulating germ sensors can calm two opposite immune errors in mice. Allergic asthma and type 1 diabetes both come from immunity overreacting, one to harmless airborne material and one to the body's own pancreas. The team gave systemic stimulation of Toll-like receptors, the sensors that detect germs, in the NOD mouse model.

The stimulation suppressed both experimental allergic asthma and autoimmune diabetes in the mice. That double success supports the hygiene idea in a controlled form: a measured immune challenge can teach the system restraint. Turning the idea into therapy will need care, since the same sensors can also fan inflammation. Still, one intervention calming both allergy and autoimmunity is a strong hint that the two errors share a tunable root.
plos-pone-0011584:
Benoit Langlois and colleagues examined a cell-surface protein called LRP-1 in PLOS ONE in 2010. LRP-1 normally clears stray molecules from outside cells. Because many of those molecules are linked to how cancer spreads, the team suspected LRP-1 might also help tumour cells invade new tissue.

Their experiments show LRP-1 does push invasion forward, and they trace how. It raises activity in the ERK signalling route while holding back the JNK route at the same time. One protein steering two routes in opposite ways helps explain its strong effect, and it marks LRP-1 as a possible target for slowing cancer spread.
plos-pone-0011684:
Johnny Habchi and co-authors looked at loose, floppy parts in proteins from two henipaviruses, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Hendra and Nipah are new viruses in the paramyxovirus family. One protein wraps up the viral genome, while a second helps the copying machine do its work. Computer tools had flagged parts of both proteins as lacking a fixed shape.

The team tested those flags with lab work. The tests confirmed the loose regions and described how they behave. Loose regions often serve as flexible docking sites, so confirming them matters for making drugs against viruses with few treatments.
plos-pone-0011784:
Marie-Ghislaine de Goër de Herve and co-authors studied regulatory T cells in young transplant patients, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The signalling molecule IL-2 was reported as critical for the survival of these calming cells in mouse models, acting through a receptor part called CD25. Whether human regulatory T cells truly need CD25 in the body was untested.

The team examined children who received a CD25-blocking antibody after liver transplant. Their regulatory T cells persisted in vivo despite the blockade. CD25 therefore appears non-essential for maintaining human peripheral regulatory T cells, rewriting part of their survival manual.
plos-pone-0011884:
Rodrigo Fuentealba and co-workers traced in 2010 how the Alzheimer's-linked protein fragment Aβ42 gets inside neurons. Alzheimer's disease features early deposits of this fragment within vulnerable brain cells, before the better-known plaques form outside them. Faults in the cell's disposal compartments are suspected to play a part.

The team showed that a surface receptor called LRP1 handles much of this uptake and routes the fragment toward lysosomes, the cell's disposal units. A defined doorway changes the question from whether neurons take in Aβ42 to how that traffic is controlled. If the doorway or the routing can be adjusted, the buildup inside neurons might be slowed.
plos-pone-0011984:
Loïc Josseran and colleagues evaluated in 2010 a French surveillance system that watches emergency department data for early signs of health crises. Such syndromic systems promise fast answers for decision makers, but speed is worthless if the data are poor. The test case was a heat wave, tracked through the Oscour network of emergency departments.

The team assessed the quality and usefulness of the morbidity data the system gathered during that event. Heat waves kill quietly, mostly among the old and isolated, and hospitals see the wave before death registers do. A system proven on a real heat wave earns trust for the next emergency, whether it is weather, flu, or something new.
plos-pone-0012084:
Robert Gatenby and Roy Frieden argued in 2010 that electric fields inside cells may help route information, not just chemistry. Normal cell function needs signals to travel accurately from membrane receptors to the nucleus. Messenger proteins were thought to reach their targets by random walking, but random drift disperses them and garbles the message.

The authors propose that Coulomb interactions between the cytoplasm's electric fields and phosphorylated, electrically charged messenger proteins optimize that information flow. Charged messengers steered by fields would arrive faster and more faithfully than drift allows. The proposal is theoretical, but it gives cell biology a testable alternative to the random-walk picture.
plos-pone-0012184:
Victor Novack, Michael Pencina, Doron Zahger, and co-authors asked what routine blood tests say about survival after heart failure, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Patients rushed in with badly decompensated heart failure all get the same standard panel: blood counts, salts, kidney tests, sugar, and a few more. Several of those values individually hint at risk, yet doctors lacked a joined-up read of the whole panel.

The authors weighed how the panel as a whole relates to death within a month and within a year of admission. Using tests already drawn on every patient costs nothing extra and could sort patients by risk on day one. That sorting helps teams decide who needs the closest watch and strongest treatment.
plos-pone-0012284:
William Mathews, Edward Cachay, Joseph Caperna, and co-authors estimated how accurate anal cytology screening really is, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The screening, a Pap-style smear, hunts early cell changes that can precede anal cancer, a growing risk in HIV-infected adults. The gold-standard check, biopsy, is itself imperfect, which distorts every accuracy figure computed against it.

Using records from a screening program for HIV-infected adults, they adjusted their estimates for the biopsy standard's own errors. Honest accuracy numbers decide whether screening programs help or waste resources and worry patients needlessly. Their approach also teaches a general lesson for any test graded against a flawed ruler.
plos-pone-0012384:
Lieke van der Aa, Magdalena Chadzinska, Edwin Tijhaar and colleagues traced inflammation signals in fish in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. In humans, the chemokine CXCL8 calls white blood cells to infected tissue. Fish carry many similar signals, but how they relate to the human one, and which do its job, had been murky.

The team sorted the fish versions into two lineages and tracked when each switches on during early inflammation. The two families showed distinct patterns, meaning fish split the job between them. Sorting out these signals helps fish health research, where infection losses are huge, and deepens the story of how immune signals evolved across vertebrates.
plos-pone-0012484:
Ludovic Reveiz, An-Wen Chan, Karmela Krleža-Jerić and colleagues audited how clinical trials report their methods on registries, in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Randomized trials are the gold standard of medical evidence, but poor reporting hides flaws. Registries were created so methods are declared in advance, letting readers check whether results were cherry-picked.

Pulling records through the World Health Organization search portal, the team found method details often missing or vague. A registry entry that omits key methods cannot do its quality-control job. The audit presses registries and sponsors to enforce complete reporting, which protects patients who volunteer for trials.
plos-pone-0012584:
Sharon Cresci, Janice Huss, Amber Beitelshees and colleagues studied a gene variant in heart patients with diabetes, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The receptor PPAR alpha responds to fatty signals and is switched on in diabetic hearts, where it may shape how heart muscle survives a blocked artery. A variant in its promoter, the gene's control region, caught the team's attention.

The variant weakened activation by a partner pathway called ERR and was linked to lower mortality after acute coronary ischemia in diabetic patients. A DNA difference that predicts survival after heart attack could guide monitoring and treatment intensity. It also flags the PPAR alpha pathway as a therapeutic lever.
plos-pone-0012684:
Nguyen, Chau, Perry and co-authors tested whether short bacteria-killing peptides can survive in blood serum. The peptides they built are rich in two amino acids, tryptophan and arginine, and were tweaked by capping their ends or closing them into rings. Their 2010 study asked how long each version lasts before serum breaks it down.

Lasting longer is essential if such peptides are ever to become real drugs. The tweaks that helped most point the way to sturdier designs. Peptide drugs could add options as bacteria grow resistant to standard antibiotics.
plos-pone-0012784:
Khoshnevis, Neumann and Ficner solved the shape of a yeast protein piece that grips RNA. The protein, eIF3b, belongs to the machine that starts protein building in cells. Its RNA recognition motif is the hand that holds the message being read.

Their 2010 crystal structure shows how the yeast version differs from the human one. Small shape differences can explain why the two machines handle messages differently. They also give drug designers footholds, since this machinery runs fast in cancers and is needed by many viruses.  Comparison across species is a strength of the study.
plos-pone-0323584:
Allison N Myers-Pigg and colleagues flooded a coastal forest on purpose to watch its first reaction to the kind of storm surge climate change is making routine. In this ecosystem-scale experiment, plots the size of several houses received nine hours of either fresh water or brackish water, mimicking heavy rain versus sea surge. Sensors tracked soil, water, and trees throughout.

The water system lurched, as expected, but most chemistry and vegetation measures barely moved, and salt water proved no worse than fresh in the short term. The forest, in other words, shrugged off a single novel soaking. Yet some belowground conditions swung sharply for a while, enough to nudge how the trees function. The authors frame the result as resistance with warning signs, baseline knowledge for judging what repeated storms will do.
plos-pone-0326984:
Umi Matsumura and co-authors compared how people who once sprained an ankle move during squats and walking. Some sprain survivors, called copers, return to full activity without lasting instability. Whether their movement truly matches uninjured people was unclear. The 2026 study fitted ten copers and ten controls with motion sensors and muscle monitors.

During half squats, copers rotated their thighs less than controls. Three leg muscles also fired less strongly in the coper group. The differences suggest copers quietly adopt a protective movement style even when they feel fully recovered. Matsumura and colleagues say training programmes should notice such hidden adaptations, since they may shift load to other joints over time.
plos-pone-0332684:
Blue cone monochromacy leaves boys and men unable to tell red and green apart, and one faulty letter in a cone pigment gene is its most common cause. Marion E Cahill and colleagues engineered mice carrying the equivalent fault on a retina made only of cones, in this 2026 PLOS One study.

The mice lost their light responses and their cone tips shrank, mirroring the human disease's blind spot region. Chemical profiling showed stressed, altered retinal metabolism. A gene therapy virus delivering a healthy human pigment gene restored light responses and rebuilt cone tips, in both young and older treated animals, lasting at least five months. The rescue supports human trial hopes.
plos-pone-0332784:
