Children with physical disabilities get fewer chances at organized community sport than their peers. Karen Davies and colleagues present a plan, in PLOS One in 2026, for a scoping review of how such programs are evaluated, focusing on young people up to age twenty-five.

The review will judge studies through two lenses: one framework tracking reach, impact, and upkeep of programs, and another grading the quality of participation itself. Studies of children whose disabilities are only cognitive are excluded. As a protocol, the paper reports no findings. The finished map should show program designers what good evaluation looks like and where evidence is missing.
plos-pone-0334584:
Anne Pettikiriarachchi and a team of collaborators built a targeted weapon against cancers that overproduce a growth receptor called EGFR. Their 2026 paper describes a tiny engineered protein that homes to EGFR on tumour cells, carrying a cargo that mimics viral genetic material and tricks the cell into self-destructing. Crucially, the homing protein does not switch the receptor on, avoiding feeding the cancer.

In dishes, the complex killed tumour cells with medium to high receptor levels while sparking immune signals that recruited blood cells to attack neighbours. In mice, it slowed human tumour grafts. The authors see potential against colon, breast, and other EGFR-heavy cancers, pending much more development.
plos-pone-0335384:
Weige Yang and co-authors scored soil quality under planted forests in China's Qinling Mountains. Planted trees can rebuild poor soils, but which species help most was unmeasured locally. Their 2026 study sampled soils under five tree types and rated thirteen physical and chemical properties by two scoring methods.

Walnut plantings held the best soil by both methods, followed by black locust. A pine and a paper mulberry sat mid-table, and an oak type scored lowest. Five measures carried most of the signal, including density, acidity, and organic matter. A shortened scoring set reproduced the full results well. Yang and colleagues offer the ranking as guidance for choosing trees that restore mountain soils.
plos-pone-0335584:
Aman Singh and colleagues silenced two recycling genes, ATG5 and ATG7, in blood vessel lining cells to see whether the cell's clean-up system, autophagy, treats them as interchangeable. Both genes are essential for autophagy and both interact with a major growth signal that maintains vessel health. The 2026 experiments measured gene activity and cell behaviour after each knockdown.

The two silences produced clearly different fingerprints on the growth pathway's components. Losing ATG5 made the cells multiply and migrate more vigorously, while losing ATG7 had weaker, distinct effects. The authors conclude the genes play non-redundant roles in vessel biology, a distinction that matters if autophagy is targeted to treat vascular disease.
plos-pone-0339084:
Verena Paul and co-workers explore how children who survived cancer settle back into daily life in the first five years after treatment. Cure is not the end of the story: school, friendships, and routines can all suffer. Their 2026 study mixes interviews with thirty parents and surveys from more than two hundred fifty families, then maps how different struggles connect.

Survivors showed snags in schoolwork, social life, and everyday tasks. Learning, communication, and taking part in big life areas sat at the center of the web, pulling overall participation with them. Many children manage, but hidden difficulties can weigh heavily. Support that joins medical, school, and emotional help, the authors argue, beats treating each problem alone.
plos-pone-0343484:
Endashaw Terefe and colleagues scan the full genomes of native Ethiopian zebu cattle in a 2026 genetics paper. These cattle thrive in heat that stresses many imported breeds, and Ethiopia holds herds shaped by dry heat and by wet heat. The team reworked public gene data from dozens of animals and compared them with zebu and taurine breeds from other regions.

Dry-heat and wet-heat herds proved close cousins, yet each carried its own marks of natural selection. Dry-heat genes clustered around cell stress, energy parts, and blood vessel change, while wet-heat genes leaned toward defense against infection. A few genes appeared in both groups. The named candidates give breeders leads for cattle that stay productive as climates warm.
plos-pone-0346284:
Joan Badia, Maria Llambrich, Rocío López-Rubio, Horacio Saggion, and Raquel Cumeras published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. Their title is a play on a famous film: the silence of the labs. The topic is ethical oversight in metabolomics research, the study of small molecules in living samples.

Metabolomics uses human and animal samples at huge scale, which raises questions about consent, privacy, and review. The authors examine how ethics oversight actually works in this fast-moving field. Research ethics boards and metabolomics teams share an interest in whether current rules keep pace with what laboratories now can measure and share.
plos-pone-0346784:
Jeannette E. Cullum and co-workers test whether a yeast infection changes how tiny freshwater crustaceans swim. Germs can steer host behavior, which then shifts spread of disease and life in the food web. Their 2026 lab study infects small water fleas with a yeast and films their swimming over time, comparing them with healthy fleas.

Infected fleas covered less distance and swam more slowly than healthy ones. How deep they swam depended on both infection and time since it began. Slower, altered movement could change how often predators meet these fleas and how the yeast spreads through a lake. The results feed into models that try to predict disease in changing fresh waters.
plos-pone-0346984:
Rafaela Carapeto, Andrew Willis, and Frances Shiely read the leaflets given to people invited into clinical trials and measured how they balance hope against warning. Every trial volunteer in the United Kingdom and Ireland receives such a leaflet before consenting. The 2026 study coded two hundred twenty-eight leaflets from twenty-six trial units, counting words that stressed possible benefits versus possible harms.

Warnings took roughly two and a half times more space than benefits, and about seventy-two percent of leaflets leaned negative. Rules require clear warning, the authors note, but the imbalance may colour how people judge a trial. They recommend plainer guidance so leaflets present both sides fairly and readably.
plos-pone-0347184:
Lisane da Silva Oliveira led a team of nine authors on this 2026 scoping review of eating disorder screening in basic health care. Clinics that see patients first are well placed to catch these serious mental illnesses early, yet staff need tools proven to work. The team searched many databases and gray sources for validated screening approaches in teens and adults.

Only a small set of studies passed full review, and solid proof of accuracy was thin, especially for poorer countries and younger patients. Lack of training and time also blocked routine use. Oliveira's map shows clinics which tools exist and where stronger testing is still owed.
plos-pone-0347584:
Laetitia Rater, Debra Marais, and Aisling Kelly interviewed seven mothers who moved to the United Kingdom by choice, for work, study, or family, and then developed depression after giving birth. Postnatal depression strikes migrant mothers more often than others, yet their own accounts are rarely heard. The 2026 study used long, open interviews analysed for the meanings beneath the words.

The women described layers of disconnection, loneliness, despair, and grief, shaped by being far from family while learning to be mothers in a foreign system. Their stories also carried resilience and slow recovery. The authors argue these mothers need community support alongside medical care, and services that understand the migrant experience.
plos-pone-0347784:
Xuanying Shen and his team fixed a flaw in views of hills from space. Slopes that face from the sun look too dark in raw shots. That warps plant readouts for whole ranges. The team used shots of the karst hills of Guizhou, China. Their fix treats lit and dim zones in unlike ways. It also counts light that bounces in from near slopes.

The fix near wiped out the false link of bright and slope in low winter sun. Bad spots fell by more than nine in ten in winter. Plant readouts held far more true through the year. The team says the fix suits hard hill lands.
plos-pone-0348084:
Note on status: this is a protocol for a planned systematic review, by Jose Cruz-Cuevas and colleagues, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. The question is whether patients with infective endocarditis, a dangerous infection of the heart's inner lining, can safely switch from intravenous antibiotics to pills partway through treatment.

Standard care means weeks of intravenous drugs, often in hospital. A major earlier trial suggested switching to oral antibiotics worked for a narrow group of patients, but other studies disagree. The planned review will pool randomized trials and comparative studies in adults and weigh cure rates against harms. A clear answer could shorten hospital stays and cut costs without risking relapse.
plos-pone-0348184:
Maria Camila Londono-Mendez and colleagues followed forty one young beef heifers grazing in western Canada across summer and winter. Animals had first been sorted into efficient and less efficient eaters, based on how much feed they needed for their growth. Blood, weight, and belly temperature were tracked every few weeks, along with weather strain measures.

Efficient heifers showed signs of calmer stress chemistry in summer, with lower levels of one alarm marker. Less efficient animals ran hotter in parts of the summer day and carried more leptin, a fullness hormone, in winter. A calming brain chemical also split the groups when weather was mild. Season, the work shows, can hide or reveal what efficiency really costs.
plos-pone-0348284:
Jiayu Li and Shiming Hu ask how truth gets settled in Chinese online news when platforms, users, and the state all push at once. Three controversies were traced from first public feeling to final official closure. Lenses came from actor network theory, which treats platforms and rules as actors alongside people, and from mapping how disputes move.

Social platforms acted as choke points where public heat met state control. User posts raised feeling and scrutiny, while ranking systems and official writing steadied the final story. Truth, the authors argue, is not simply found. It is made jointly by people, platform logic, and government action, in a constant tug of negotiation.
plos-pone-0348584:
Xu Jun, Li Shasha, and Mao Dandan surveyed five hundred three nurses at two large hospitals in China about their quality of life. Rather than test one factor at a time, they used a set-based method that looks for combinations of conditions. Stress, distress, support, burnout, and work-family conflict were all measured.

Four different combinations led to a good quality of life, and each paired low strain with strong social support in some form. No single fix worked on its own; support from others appeared in every good path. Two combinations led to poor quality of life. For managers, the lesson is that nurse well-being comes in bundles, not single causes.
plos-pone-0348784:
Qiang Han and colleagues built a prediction model for one of China's best-known spirits, strong-aroma baijiu. Brewers steam and distill fermented grain, and small changes in process settings change how much liquor comes out. Their 2026 paper combines several machine learning ingredients: a flexible neural network design, a method that compresses tangled input data, and a swarm-based search that tunes the whole ensemble.

Tested against simpler versions, the tuned model predicted yield more accurately and was less prone to memorising its training data. It also ran efficiently. The authors argue distilleries could use such models to set process parameters before production rather than learning by trial and error.
plos-pone-0348884:
Haoyi Zhao and colleagues designed an algorithm for scheduling reconfigurable assembly lines, factory lines that must switch between many product variants. A good schedule must hold down changeover costs, balance work evenly across stations, and smooth the flow of parts, three goals that pull against each other. Their method uses a reinforcement learning agent to direct a toolbox of search strategies.

The agent learns, from live feedback during the search, which strategy to apply at each stage, choosing among swarm, teaching-based, whale, and wolf-inspired optimizers. A new leader-selection rule favors solutions that are both strong and long-lived. Better scheduling of flexible lines is central to mass customization, where factories win by making variety affordable.
plos-pone-0349284:
Ibrahim Erarslan, Miray Budak, and Devrim Tarakci report a small trial testing whether music can strengthen therapy for children who have attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. Thirty-nine children between five and twelve took part. Half received occupational therapy built around harmonica and drum activities, while the rest received standard structured therapy, once a week for six weeks.

Both groups improved in attention over the trial, and the music group gained more on attention than the comparison group. Gains in broader thinking skills and in caregiver strain were smaller and less clear. The authors suggest that rhythm and melody, matched to each child's needs, can make therapy sessions work harder, and they call for trials that use a wider range of instruments.
plos-pone-0349384:
Stomach cancer rates in South Korea have fallen since 2012, helped by national prevention programs. Ji Hyun Kim and colleagues mapped where cases cluster across more than two hundred districts, comparing the years just before and after the decline, in this 2026 PLOS One study.

Two mapping methods agreed on the high-risk and low-risk zones. Average rates dropped in both kinds of district, though the hot spots stayed hotter. The team then compared twenty-three geographic traits, from income to clinic access, between zones and periods. The work aims to aim screening and prevention money at the places that still carry the heaviest burden.
plos-pone-0349584:
Florence Gyembuzie Wongnaah and colleagues tracked full vaccination coverage for two year olds in Ghana across survey rounds from 1993 to 2022. Equity was cut six ways: mother age, wealth, mother schooling, town versus village, child sex, and region, using a world equity toolkit.

Coverage rose from about fifty six percent to about seventy two percent, peaking near seventy eight percent in 2008. Wealth, schooling, and town gaps shrank by 2022. Two gaps refused to close: children of teen mothers lagged by near twenty seven points, and regions split by near forty points. National averages flatter progress while place and young motherhood still decide a childs shots.
plos-pone-0349684:
Sandy Rao, Kristin Cleverley, and co-authors published a 2026 protocol for a review that will map how equity, diversity, and inclusion show up in research on college and university student mental health. Student mental health studies have multiplied, and inclusion has become a stated priority, yet nobody has charted how the two actually meet inside research practice. As a protocol, the document sets out a plan rather than findings.

The planned review will search six major databases plus grey literature, screen studies in duplicate, and extract how inclusion is defined and used at each research stage. Results will be mapped in tables and charts with descriptive summaries. The authors say the map will show where inclusion is genuine, where it is token, and where it is missing entirely.
plos-pone-0349784:
Hüseyin Cihat Solmaz and colleagues tested whether vitamin D can protect baby mice from brain harm caused when their mothers receive the anesthetic propofol during pregnancy. Anesthesia in pregnancy is sometimes unavoidable, yet propofol can injure the developing brain. Twenty pregnant mice were split into groups receiving vitamin D, propofol, both, or neither.

In the pups, vitamin D lowered the inflammation and cell-death signals that propofol raised in the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex, two regions vital for learning. Behavior tests at six weeks checked movement and anxiety. The result is early animal evidence, not a clinical recommendation, but it suggests a cheap and familiar nutrient might blunt a real risk worth studying further.
plos-pone-0349884:
Steven David Pickering, Dorothy Yen, and co-authors surveyed adults in England about trust in the National Health Service, comparing ethnic minority and White respondents. Minority patients often report worse experiences, and the study asked where exactly the gap lives. Their 2026 survey of more than eleven hundred adults covered communication, ethics, competence, trust, and discrimination.

Minority respondents rated the service significantly worse on ethical behavior, personal care, trust in frontline staff, and perceived discrimination. The widest gap concerned the belief that how well the service treats you turns on your ethnicity or birthplace. Yet no differences appeared on honesty, keeping promises, general skill, or faith in those at the top. The authors conclude the divide is relational, rooted in day-to-day encounters rather than doubts about skill.
plos-pone-0350084:
Helena Pernice and co-authors described a registry for systemic amyloidosis at a Berlin centre in 2026. In this rare disease group, misfolded proteins build up in organs and slowly disable them, and varied courses make long term data precious.

The protocol sets out how patients are worked up, which clinical, lab, imaging, and genetic data are gathered, and how follow-up runs over time. Samples are banked and patients report their own outcomes. A single centre registry built this carefully can anchor wider collaboration, giving researchers the steady, comparable records that rare disease progress depends on.
plos-pone-0350184:
Marina Burakova tested a French-language questionnaire that measures a person's sense of occupational calling, adapted for volunteer firefighters who receive a stipend. Calling, the feeling of being summoned to meaningful work, can motivate deeply but also burn people out. Her 2026 study collected responses from more than eleven hundred volunteers online and checked whether the twenty-two-item scale measures what it claims, equally well across gender and age.

The scale held up: its scores were consistent, and its structure worked the same across groups. Facets behaved differently, though. Feeling summoned by something beyond oneself, and having the calling spill into all of life, tracked with negative outcomes, while purposefulness predicted nothing. The author discusses calling as a double-edged sword and what that means for supporting volunteers.
plos-pone-0350284:
Yu Deng, Lu Jiang, and Juan Wang built a risk scoring method for ice floods on the Yellow River in Inner Mongolia. When river ice jams and breaks, flooding can strike fast during the winter-spring thaw, threatening homes and slowing the region's economy. Standard assessment methods handle the deep uncertainty in such hazards poorly. Their 2026 study merged two mathematical approaches designed for fuzzy, uncertain judgments into one model.

Applied to three reaches of the river, the model rated two counties as medium risk and one banner district as high risk. Those ratings matched the pattern of past disasters closely, which the authors take as a check on the method's reliability. They offer the framework as a firmer basis for planning defenses and responses along cold-region rivers.
plos-pone-0350384:
Silvia Spivakovsky, Joyce Figueroa, and Ryan Richard Ruff built and checked a Spanish oral health knowledge quiz for Spanish speaking adults in the United States. One hundred and seventy five adults at a New York dental college, most born abroad, took the spoken quiz plus two comparison tools. Scores were checked for consistency, agreement between raters, and gains with schooling.

Average knowledge was low. Quiz consistency was good and rater agreement high. Scores tracked a broader knowledge tool moderately and rose with education, as a valid quiz should. Fit checks for its factor pattern were middling. A trusted Spanish quiz lets clinics spot knowledge gaps and tailor teaching for a group facing steep dental gaps.
plos-pone-0350484:
Steffen De Vreese and seven colleagues map the dolphin ear in fine detail in this 2026 anatomy study. Dolphins hear underwater through a specialized apparatus of bone, fat bodies, air sinuses, and nerves, but how these parts interconnect, especially the nerve supply, was poorly mapped. The team combined dissection, contrast-enhanced micro-CT scanning, tissue microscopy, and high-resolution confocal imaging across several dolphin species.

They charted the acoustic fat bodies, including a little-known rearward extension, and traced the branching of the main jaw nerve. Around the ear canal they found a layered web of blood vessels and sensory structures, including touch corpuscles that merged and split into a continuous three-dimensional nerve network. The authors conclude the outer ear region works as a sophisticated sense organ in its own right, likely helping dolphins judge pressure and position in the water.
plos-pone-0350584:
Quercetin, a plant compound in many foods, slows liver cancer cells in dishes, and Zhijuan Wang and colleagues tested how it acts against liver cancer tied to hepatitis B virus. Their 2026 PLOS One study combined cell tests, computer target hunting, and mouse tumors.

The compound curbed cancer cell growth, movement, and colony formation. Network analysis pointed at a growth signal switch on the cell surface, and lab checks confirmed the pathway quieted. Tumors in mice responded, and pairing quercetin with a drug that blocks the same switch strengthened the effect. The authors present the mechanism as a lead for further drug work, not a treatment yet.
plos-pone-0350884:
Zhongzheng Li and five colleagues design scheduling software for hydrogen based microgrids that keeps operators' private data private, in PLOS ONE in 2026. A microgrid juggling solar power, batteries, heat, and hydrogen storage must coordinate with neighbors, but the back and forth messages can leak how each site runs. Their framework pairs day ahead distributed planning with rolling short term control, and scrambles the exchanged numbers with noise that fades over time.

The fading noise scheme closed most of the cost penalty that privacy usually imposes, nearly matching a fully open central plan, and reached agreement in fewer rounds than fixed noise. Attack tests that try to reconstruct private values from the message trail found a real trade off, more exposure late in the process. The authors present the balance honestly: privacy here is a dial, and their method turns it more efficiently.
plos-pone-0350984:
Lu Zhang and colleagues tested a multi-ingredient treatment for diabetic nerve damage in rats in 2026. The painful condition, a common result of type two diabetes, is tied to inflammation and a disordered immune response.

Diabetic rats got the treatment for eight weeks. Nerve signal speeds, behaviour, and nerve tissue all improved compared with untreated diabetic animals. Gene activity in the spleen shifted in immune pathways, and related proteins in the sciatic nerve changed too. The exploratory results suggest calming immune signals may protect nerves, a lead that needs testing before any thought of human use.
plos-pone-0351084:
Some heritage trips stay with travelers for years, and Ming Lou and colleagues asked what turns a visit to a living craft tradition into a profound experience. Their 2026 PLOS One study built a model from online accounts of Chinese intangible heritage tourism.

Four building blocks emerged: the conditions on offer, how visitors judge the experience, what it means to them personally, and what it means socially. Fifteen finer categories fill the frame. Skilled service, fresh content, atmosphere, modern technology, and social interaction set the stage; feelings of participation, wonder, and immersion carry the middle. The model gives heritage sites a design checklist beyond ticket sales.
plos-pone-0351884:
Somayeh Taghidoust Chahardeh, Seyyed Hosseini, and Ali Shamsi Majelan compared three warm-ups in elite female taekwondo athletes. Thirty-six athletes took part. After a standard treadmill warm-up, each group used a different method. The choices were dynamic stretching, foam rolling, and resistance band drills. Wearable sensors then measured the force and timing of drop jumps.

The groups differed in push-off timing, force, and power. Dynamic stretching raised push-off force and power the most. Foam rolling primed a different mix of jump traits. In a sport built on sudden kicks, the warm-up is not a ritual. It tunes the exact jump the athlete is about to use. Coaches can pick the drill that fits the day's need.
plos-pone-0351984:
Changming Song, Yang Zhou, and Wenguang Ji improve face recognition when examples are scarce. Their 2026 paper proposes a sparse representation model built for exactly that shortage. A fusion dictionary blends complementary views of the face data. A nuclear norm term protects fine image detail during reconstruction. Errors are modelled with a blended distribution that tolerates both small noise and gross outliers, such as occlusion or bad lighting.

The mathematics stayed friendly. The model is convex, so a classic splitting algorithm solves it reliably. The authors prove the solver converges. Head-to-head experiments then did the persuading. Their method beat rival approaches on recognition rate and on robustness together. Security and device unlocking both meet faces under poor conditions with few stored samples. A recogniser designed for scarcity, rather than despite it, fits how the technology is actually used.
plos-pone-0352184:
Sharif Alsoudi, Amina Benkouider, and Huda Al-Manjiya test whether a well-known well-being questionnaire works in Arabic, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study from Oman. The short survey measures positive mental health across emotional, social, and psychological well-being. More than eleven hundred adults aged eighteen to sixty-five completed the Arabic version online.

Statistical checks supported the scale, with one strong general well-being factor sitting behind the three parts. Scores were consistent across the questions, and people with higher well-being tended to report lower anxiety. The authors conclude the Arabic scale is a sound, brief tool for studying positive mental health in Oman and other Arabic-speaking settings.
plos-pone-0352384:
Kimia Taki and Bahram Hosseinzadeh Samani present this 2026 PLOS One simulation study of a solar-powered milk pasteurization system for off-grid dairies. Their design pairs solar heat collectors and photovoltaic panels with a venturi reactor and cold plasma treatment, sized to handle several hundred liters a day. Performance was modeled for three Iranian cities with cold mountain, hot dry, and hot humid climates.

The system held its target pasteurization temperature in all three settings, with solar energy supplying up to about a third of the energy needed, depending on place and season. The hot desert city offered the richest solar resource, while the mountain city gave the steadiest spring and summer heat. The authors conclude the hybrid design can meaningfully cut fossil fuel use for milk safety in remote areas.
plos-pone-0352584:
Michael Zakharin and Timothy Bates examine how moral values vary with age and gender in a 2026 study. They used a modern questionnaire that measures moral foundations. These include care, equality, loyalty, authority, and purity. Their samples covered more than eight hundred Americans and over sixteen hundred people in the United Kingdom.

Respect for loyalty, authority, and purity rose steadily with age in both countries. The yearly rise was small, but it built into a large gap between youngest and oldest adults. Concern for equality faded with age, while care stayed level. Women scored higher on care and equality. Men scored higher on the binding values of loyalty, authority, and purity. The patterns suggest that generational moral change is gradual, not a sudden break.
plos-pone-0352684:
Haibo Lyu and three co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One soil study on weathered granite soil reused as foundation fill. The safety of that reuse depends on how the soil is packed down. The team prepared samples across a range of starting moisture levels. They packed them at varied effort levels. Then they measured how easily water seeps through, and how much the soil compresses under load.

Packing effort dominated seepage. Squeezing harder cut water flow sharply, until it leveled off. Wetter starting soil deformed more under load. The authors blame thicker water films coating the grains. Harder packing stiffened the soil and shrank its pore space. They built a formula that predicts seepage from packing effort. It matched their measurements closely, and they offer it for designing safer fills.
plos-pone-0352784:
Mandari and Nyundo present a 2026 protocol for a study of depression after stroke in Dodoma, Tanzania. Depression strikes many stroke survivors, worsens recovery, and raises the risk of another stroke and of death, yet in this setting its frequency and causes are barely documented. The study will follow adults admitted with a first stroke at referral hospitals.

Patients will be enrolled within two weeks of the stroke and checked at one and three months. A standard interview will confirm major depression and screen out anyone with a past history, while a nine-question scale will track severity over time. Social and medical details gathered at admission will be tested as predictors. Care will be taken with consent and data sharing under local ethics approval. As a protocol, the paper promises a careful design; its findings on how common post-stroke depression is, and who is at risk, will follow.
plos-pone-0352984:
Mert Keles and six colleagues compare two ways of spotting early bone change around dental implants in a 2026 study. Standard panoramic measures, like cortical width, may miss subtle shifts in spongy bone. Fractal analysis offers a finer tool. It scores the complexity of bone texture visible on X-rays.

The study covered sixty single-tooth implants, imaged at placement and again three months later. Fractal scores rose significantly in every region around the implants. The conventional width and index measures, by contrast, showed no change. Gum inflammation also eased over the same period. Fractal analysis therefore detects healing changes months before standard measures move, which could help dentists judge implant success earlier and more reliably.
plos-pone-0353184:
Toompere and colleagues sorted clinic visitors in Estonia into risk profiles for sexually spread infections in a 2026 study. More than eleven hundred people seeking testing answered questions about partners, condom use, past infections, and substance use. Grouping patterns can guide prevention better than one general message.

Three profiles appeared for men and three for women. The largest male group reported many partners with raised risk habits, while another male group carried many overlapping risks plus past infections. Female groups split by new partners, condom consistency, and partner-linked exposure. Clinics can use such profiles to focus talks on condoms, partner notice, and substance use where each profile needs it most.
plos-pone-0353284:
DiLillo and colleagues estimated past COVID-19 exposure in Kenyan children with cancer in a 2026 study. Blood samples collected from 2014 to 2022, from children with and without cancer, were tested for antibodies to the pandemic virus and to older common cold coronaviruses. Grouping methods flagged children whose pandemic-virus signals rose above pre-pandemic levels.

Hospital care during the pandemic raised fears of extra infection risk for these children, yet data were scarce. Antibody patterns also tested whether past cold viruses shaped responses to the new one. Evidence like this helps cancer centers in low-resource settings weigh isolation burdens against real exposure risk.
plos-pone-0353384:
Li and Shi surveyed what drives people to use AI fitness assistants in a 2026 study. Chat-based coaches can draft and refine training plans, but users weigh quality against risk. More than three hundred questionnaires fed a model linking system quality, social norms, attitudes, and sense of control to intention to use.

Higher system quality tied strongly to friendlier attitudes and stronger felt control. System quality carried the greatest weight within overall quality. Perceived value helped turn those views into actual intention. Builders of fitness AI should thus polish reliability and clarity first, since users judge the whole category by the quality they experience.
plos-pone-0353484:
Cui Jian and co-authors surveyed Chinese hospital laboratories on how they handle respiratory samples and test for pneumococcus. Consistent processing and drug-resistance testing guide treatment of pneumonia, a major killer. Their 2026 national survey drew several thousand valid replies from hospitals in the national resistance surveillance network.

Sputum was the most common sample type, ahead of blood and urine. Most laboratories stained sputum and lung washings routinely and applied the same cell-count rule to accept or reject sputum. Identification leaned on classic chemical tests and automated cards, with mass spectrometry in a minority of labs. Jian and colleagues map wide practice variation that national standards could narrow.
plos-pone-0353684:
Shaoqiang Wang led a team of eight authors on this 2026 medical imaging paper about outlining thyroid lumps in ultrasound scans. Nodules vary in size and blur at the edges, so software has to hold fine detail and wide context together. Their network stacks two U-shaped stages for a rough then refined outline, with modules that model long-range patterns cheaply and spotlight key features.

On standard tests the design beat leading rival methods on most core measures. Wang releases the code openly, aiming at more reliable computer help for thyroid diagnosis.
plos-pone-0353784:
Petr Bahenský and five colleagues strap breathing monitors to competitive runners to see how a respirator mask changes the mechanics of breath, in this 2026 PLOS ONE trial. Twenty young runners, ten men and ten women, ran a graded treadmill test twice — once masked, once not — while sensors divided each breath among upper chest, lower chest, and belly. Overall air volume and breathing rate stayed the same with the mask on.

Underneath, the pattern shifted at high effort: the upper chest contributed less and the belly more. Women tended to favour the upper chest more than men, though with wide variation. Masks do not suffocate trained runners, the authors conclude, but they quietly reroute the work of breathing.
plos-pone-0354184:
Li and colleagues, in a 2026 study, wrap a common cholesterol drug in a disguise made from platelet skins to treat ischemic stroke. Simvastatin can help repair the blood-brain barrier and calm inflammation after a stroke, but little of it reaches the brain, and high doses risk side effects. Platelets naturally home to injured blood vessels, so their membranes make a smart cloak.

The team coated drug-loaded particles with platelet membrane and confirmed the cloak took. In cell tests, the coated particles mopped up harmful oxygen chemicals and nudged immune cells from an angry state toward a healing one. In rats with stroke, the coated drug shrank the damaged brain area far more than the plain drug. Over three weeks, treated animals regained movement and weight faster. The authors present the platelet cloak as a way to get more benefit from an old drug at a lower dose.
plos-pone-0354384:
Yujia Huang, Chaojun Shan, Xueni Xiao, and Chuanya Huang present a protocol, published in 2026, for the first systematic review of computer models that predict which nurses will quit. Hospitals worldwide bleed nursing staff, and prediction models have multiplied, but nobody has audited their quality or compared their performance in one place.

The registered review will search nine English and Chinese databases for model-building studies, extract each model's ingredients and accuracy, and grade bias risk with a standard tool designed for prediction research. Two reviewers will work independently, with a third settling disputes. The finished synthesis aims to tell administrators which models, if any, deserve trust when planning retention spending, and where model builders keep going wrong.
plos-pone-0354484:
Demeke and colleagues, in a 2026 review, pool what is known about work-related muscle and joint disorders among nurses in Ethiopia. Nurses lift, bend, and stand for long shifts, and these disorders are among the most common job-related health problems anywhere. No pooled national figure existed, so the team gathered the Ethiopian studies and combined them.

Sixteen studies covering nearly six thousand nurses gave a pooled rate of about six in ten nurses affected. Four factors raised the odds: being female, job stress, long periods of standing, and five or more years of experience. The authors judge the burden considerably high and point to practical fixes, including supportive management and ergonomic training. A fuller, careful review design, with quality checks and bias tests, backs the headline number. The paper gives hospital leaders in Ethiopia a national benchmark to argue from.
plos-pone-0354684: Candida infections in a Colombian high-complexity hospital — a decade of epidemiology. This Tolima study covered 2014–2024. The findings track fungal threats through ten years — guiding antifungal stewardship where resistance is rising.
plos-pone-0354884:
Claudia Stracke and seven colleagues report a subgroup analysis from a German randomized trial, published in 2026. The trial tested decision coaching for healthy women who carry a cancer-risk variant in the BRCA1 or BRCA2 genes. These women must weigh preventive surgery against intensified screening while also deciding about having children, an unusually tangled choice. The coaching program paired personal sessions with a structured, evidence-based decision aid; the comparison group received usual care.

Women whose family planning was still open started with more decisional conflict than those whose families were complete. Coaching reduced conflict across the trial, and the open-family-planning women in the coaching group improved the most. Among initially undecided women in that subgroup, far more coached women had reached a decision by twelve weeks, and more chose intensified breast surveillance. The authors say tailored coaching seems especially valuable where prevention and childbearing collide.
plos-pone-0355284:
Yujiao Dong and co-authors investigated a cell-surface protein, CD93, in stomach adenocarcinoma, a leading cause of cancer death. The protein had been tied to vessel growth and spread in other solid tumours. Their 2026 study checked its levels in tumour data and patient samples, then raised and cut it in cultured cancer cells.

Tumours carried far more CD93 than normal tissue, and high levels tracked with shorter patient survival. Extra CD93 made cancer cells multiply faster and helped vessel cells form tubes, a step in building tumour blood supply. Animal grafts tested growth effects in living tissue. Dong and colleagues nominate CD93 as a marker of aggressive disease and a possible treatment target.
plos-pone-0355384:
Chioma Mbachu and colleagues launch in 2026 a screening study across Nigeria for Fragile X disorders in children with learning and development problems. Little is known about these genetic conditions in Nigeria, and no national figures exist. Six hospitals, one in each region, will enrol children with intellectual disability, autism, or broad developmental delay.

Dried blood spots will travel to a central lab for gene testing that sizes a repeated DNA stretch. Families of children who test positive will get careful explanation, counselling, and referral, with one drug treatment offered for the full syndrome. Results aim to give first prevalence figures and build local testing skill.
plos-pone-0355484:
Elaine Berkery, Nuala Ryan, and Helen Purtill ask in 2026 what makes nurses in Ireland want to move into management. Nurses from a group of public hospitals answered questions about themselves, their jobs, and their workplace. Shortages of nurse managers give the question practical weight for planning who leads wards in future.

Many traits linked to management ambition in simple checks, with bouncing back from setbacks the strongest. When factors were tested together, holding a higher degree and stronger resilience stood out on their own. The authors suggest backing further study and building resilience could grow a steady supply of future managers.
plos-pone-0355684:
Asebe Hagos and colleagues measured the urban-rural gap in treatment for childbirth complications in Ethiopia. Emergency obstetric care saves mothers, yet access splits sharply by place. Their 2026 study used a national cohort of postpartum women who reported complications, then decomposed the gap to find what drives it.

About six in ten women received treatment for their complications. Urban women were treated at higher rates than rural women. The decomposition method separates the gap into parts explained by differing characteristics, like education and wealth, and parts explained by differing returns to those traits. Hagos and colleagues argue closing the gap needs targeted rural investment, not only national averages that hide it.
plos-pone-0355784:
Danielle Barth and seven colleagues, with a large collaborating team, test whether the grammar of a language predicts how often its speakers talk about family, in this 2026 cross-linguistic study. Kinship organizes every human society, yet languages differ in how much grammatical machinery they devote to relatives. Using a picture-based communication task, the team measured the share of references to people that were phrased as kin terms across twenty-two typologically diverse languages.

That share differed between languages. Four candidate influences all mattered, including the complexity of each kin vocabulary, the kind of interaction, and the topic at hand. The headline result concerns grammar itself: languages with grammatical means for encoding kinship, a feature the authors call kintax, led their speakers to choose kin words more often. The finding supports the old hypothesis that grammars code best what speakers do most, and shows the traffic runs both ways.
plos-pone-0355984:
Sara Hosseinpoor and colleagues layered systems biology and machine learning over blood gene data to nominate molecular leads for autism spectrum disorder. Their 2026 study combined differential expression and gene co-expression networks. It added protein interaction maps and two feature selection algorithms. The winners were then checked in a rat model of autism induced by a prenatal drug exposure.

Two genes survived every filter: TLR8, an immune sensor, and CASP4, an inflammation-linked executioner protein. Both ran higher in the model animals. TLR8 rose in blood and brain, and CASP4 in brain alone. Network analysis attached a few small regulatory RNAs to each. The authors frame the pair as candidate biomarkers. Their immune flavor reinforces the view of autism as partly an immune story.
plos-pone-0356184:
Amy B Rubis and colleagues summarize United States surveillance for meningococcal disease across the first four years of the twenty twenties. The illness is rare but swift and deadly, so health officials track every case and fingerprint the bacteria by genome. Reports gathered through national systems covered well over a thousand confirmed and probable cases, with detailed strain typing.

Case rates bottomed during the pandemic's second year and rose to their highest in the final year studied. One bacterial group, type Y, climbed from a small share to more than half of cases, and within it a strain family once rare in the country came to dominate. Nine outbreaks began in the period, some years accounting for a large share of all cases. Rubis and colleagues say shifting strains must guide vaccine and response planning.
plos-pone-0356284:
Young Do Song and seven colleagues create two mouse models of retinal degeneration with different speeds of disease, in this 2026 study. Dry age-related macular degeneration, a leading cause of blindness, destroys the eye's support layer over years, and existing lab models mimic that slow course poorly. The team engineered mice to overproduce a protein called RIP3, which drives a form of cell death thought to be involved.

One line, with RIP3 raised throughout the body, lost retinal thickness and vision gradually over many months, much like the human disease, alongside steady inflammation. A second line, with extra RIP3 concentrated in the eye's support layer, degenerated within a couple of months. Together the pair gives researchers a matched slow and fast platform for tracing mechanisms and testing treatments aimed at this cell death pathway.
plos-pone-0356384:
Sobia Khan and colleagues tested a root-dwelling fungus as a helper for okra plants facing salt and cadmium stress. Salt and heavy metals cut okra yields worldwide, and friendly fungi can buffer plants against both. Their 2026 study took the fungus from wild jujube roots and applied it to okra under harsh growth conditions.

Treated plants grew notably taller and heavier than untreated stressed plants. Leaf green pigment more than doubled, and shoot dry weight rose over threefold. Stress hormone levels fell while growth hormones rose, and leaves stored more sugars and protective compounds. Khan and colleagues present the fungus as a candidate bio-tool for farming on salty, metal-tainted soils, pending field trials.
plos-pone-0356684:
Feng Gao and colleagues simulated the temperatures inside a coal shearer cable. This is the thick power cable that drags behind mining machines as they chew along a coal face. Sensor fibers are woven inside it. Their 2026 engineering study modeled three ways of embedding the optical fibers. It ran the virtual cable through straight and bending motion, at varying loads and room temperatures.

Bending was the enemy. Fiber temperatures jumped by roughly a dozen degrees compared with straight running. One fiber layout ran distinctly hotter than the other two. Heat also climbed with electrical load and ambient temperature. Fitted formulas now link the fiber's reading to the temperatures of the cable's core parts. That turns the embedded fiber into a trustworthy thermometer for a cable nobody can open underground.
plos-pone-0356784:
Roger Montenegro Mendoza and colleagues used Panama's 2019 national health survey to weigh the double burden of malnutrition among women of reproductive age: carrying excess weight and anemia at the same time. Their 2026 analysis estimated how common each condition is alone and combined among non-pregnant women aged fifteen to forty-nine, and modeled which social and biological factors travel with the combination.

Nearly one woman in five carried the double burden. It clustered among women in their forties, those who had given birth, those with little schooling, and above all those with high inflammation, whose odds ran many times higher. The authors argue Panama's nutrition programs, built for a thinner era, must now treat under- and over-nutrition as one intertwined problem.
plos-pone-0356884:
Abdulwali Sabo and colleagues checked whether a questionnaire about social determinants of health, the living conditions that shape illness, measures the same thing in two very different countries. Their 2026 study surveyed 860 university students, half in Malaysia and half in Nigeria, and tested a trimmed version of the questionnaire with twenty questions grouped into structural and day-to-day factors.

Statistical checks showed the two-factor version held together well in both samples, with strong internal consistency and stability over retesting. Formal invariance tests passed, meaning scores can be fairly compared across the two settings rather than reflecting translation quirks. A validated shared instrument lets researchers study how housing, work, and policy shape health across countries on equal footing.
plos-pone-0357284:
Turki A Alamoudi and Saif A Alarifi worked on safer roadsides for rural highways in Saudi Arabia, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Crashes in which cars leave the road or roll over are among the deadliest on rural roads. The roadside clear zone, the open space kept beside the road, decides how forgiving the road is when a driver errs.

Alamoudi and Alarifi built an evidence-based design for those clear zones, tuned to Saudi rural highways. Their rules give road engineers proven ways to cut deaths from vehicles leaving the road. Roadsides designed to forgive mistakes save people who would otherwise hit poles, ditches, or steep slopes. Local evidence matters because speeds, vehicles, and terrain differ from the countries where older standards were written.
plos-pone-0357384:
Shimeng Wang and co-authors survey late teenagers to untangle how physical activity relates to executive function, the mind's control system. Activity is often assumed to sharpen thinking, yet the psychology between them is murky. Several hundred students aged seventeen to nineteen reported activity, two kinds of rumination, and mindfulness, and completed three timed computer tasks covering focus, memory updating, and switching.

Surprisingly, higher activity tracked with slower task scores overall in this sample. Both kinds of rumination carried part of the link, and mindfulness changed how strongly activity fed into intrusive rumination and how rumination fed into performance. Wang and colleagues urge care in reading the result: the study is a snapshot, and its message is that activity and thinking connect through mental habits, not by a simple boost.
plos-pone-0357484:
Yan Shen, Wenxiu Hu, and Xin Wang study whether knowing how to use digital money tools changes how Chinese households spend. Using a national household finance survey, they link digital financial skill with total spending and with the mix of what families buy. The work asks a policy question directly: can teaching digital finance skills lift demand, especially where incomes are low?

Higher digital skill tracked with higher total spending, and the link ran strongest among low-income households. Borrowing was the main channel connecting skill to spending, with investing and insurance playing smaller parts. The mix of spending, however, did not shift in a robust, systematic way. Shen and colleagues say skill programs can lift spending, but changing its shape needs help from education, health, and cultural policy too.
plos-pone-0357584:
Hongxia Guo led a team of six authors looking for prognostic signs in lung cancer, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Melatonin is best known for governing sleep, but its related genes form a network with wider effects. The team studied genes tied to melatonin in lung adenocarcinoma, a common form of lung cancer.

Guo's group found that a signature made from those genes carries prognostic value, separating patients by likely course. Oncologists could use such a signature to forecast which patients face the toughest outlook and treat them accordingly. Gene signatures are cheap to run once defined, so a validated one can spread fast. The study adds a sleep-related angle to a field that usually looks elsewhere for its markers.
plos-pone-0357784:
David Coy-Mesa, Yilsy Núñez Guerrero, and Gustavo Morales-Alonso published a 2026 qualitative study in PLOS ONE on why some people get left out of the sharing economy. Platforms for rides, stays, and bookings assume confident app users, yet digital skills and access are uneven. The authors ran two focus groups with adults in Madrid, then analyzed transcripts with a structured qualitative method plus text-mining tools.

Five linked barriers shaped participation: how usable the platforms felt, the technology itself, personal digital skills, trust and safety worries, and other limits such as payment conditions. People with weaker skills or fewer resources described these barriers stacking on top of each other until taking part stopped feeling worth it. Exclusion, they argue, comes not just from lacking internet access but from design, trust, and payment rules too, and the framework is offered to designers and policymakers aiming at fairer platforms.
plos-pone-0357984:
Kyoung Hye Kong, Kyungwon Yang, and Jung-Hwa Ryu published a 2026 cell study in PLOS ONE on a gut-made toxin that builds up in kidney failure. The toxin damages blood vessels in dialysis patients. The toxin, indoxyl sulfate, drives inflammation in macrophages, the immune cells that also manage cholesterol. Because kidney patients are often short of vitamin D, the team pretreated lab macrophages with its active form before exposing them to the toxin.

Vitamin D pretreatment calmed several inflammatory signals the toxin provoked and raised markers of the calmer, repair-style macrophage state. It also protected the cells' ability to unload cholesterol through their usual transporter channels, which the toxin otherwise disrupts and which matters for keeping vessel walls clear. Active vitamin D may defend vessel health in dialysis patients on two fronts, inflammation and cholesterol handling, though the work is so far only in cultured cells.
plos-pone-0358184:
Euntaek Yoon led a team of eight authors refining carbon-ion therapy planning for chest cancers, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Carbon-ion beams can hit tumors hard while sparing nearby tissue, but only if planners know exactly how the beam slows in the body. That slowing is captured by the stopping power ratio.

Yoon's team measured how using values from dual-layer spectral CT changes treatment plans built from standard single-energy scans. Sharper stopping power maps mean beams stop where intended, in the tumor, not beyond it. Thoracic cancers sit near the heart and lungs, so precision is not a luxury. The comparison helps centers decide whether advanced scanning is worth adopting for this demanding therapy.
plos-pone-0358484:
Yuhang Zhang and five colleagues score China's rules for selling prescription drugs online, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Beijing has loosened online sales since the pandemic years, but the rulebook is young and gaps could endanger patients. Using text mining and a policy scoring model with ten main variables, the team graded eighteen national policies issued between 1999 and 2023 for completeness and consistency.

The average score landed in the range the model calls good. Six policies rated excellent and twelve good, with none perfect and none failing. Current rules lean hard on smart, technology driven supervision, and the system has clearly matured over two decades. The authors still find room to strengthen several areas, which they leave unnamed in broad terms but frame as the next reform targets. The exercise gives regulators a measured baseline rather than impressions.
plos-pone-0359084: Ahmed, writing alone, published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on rebuilding torn tendons. The work develops scaffold and stem cell constructs that copy natural tendon traits, called biomimetic hybrids. The design was tuned for mechanical strength so the repair could bear load. The goal is a repair that restores a tendon's working strength, not just its shape. Tendon injuries are common and heal slowly.
plos-pone-0359784:
Chengqun She and colleagues searched in 2026 for signs in the body that two unlike diseases share. One is sepsis, the body's harsh, damaging response to infection. The other is a swelling of the aorta, the great artery, in the chest, which can burst with little warning. The team mined gene data with machine learning to find markers that flag both.

Their hunt centers on immune pathways, since inflammation runs through both diseases. A shared marker could help doctors spot either disease sooner, and could point to one treatment idea that serves both. The work is done on computers, using data gathered by others. Its candidate markers still need tests in the lab and the clinic before they can be trusted.
pmc-13217184:
Elbeltagi and colleagues review drug treatment for autism spectrum disorder in children. Autism brings varied challenges, and no approved drug treats its core social and communication differences. Medicines are therefore aimed at problems that ride along with it, such as aggression, irritability, gut trouble, and sleep disturbance.

The review weighs five major drug classes for benefit and harm. It also judges early work on biomarker-guided care, where a child's biology might steer drug choice. Controversies run through the field, from weak trial evidence to long-term safety worries. The authors call for careful, individual prescribing, and for trials that match treatments to the children most likely to gain.
pmc-13237284:
Abdeltawab and colleagues train object-detection AI to read fused PET and CT scans of lymph node tumours. Lymph nodes guard the immune system and guide cancer treatment choices. Judging whether a node holds tumour is tricky, and a wrong call cuts both ways: too little treatment, or surgery harsher than the disease demands.

Their system finds nodes on scans that blend metabolic glow with anatomical detail, then classifies them automatically. Errors in node status raise recurrence risk and surgical complications, so a tireless second reader could steady staging. The study tests whether detection models, proven on photos, can carry that accuracy into fused medical images.
pmc-13240184:
Pan and colleagues pin down the small set of master switches that turns on production of the cancer drug paclitaxel in yew cells. The drug is scarce in nature and hard to build chemically, so supply stays tight. The team grew cultured yew stem cells, a system where a plant hormone already boosts output, and searched the cells' control network comprehensively.

They found that a minimal network of transcription factors, proteins that switch gene sets on, suffices to drive the drug's manufacture. That is a practical prize: instead of coaxing the whole tree pathway, engineers can flip a few switches. It opens a cleaner route to growing the drug in cell cultures at useful scale.
pmc-13240884:
Dong and colleagues in Chengdu modeled how starting hormone levels steer each stage of a first fresh IVF cycle. Static predictions miss that success unfolds through several gates. Their cohort covered twelve thousand six hundred seventy-four Chinese women. A multistate model tracked biochemical pregnancy, clinical pregnancy, and live birth as separate transitions.

Anti-Müllerian hormone, luteinizing hormone, and follicle count all acted non-linearly. Mid-range windows, not the highest values, lined up with success, challenging the more-is-better habit. The first two hormone levels predicted progress at every stage. Follicle count weighed only for reaching the initial pregnancy, the model showed.
pmc-13241484:
Mercier's team in Birmingham asked caregivers whether online peer mentoring helps children with learning differences. Mentees carried labels like a named learning disorder and ADHD. Caregivers rated ten outcomes looking back, before mentoring and since it began. Anxiety, sleep, self-care, behavior, and confidence all featured.

Caregivers saw clear gains on every one of the ten outcomes. Gains spanned mood, behavior, planning, and social skills alike. No control group tempers the zeal, and recall may flatter the program. Mercier frames mentoring as a hopeful support that merits strict controlled trials ahead. The ratings came from caregivers alone.
pmc-13242484:
Candemir Özcan and co-authors looked for hormone links to the width of the optic nerve sheath in healthy female dogs. Their study appeared in Veterinary Research Communications in 2026. The sheath's diameter, measured by ultrasound through the orbit, serves as a stand-in for pressure inside the skull. Thirty-four dogs of varied ages and sizes had the measurement taken alongside blood tests for estradiol and progesterone.

Progesterone showed a moderate negative link with sheath diameter: dogs with higher levels tended to have narrower sheaths. Age, body mass, and estradiol showed no clear relationship with the measurement. The authors are careful to call the progesterone finding modest and in need of confirmation. Even so, it suggests hormone state belongs on the list of factors vets should weigh when reading this scan. Reference values built without that context could mislead.
pmc-13242584:
Haiyan Liang and co-authors report the case of a young woman treated for aggressive lymphoma during late pregnancy. Their case report appeared in SAGE Open Medical Case Reports in 2026. At thirty-one weeks pregnant, she received a diagnosis of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma pressing on the great vein of the chest. The swelling caused superior vena cava syndrome, leaving her breathless and unable to lie flat.

She received a multi-drug chemotherapy regimen adapted for her situation, and the tumors shrank while her breathing eased. Doctors then delivered a healthy baby by cesarean section. A planned stem cell transplant was set aside because of her young age, and her overall outcome was judged satisfactory. Unusual natural killer cells seen early in treatment later disappeared, a detail the team flags for interest. The case supports chemotherapy as workable for mother and baby in late pregnancy.
pmc-13243184:
Minhong Zhao, Shuai Zhou, and Ying Zhang present a comparative report on paraquat poisoning that hides its cause. Their article appeared in Clinical Case Reports in 2026. Paraquat, a potent herbicide, destroys the lungs through scarring, and poisoning is called occult when the exposure is not obvious at presentation. Comparing cases across different exposure routes, the authors show how easily the diagnosis is delayed, and how delay worsens the outcome whatever the route.

Their management message is precision timing. Urine screening should start early whenever poisoning is suspected, rather than after symptoms declare themselves. Antioxidant and anti-fibrotic treatments should be scheduled around how the poison moves through the body in each route of exposure, aiming to blunt irreversible lung damage. The authors also call for stronger regulation and clinician awareness. The report's value lies in turning scattered hard cases into a shared playbook.
pmc-13244384:
Arman Sayuti and colleagues validated a stress hormone test for Sumatran elephants and then used it to ask what stresses the animals in rescue care. Their study appeared in Veterinary Medicine International in 2026. The subspecies is critically endangered, and Aceh Province's rescue units house twenty elephants aged ten to forty-nine. The team first proved a standard cortisol ELISA kit reads elephant samples faithfully, checking it against stress during medical treatment and recovery.

With the assay trusted, they modeled what moves cortisol day to day. Body condition, air temperature, humidity, and the combined temperature-humidity index all tracked with hormone levels across the six units. Leaner or more heat-pressed elephants carried different stress signatures than their peers. The authors argue managers now have a cheap, noninvasive gauge for welfare checks. Feed, shade, and workload decisions can be tested against the hormone rather than guessed from behavior alone.
pmc-13247984:
Reyes and co-authors describe a precarious neck-artery case in this 2026 Case Reports in Radiology report. A patient arrived with acute neck pain and visual disturbances. CT angiography showed the left vertebral artery had dissected at the second cervical level, bulging into a small pseudoaneurysm. The right vertebral artery was completely blocked from chronic disease. The injured vessel was therefore the brain's only posterior supply route.

MRI found no stroke, and the team chose conservative management with antiplatelet therapy rather than risking intervention on the sole remaining artery; symptoms improved. Recent methamphetamine use was noted as a likely contributor to the dissection. The case warns clinicians to recognize bilateral vertebral disease and read its imaging carefully. It also asks them to weigh substance use in dissection risk, especially when collateral flow cannot rescue a bad outcome.
pmc-13248984:
Ye and co-authors found that deleting part of a virus protein made it stickier, in a 2026 study. Their subject was a bacterial virus, a phage, that clings to gut mucus through a capsid protein called Hoc. Expecting a weaker grip, they used gene editing to remove the five building blocks thought to form the binding key.

Instead, the edited phage adhered to intestinal lining far better, in dishes and in animals. Structural analysis showed the deletion reshaped the protein and multiplied its binding spots for a sugar called fucose. The authors say the result breaks the simple lock-and-key picture and suggests designs for phages that linger in the gut as medicines.
pmc-13249984:
Iso and colleagues captured a rescue protein freeing a stuck ribosome, in a 2026 Nature Communications study. Ribosomes, the cell's protein factories, sometimes stall on troublesome messages, and in E. coli bacteria a protein called YheS specializes in freeing stalls caused by the SecM sequence. The team imaged the ribosome with a disabled version of the rescuer attached, at near-atomic resolution.

YheS docks at the ribosome's exit side and reaches in to shove the transfer RNA holding the unfinished chain. That nudge breaks the stuck chain's grip on the tunnel walls, and the density for the trapped chain largely vanishes in the images. Computer simulations supported the mechanism. The authors contrast this crowbar style with the cell's other, translocon-based rescue route.
pmc-13250084:
Gräf and colleagues tested a passive shoulder frame on women doing overhead drilling, in a 2026 crossover study. Fourteen women tightened twenty bolts into a sensor workstation, with and without the spring-assisted frame. Muscle activity, accuracy, and comfort were recorded in both rounds. Overhead work is a classic source of shoulder disorders, and such devices are rarely tested on women.

The frame cut shoulder muscle activity while the arm was lowering, and it lowered felt strain. But accuracy on target dropped, and users rated the device unacceptable, faulting its complexity and learning effort. The authors argue these aids need designs fitted to women, since help that ruins precision will be left in the locker.
pmc-13250384:
Yao and co-authors review how rice protein leftovers can be turned into valuable health peptides.
