Volume two of Tylor's Primitive Culture turns to religion itself. His famous theory of animism holds that belief in souls and spirits is the seed from which all religion grew. Early humans, he argues, reasoned from dreams and death to a world full of spirits.

From that seed Tylor traces growth: spirits of ancestors, gods of nature, and at last one high God. He also shows how old rites survive inside modern life, long after their meaning fades. Students of religion still start with animism, even when they argue against it. Tylor's calm, orderly case changed how the West explained faith.
tob-4184:
Diogenes Laertius compiled The Lives and Opinions of Eminent Philosophers around 200 AD, and C. D. Yonge's translation presents ancient philosophy's great gossip column. Thales falls down a well while stargazing. Diogenes the Cynic, living in his tub, tells Alexander the Great to step out of his sunlight. Epicurus's will disposes of his garden and his slaves' freedom.

Serious treatises omit such things; Diogenes preserves sayings, scandals, wills, and death stories for dozens of Greek thinkers, from the Seven Sages to the Stoics and Epicureans. Much would be lost without him, since the originals of many works perished. Philosophy with the bark on, the Lives remain the liveliest introduction to the Greek schools.
tob-4284:
Ancient Egyptians placed guides to the afterlife in tombs so the dead could pass safely through the underworld. E. A. Wallis Budge, the British Museum keeper of Egyptian antiquities, translated and edited those texts for English readers. His version of the Book of the Dead became the one most readers have known.

Inside are spells and prayers for breathing air after death, for not dying a second death, and for living on as a spirit. Chapter by chapter, the dead face judgment, demons, and dark gates. The work shows how strongly Egyptians hoped for life beyond the grave.
twain-huckleberry-finn-1884:
Mark Twain published Adventures of Huckleberry Finn in 1884, complete in the first edition text. Many call it the great American novel, the book modern American writing starts from in earnest. Twain set it in the slaveholding South of his own boyhood on the Mississippi River.

Huck, fleeing his drunk father's beatings, fakes his death and takes to the river. Jim, fleeing slavery, joins him on a raft down the wide Mississippi at night. Feuding families, con men, and a lynch mob test Huck's growing conscience on shore. He decides to help Jim though he believes it damns his soul to hell. Twain's vernacular voice and moral depth keep the book central and contested still.
un-ga-res-384:
Chinese troops had poured into Korea by the time the General Assembly passed Resolution 384 on 14 December 1950. The Assembly views the state of the Far East with grave concern. Its aim is twofold: keep the Korean fight from spreading to fresh ground, and end the fighting in Korea itself. A lasting fix for the open questions must then follow, on the terms of the Charter.

The vote asks the President of the General Assembly to form a group of three people, himself among them. The group must find the base on which a sound cease-fire in Korea can be struck. It must then report its counsel to the Assembly as soon as it can. The bid failed, and the war ran on for over two more years.
un-ga-res-a-69-84:
Radiation and its effects on people and the earth are tracked in Resolution A/69/84, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The work falls to the United Nations Scientific Committee on the Effects of Atomic Radiation, set up in 1955. The text voices worry at the harm that present levels of radiation may do to those alive now and to those yet to come.

The need to gather and weigh facts on atomic radiation grows, the text holds, as the stock of such facts grows in size and range. Fresh worry came from the wreck of the Fukushima plant in Japan in 2011, after the quake and wave that struck that year. The committee's work is backed, and its growing load is noted.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: General Assembly Resolution 384 (V) was adopted on 14 December 1950. It answered the entry of Chinese forces into the Korean War. The Assembly viewed the Far East situation with grave concern. It asked its president to form a group of three persons, himself included. The group was to work out the basis on which a sound cease-fire in Korea could be arranged. It was to report back with proposals as soon as possible.

Resolution 69/84, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session in 2014, concerns the effects of atomic radiation. It concerns the work of the United Nations Scientific Committee, set up in 1955 to study them. It commends the Committee's 2014 report on radiation exposure from the Fukushima Daiichi accident. The accident followed Japan's March 2011 earthquake and tsunami. It endorses its next global survey of medical radiation use and exposure. It stresses secure funding and wide publication of its findings.
un-sc-res-1284: Official record keeping at the United Nations preserves Resolution 1284, a Security Council text the catalog dates to 1995. A resolution may address a conflict, a court vacancy, a new member, or the running of the United Nations itself. Anyone studying UN practice can read the decision itself here, in the Wikisource transcription of the official record. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-1384:
On 14 December 2001 the United Nations Security Council adopted Resolution 1384 on Cyprus. The island's peacekeeping force faced another mandate deadline. Cyprus again agreed the force should stay. Limits placed on its patrols in June 2000 were still in force.

The Council extends the force, called UNFICYP, until 15 June 2002. It repeats the call to lift the limits placed on the force in 2000. The old military position at Strovilia should also be restored. The parties are pressed to treat missing persons as an urgent human issue. A report on the work is due by 1 June 2002.
un-sc-res-1484:
Fighting and atrocities in Ituri pushed the Council to act fast in May 2003. The town of Bunia in the eastern Congo faced a grave humanitarian crisis. On 30 May 2003 the Council authorized an emergency multinational force for Bunia. It would deploy until 1 September 2003. The force worked closely with MONUC troops already in the town. Its task was to steady security and improve conditions for civilians.

The deployment was strictly temporary. It bought time for the Secretary-General to reinforce MONUC in Bunia. States were called on to give troops, equipment, and money. The force acted under Chapter VII of the Charter. The French-led mission that followed became known as Operation Artemis.
un-sc-res-1584:
Côte d'Ivoire's arms embargo gained inspectors on the ground on 1 February 2005. The embargo had been set by resolution 1572 (2004) that November. Ceasefire breaches by Ivorian parties continued, and both the government and the Forces nouvelles owed full cooperation to UNOCI. African Union mediation under South Africa's president was under way.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council restated the embargo decision in full. It authorized UNOCI and the French forces backing it, within their means and areas of deployment, to monitor the embargo. They could inspect, without notice, the cargo of aircraft and vehicles and any site where they suspected arms were held. Seized weapons and documents were to be collected and disposed of safely. The Secretary-General was to set up a small expert group to gather and analyze information on arms flows. All Ivorian parties were told to give the inspectors free access at once.
un-sc-res-1684: Resolution 1684 stands in the Security Council's numbered run, held here as an English Wikisource transcription of the official record. Such acts are short by design, meant to be implemented rather than admired. Reading one closely shows how much weight a single operative verb can carry for the governments and missions it governs.
un-sc-res-1784:
The question of Sudan came to a vote in Resolution 1784, adopted on 31 October 2007. Work on the Comprehensive Peace Agreement lagged behind schedule. The pullback of forces due by 9 July 2007 was late and unverified. The north-south border still lacked marks on the ground, and Abyei stayed disputed.

The text extends the United Nations Mission in Sudan, called UNMIS, until 30 April 2008. Reports on the peace deal and the cease-fire are due every three months. Both sides must speed the pullback of forces and accept full monitoring in Abyei. The mission should help ready the census and elections, back disarmament work, and support the new Darfur mission as it takes over.
un-sc-res-1884:
UNIFIL was extended for a further year at Lebanon's request on 27 August 2009. The foreign minister's letter of 4 July asked for one more year without change. The Secretary-General advised the same on 6 August. Fresh breaches of resolution 1701 (2006) caused deep concern. The zone between the Blue Line and the Litani River had to stay free of arms outside the state's and UNIFIL's hands.

The Council extended UNIFIL's mandate until 31 August 2010. The force's positive role beside the Lebanese Armed Forces was praised once more. All parties were strongly called to respect the halt to hostilities and the Blue Line in its whole length, Ghajar included. The parties were urged to mark the Blue Line visibly with UNIFIL's help. The Secretary-General had to keep reporting on resolution 1701's working. The Council welcomed the coming findings of the force's strategic review.
un-sc-res-2684: On 2 June 2023, Resolution 2684 on Libya was adopted. An arms embargo on Libya has stood since 2011. Since 2016 the Council has let states inspect suspect ships on the high seas off Libya to enforce that ban. Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends those inspection powers for twelve more months. The Secretary-General must report on how the powers are used, first within six months and again within eleven.
un-sc-res-284: The text numbered Resolution 284 belongs to the Security Council's official record, catalogued at 1970. Year by year, these decisions build the written history of how the world body handled the crises of its time. The transcription keeps the preamble and numbered clauses in their official order, as the Council adopted them. As a public record, it has long been open to scholars and general readers alike.
un-sc-res-384: The record catalogued as Resolution 384, dated 1975, preserves one formal decision of the United Nations Security Council. The Charter gives the Council power to bind member states, which is why its resolutions are kept with such care. Here the primary source stands on its own, with the formal phrasing that lawyers and historians rely on. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-84:
One command for all forces in Korea was set up in Security Council Resolution 84, passed on 7 July 1950. North Korea's armed attack on the Republic of Korea had been held a breach of the peace. Member states had been urged to give the Republic such aid as it needed to throw back the attack and restore peace in the area.

The prompt and strong aid of states and peoples is welcomed. States that send forces are urged to place them under a single command. That command would be led by the United States, whose flag the force would fly beside the UN's own. Reports on the course of the war must come back to the Council. So began the U.S.-led UN war in Korea.
un-sc-res-884: Year 1993 in the catalog holds Resolution 884, a formal Security Council decision of the United Nations. Voting in the Council requires support from its permanent members, so each adopted text marks a point of agreement. Readers will find the full wording here, taken from the English Wikisource transcription of the UN official record. The entry belongs to the library's DECLASSIFIED group of public official records.
un-sc-res-984: The text numbered Resolution 984 belongs to the Security Council's official record, catalogued at 1995. Year by year, these decisions build the written history of how the world body handled the crises of its time. The transcription keeps the preamble and numbered clauses in their official order, as the Council adopted them. As a public record, it has long been open to scholars and general readers alike.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Security Council resolution 1284, adopted on 17 December 1999 under Chapter VII, rebuilds Iraq's weapons inspection system. It establishes the United Nations Monitoring, Verification and Inspection Commission, UNMOVIC, as a subsidiary body of the Council. UNMOVIC replaces the Special Commission (UNSCOM). It gives it the old commission's job of verifying Iraq's compliance with resolution 687 (1991). A reinforced system of ongoing monitoring and verification backs that work.

The Council decides that Iraq must allow UNMOVIC teams immediate, unconditional and unrestricted access to any site, record or person they wish to inspect. It keeps the IAEA in charge of the nuclear file, and has Iraq pay the full costs of both bodies. On the humanitarian side, it lets Iraq sell any volume of oil under the oil-for-food programme of resolution 986 (1995). It speeds approval of humanitarian goods. It asks for a high-level coordinator on missing Kuwaiti and third-country nationals and stolen Kuwaiti property.

On 14 December 2001 the Council returned to its oldest peacekeeping file: Cyprus. Resolution 1384 passed unanimously. The Secretary-General's report of 30 November 2001 had reviewed the UN operation there. It urged both communities to face the painful issue of missing persons. Cyprus's government agreed the UN force should remain.

Members extended UNFICYP's mandate until 15 June 2002. A report on progress was due by 1 June 2002. The text repeats a demand from the previous year. Turkish Cypriot restrictions on the peacekeepers, in place since June 2000, had to end. The military situation at Strovilia was to be restored. Routine renewals like this one kept the buffer zone stable.

Mass killing tore at Bunia, a town in Congo's Ituri region, in May 2003. Local militias fought for the town's streets. The UN force there was too thin to stop the bloodshed. The chief wrote on 15 May to plead for help. Congo's president backed the plea. Resolution 1484 passed with no dissent on 30 May 2003.

A stopgap world force could deploy to Bunia at once. Its life was fixed: to 1 September 2003. It would guard the airfield and camps for the displaced. If need be, it would shield townsfolk and aid staff too. Its troops could use all means the task required. In that gap, the UN force in Congo would grow stronger. All sides in Ituri were told to halt the fight at once.

Resolution 1584, adopted unanimously on 1 February 2005, gives peacekeepers in Côte d'Ivoire the job of hunting embargoed weapons. An arms embargo had been imposed in November 2004, and ceasefire violations by both the government and the Forces nouvelles kept breaking out despite the Linas-Marcoussis and Accra agreements. Both sides were reminded of their duty to honor the May 2003 ceasefire and shield civilians.

The Council authorized UNOCI, with the French forces supporting it, to monitor the embargo's implementation. That included inspecting, without notice, the cargo of aircraft and vessels and seizing illicit arms. The decision turned peacekeepers into customs enforcers for a war the Council was determined to starve of weapons.

Eleven permanent judges of the Rwanda war crimes tribunal have their terms extended on 13 June 2006. The judges had been elected in 2003 for four years ending in May 2007. Their trials, however, were not on course to finish within that time, and the Secretary-General had asked for the extension.

The eleven judges named in the text will stay in office until 31 December 2008, setting aside the usual term limits in the tribunal's Statute. States are also asked to keep working to ensure their nationals serving as ad litem judges can be made available to the tribunal. The aim is to keep experienced benches in place until the tribunal's remaining trials conclude.

Sudan's peace agreement is behind schedule in Resolution 1784, adopted on 31 October 2007. The Comprehensive Peace Agreement's deadline for verified redeployment of forces, 9 July 2007, had passed unmet. The North-South border was still undemarcated and the Abyei dispute unresolved. Displaced people were returning to the South, and UNMIS was also helping the new Darfur mission, UNAMID, take over there.

The Council extends the UN Mission in Sudan, UNMIS, until 30 April 2008. It demands full, fast implementation of the peace agreements and unrestricted UNMIS monitoring in Abyei. It urges both sides to pull their forces back from the disputed 1956 border line there. It also urges them to set up an interim administration. It presses for faster redeployment, working Joint Integrated Units, disarmament planning, and support for the national census and the elections and referenda the agreement promises. Reports are due every three months.

An isle of spice won its freedom days before this vote. Zanzibar left British rule on 10 December 1963. Its sultan took the throne of a free state. A bid for a UN seat came at once. Resolution 184 passed with no dissent on 16 December 1963. The vote shared a meeting with Kenya's own seat bid.

The Council told the General Assembly to admit Zanzibar. The Assembly did so with speed. The free state did not live long. A revolt toppled the sultan in January 1964. By April, the isle had merged with Tanganyika. That union grew into Tanzania. The UN seat passed to the merged state. This text marks one of the UN's briefest lives: a state that joined, fell, and merged in the span of a few months.

Southern Lebanon and the UN Interim Force there, UNIFIL, are the subject of Resolution 1884, adopted on 27 August 2009. Lebanon's government asked for one more year of the force with no change to its mandate. The Council voiced deep worry about breaches of Resolution 1701, which had ended the 2006 war. It worried about keeping the zone between the Blue Line and the Litani River free of armed groups other than Lebanon's own forces and UNIFIL.

The Council extends UNIFIL until 31 August 2010. It praises the force's work with the Lebanese Armed Forces in setting a new pattern in the south. It strongly calls on all sides to respect the halt to fighting and the Blue Line in full, guard UN staff safety, and give UNIFIL free movement. Reports on Resolution 1701 are to come every four months, along with a review of the force's size and gear.

Resolution 2684, adopted by the Security Council on 2 June 2023, renews the Libya arms-embargo enforcement regime at sea. Acting under Chapter VII, it extends for a further 12 months the authorizations set out in Resolution 2635 (2022). Those authorizations allow member states to inspect vessels on the high seas off Libya. The vessels are suspected of violating the arms embargo imposed by Resolution 1970 (2011). Member states may seize and dispose of banned items. The Secretary-General must report on implementation within six months and again within eleven months.

The Namibia question went to the International Court of Justice in 1970, sent there by Resolution 284. A sub-committee set up under Resolution 276 had suggested asking the Court for an advisory opinion. The Council agreed that the Court's answer would guide its next steps. The resolution was adopted on 29 June 1970.

The Council put a single question to the Court. What are the legal consequences for states of South Africa's continued presence in Namibia? Resolution 276 had already declared that presence illegal. The Secretary-General was told to send the resolution to the Court. All documents that could shed light on the question went with it. The Court was asked to give its answer at an early date.

East Timor slid toward war in December 1975 as Indonesian forces moved into the territory. East Timor had been a Portuguese colony, on the path to independence. Representatives of its people spoke to the Council in their own voice. Resolution 384 was adopted unanimously on 22 December 1975.

The Council recognized the right of the people of East Timor to self-determination and independence. It deplored Indonesia's military intervention. Indonesia was called on to pull all its forces out of the territory without delay. The Council also regretted that Portugal, the power in charge, had not fully met its duties. Portugal was told to work with the United Nations. The people of East Timor had to be free to choose their own future. A special envoy was to be sent at once to assess the situation on the ground.

The Korean War was two weeks old when the Council organized the forces sent to fight it. North Korea's attack on the Republic of Korea had already been judged a breach of the peace. Member states had been asked to help repel the attack. Governments had responded with prompt and strong support. Resolution 84 was adopted on 7 July 1950.

The Council welcomed that support and noted the offers of help sent in. It recommended that all members providing forces or other aid place them under a unified command. The United States would lead that command, and Washington was asked to name the commander. The unified command could fly the United Nations flag in the course of operations. It would fly alongside the national flags of the states taking part. The United States also had to report to the Council on the course of the action taken.

The war over Nagorny Karabakh flared again in the autumn of 1993. The region lies inside Azerbaijan and has a mostly Armenian population. Fighting had broken earlier cease-fires. Civilians were fleeing the Zangelan district and the city of Goradiz, which had been occupied. Resolution 884 was adopted on 12 November 1993.

The Council condemned the renewed hostilities. The occupation of the Zangelan district and Goradiz was condemned in particular, and so were attacks on civilians. Armenia's government was called on to use its influence. The Armenians of Nagorny Karabakh had to be made to obey the Council's earlier resolutions, 822, 853, and 874. The cease-fire proposals of the Minsk Group, which led the peace process, were welcomed. The Council restated Azerbaijan's sovereignty and the rule that territory may not be taken by force.

Countries that had given up nuclear weapons wanted safety in return, and the Council answered on 11 April 1995. More than 170 states had joined the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons. The states without such weapons had promised not to build them. Resolution 984, adopted unanimously, gives them security assurances.

The Council welcomed statements by the five nuclear-weapon states. Each had promised not to use nuclear weapons against non-nuclear parties to the treaty, with limited exceptions. The Council recognized a key right. A victim of nuclear attack, or a state threatened with one, could bring the matter straight to the Council. The Council would then act at once. The text set out how states could help such a victim, with aid and with claims for compensation. All states were also urged to pursue talks on nuclear disarmament in good faith.
upanishads-muller-vol2-1884: Volume two of the Upanishads in Müller's Sacred Books of the East series, 1884. More of the forest teachings on Brahman and Atman. This edition preserves those profound scriptures. The archive guards it with care.
zola-joy-of-life-1884:
Chatto and Windus issued The Joy of Life in 1901, edited with Vizetelly's preface. The French title, La Joie de Vivre, promises more cheer than the tale delivers. Chapter one opens as a cuckoo clock strikes six and Chanteau loses all patience.

On the stormy Brittany coast, kind Pauline gives her life to others. She nurses her cousin Lazare through endless failures and fears of death. His gloom wars with her selfless love of living across the years. Tender above all Zola's books, this 1884 novel forms the gentle counterweight to his darker visions, and Vizetelly prized it highly.
zosimus-new-history-1684:
Zosimus, a pagan official at Constantinople, wrote his New History around 510 CE to explain why Rome was falling. The English text here is the anonymous version of 1684, the only one in the public domain. His six books run from Augustus to the sack of Rome in 410.

Zosimus blames the emperors who dropped the old gods, above all Constantine and Theodosius, for the empire's wounds. He gives the fullest narrative of the late empire's fall that survives. His voice is the last great pagan answer to Christian Rome. The old spelling of the 1684 print, with its long s, takes a page to get used to.
